title: BUG: Timespan.timestamp() surprisinly different from datetime.datetime.timestamp() for naive timestamps
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
now = time.time()

pdts = pd.Timestamp.fromtimestamp(now)    # naive TS 
print("PD", pdts)
pyts = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(now)  # naive TS
print("PY", pyts)

print("PD", pdts.timestamp())   # we get back what we put in
print("PY", pyts.timestamp())   # get back modified by local TZ offset! 

print("DIFF", pdts.timestamp()-pyts.timestamp())

# Output:
# PD 2022-12-16 16:44:38.732732
# PY 2022-12-16 16:44:38.732732
# PD 1671209078.732732
# PY 1671205478.732732
# DIFF 3600.0
```


### Issue Description

I found it very surprising that pd.Timestamp.timestamp() behaves differently from datetime.datetime.timestamp() and in a very unfortunate way: basically it means that with naive timestamps: 
```
pd.Timestamp.fromtimestamp(ts).timestamp() != ts
```
in all timezones except UTC, while 
```
datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts) == ts
```
always. 

### Expected Behavior

Since Timestamp is meant to behave similar to datetime, this should also be the case for the `timestamp()` method by default. 

Sadly the documentation does not point out those differences prominently enough, e.g. this page: https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.Timestamp.html
merely states "timestamp  Return POSIX timestamp as float." which is really incorrect as it returns the POSIX timestamp adjusted by the local timezone offset as a float if the timestamp is naive. 

### Installed Versions

Tested with versions 1.5.2 and 2.0.0.dev0+933.g70eef55e43

title: BUG: to_json(date_format="iso") segfaults on a failed allocation — NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback returns NULL without setting errorMsg
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

`int64ToIso` returns `NULL` only when its allocation fails, so the example injects a single
failed `malloc` of the exact size it requests (42 bytes for `date_unit="ms"`) with an
`LD_PRELOAD` shim. Nothing else about the frame is unusual.

```c
// failmalloc.c — gcc -shared -fPIC -o failmalloc.so failmalloc.c -ldl
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <dlfcn.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static size_t target_size = 0;
static int armed = 0, fired = 0;

void failmalloc_arm(size_t size) { target_size = size; armed = 1; fired = 0; }

void *malloc(size_t size) {
  static void *(*real)(size_t) = NULL;
  if (!real)
    real = dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "malloc");
  if (armed && !fired && size == target_size) {
    fired = 1;
    fprintf(stderr, "[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=%zu\n", size);
    return NULL;
  }
  return real(size);
}
```

```python
# repro.py
import ctypes, faulthandler
import pandas as pd

faulthandler.enable()

frame = pd.DataFrame({"t": pd.to_datetime([1616409000123] * 50, unit="ms").as_unit("ms")})

ctypes.CDLL("./failmalloc.so").failmalloc_arm(ctypes.c_size_t(42))

print(frame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso"))
```

```
$ PYTHONMALLOC=malloc LD_PRELOAD=./failmalloc.so python repro.py
[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=42
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x0000004002102f00 [python] (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 292 in write
  File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 241 in to_json
  File ".../pandas/core/generic.py", line 2623 in to_json
  File "repro.py", line 12 in <module>

Current thread's C stack trace (most recent call first):
  ...
  Binary file ".../pandas/_libs/json.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so", at +0x8ae0
```

### Issue Description

A failed allocation inside the ISO datetime conversion is dereferenced as a `NULL` string
instead of raising, because the encoder's `NULL` signal is `enc->errorMsg` and this path never
sets it:

1. `int64ToIso` (`pandas/_libs/src/datetime/date_conversions.c`) allocates the output buffer and
   returns `NULL` after `PyErr_NoMemory()` if that fails. It also returns `NULL` when
   `make_iso_8601_datetime` fails.
2. `NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback` (`pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c`) forwards
   that result unchanged, without setting `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg`.
3. `ultrajsonenc.c`, `case JT_UTF8`, tests only `enc->errorMsg` before using the value:

```c
    value = enc->getStringValue(obj, &tc, &szlen);
    if (enc->errorMsg) {
      enc->endTypeContext(obj, &tc);
      return;
    }
    Buffer_Reserve(enc, RESERVE_STRING(szlen));
    ...
      if (!Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated(enc, value, value + szlen)) {
```

So `Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated` runs on `value == NULL`, which segfaults.

Sibling callbacks in the same file follow the opposite convention and do set `errorMsg` before
returning `NULL` — `PyTimeToJSON` and the type-check branch of `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` both
do `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg = "";`. Two more callbacks look to have the
same gap as the one above:

- `NpyTimeDeltaToIsoCallback` forwards `int64ToIsoDuration`, which has the same two `NULL`
  returns.
- `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` sets `errorMsg` for the type check, but forwards the result of
  `PyDateTimeToIso` (which has several `NULL` returns) unchecked.

This looks like a remaining instance of the class of bug reported in #66356 and fixed by #66357
and #66797 — neither of those passes touched the ISO datetime/timedelta callbacks.

Reproduced on 3.0.5 and on `main` at `3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e`, both Python 3.14 /
linux-x86_64. 3.0.6 contains no changes to these files.

For context on why this isn't only theoretical: we hit a SIGSEGV in `pandas/_libs/json...so`
beneath `DataFrame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso")` in CI, serialising a ~45k-row
frame with a tz-aware `datetime64[ms, UTC]` column under memory pressure from several parallel
test workers. I can't attribute that crash with certainty — the shipped extension module is
stripped, so the C stack has no symbols — but this is the only unchecked-`NULL` path I could
find on it, and the per-value allocation count makes a transient failure plausible.

### Expected Behavior

`MemoryError` (or the relevant exception) propagates to the caller, consistent with how other
allocation failures in the encoder are handled — e.g. `Buffer_Realloc` calls
`SetError(NULL, enc, "Could not reserve memory block")`.

Setting `errorMsg` in the three callbacks before returning `NULL` would be enough; adding a
`value == NULL` check alongside the `enc->errorMsg` check in `JT_UTF8` would make the encoder
robust to any future callback with the same omission.

### Installed Versions

```
python                : 3.14.7

```

</details>

2. **np.nan to None Consistency**: Fixed an inconsistency where scalar replacement (`df.replace(np.nan, None)`) would fail to replace values or upcast to object correctly, whereas list replacement (`df.replace([np.nan], [None])`) succeeded. The scalar replacement path (`Block.replace`) incorrectly filtered out `None` in the fast-path `_can_hold_element` for certain dtypes, preventing the necessary object upcast. We added a check for `value is None` to ensure parity between scalar and list replacements. Robust monkey tests and unit tests were added to assert equivalence.

title: BUG: groupby then resample on column gives incorrect results if the index is out of order
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(dict(
    datetime=[pd.to_datetime('2024-07-30T00:00Z'), pd.to_datetime('2024-07-30T00:01Z')],
    group=['A', 'A'],
    value=[100, 200],
), index=[1, 0])

df.groupby('group').resample('1min', on='datetime').aggregate(dict(value='sum'))
```


### Issue Description

The example above gives the following incorrect output:

```
                                 value
group datetime                        
A     2024-07-30 00:00:00+00:00    200
      2024-07-30 00:01:00+00:00    100
```

### Expected Behavior

The correct output is:
```
                                 value
group datetime                        
A     2024-07-30 00:00:00+00:00    100
      2024-07-30 00:01:00+00:00    200
```

The correct output can be got using either of the following - either reset the index, or use the datetime column as the index.
```python
df.reset_index().groupby('group').resample('1min', on='datetime').aggregate(dict(value='sum'))
df.set_index('datetime').groupby('group').resample('1min').aggregate(dict(value='sum'))
```

It seems the out-of-order index (`[1, 0]` instead of `[0, 1]`) is affecting the resampling, even though the index should be ignored when using the `on` keyword argument to `resample`. This may be related to #35275 where it seems the index also affects the operation of resampling on a column (in that case giving an IndexError if the index value is not less than the length of the data frame.)

AI Usage Details: I used Gemini 3.1 Pro strictly to assist with the analysis part of the C/Cython codebase. I personally wrote, reviewed, and understand every line of the final code and tests. We also ran 100,000 fuzzing scenarios and the full test suite to guarantee correctness.

### Background
Fixes #20442. Pure Python specifies that `None == None` evaluates to `True`. However, in pandas, comparing a Series of objects with scalar `None` previously short-circuited into NumPy's NA logic (treating `None` like `np.nan`), returning `False` universally for `None == None`.

### Fix
Modified `pandas/core/ops/array_ops.py` to intercept scalar `None` operations when comparing against object arrays, dispatching to `comp_method_OBJECT_ARRAY`.
Updated Cython logic in `pandas/_libs/ops.pyx` (`scalar_compare` and `vec_compare`) to explicitly match `None` with `None`, returning `True` for `Py_EQ` and `False` for `Py_NE` before evaluating `checknull`.

### Verification
Included new unit tests covering 50+ combinations of `None` equality, including massive scale benchmarking which showed zero performance regressions. Tested against other missing datatypes (`pd.NA`, `np.nan`, `NaT`) to ensure their logic remained untouched.

Fixes #69443

## What was happening

Assigning a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow-backed column of a 1-row frame blew up with `TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]'`:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df.loc[:, "A"] = df["A"].astype(float).round(6)  # TypeError
```

The trail: `SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace` unwraps a length-1 1-d array down to 0-d before handing it to the EA, and `ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa_scalar` then passed that 0-d array straight into `pa.scalar`, which cannot consume an ndarray. PyArrow raised `ArrowInvalid`, which surfaced as the `TypeError` above.

## The fix

In `_box_pa_scalar`, a 0-d ndarray is now unboxed to its NumPy scalar with `value[()]` before reaching `pa.scalar`. I used `[()]` rather than `.item()` deliberately: it preserves the dtype, so a `datetime64` stays a `datetime64` scalar instead of collapsing to an int. The same 0-d value also tripped `ArrowStringArray._validate_setitem_value` on its `len(value)` check, so it gets the same unboxing there and flows into the existing scalar branch. Genuinely invalid values still raise `TypeError` exactly as before.

## Tests

- New regression test `test_setitem_0d_ndarray` in `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py`, covering the exact issue repro, the multi-row broadcast case (a length-1 array assigned into a 2-row frame), and the `string[pyarrow]` path.
- `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py -k setitem`: 3282 passed, 42 xfailed.
- `pandas/tests/extension/test_string.py -k setitem`: all passing.
- The repro script additionally verified `int64[pyarrow]` and `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]` columns, plus that invalid values (e.g. strings into a float column) still raise `TypeError`.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on all changed files; whatsnew entry added under ExtensionArray in `v3.1.0.rst`.

## AI use

Developed through Sanjay's Muse agent (model: Muse Spark). It reproduced the issue, traced the root cause through the setitem path, drafted the fix, the regression test, and the whatsnew entry, and ran the test suites above. The diff is the complete change set: two small unboxing guards, one regression test, one whatsnew line.

body:
Closes https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/66333

Follow-up to the scalar-broadcast clarification in #66334. The docstring says fields may be "scalar or array-like", but `range`, `Index`, and nullable pandas arrays are not accepted; only `list`, `tuple`, `np.ndarray`, and `Series` are treated as array-like by `_make_field_arrays`.

body:
### Feature Type

- [X] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wanted to make a function to create and format a table with experiment results. However I am facing some problems due to the way Pandas actually works:

- It is impossible to actually return an styled `DataFrame` as far as I know, one must return a `Styler` object instead. Thus, users must know about the `Styler` class, and it also has a bad text representation in terminal.
- The most flexible approach to styling is to set CSS classes (for example, a class for a significant result) and then add styling to the classes. This is again problematic for several reasons:
    - There is no analog of `set_td_classes` for index and column titles, that is, a `set_th_classes` or something like that.
    - Although the classes with a posterior call to `set_table_styles` work well for HTML output, when a user has to format the table for a publication (with `to_latex`), the style for the classes is not applied. Instead the CSS selector and properties are prepended to the Latex output. This occurs even when using `convert_css` and we restrict ourselves to the supported CSS conversions.
- I wanted to append an asterisk to cells of some class, but I was unable to do it. I tried both of the ways [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/68914546/2455333) but they did not work (or I did it wrong somehow).

### Feature Description

- (Optional): Allow to set the styler object for a particular `DataFrame`.
- Improve `Styler` text representation.
- Allow to set per-CSS-class styles that work for `Latex` output (ideally, also allow for styles that work for both HTML and Latex).
- Allow to append/prepend text (or maybe something more general) to both HTML and Latex outputs based on the CSS class.

### Alternative Solutions

The only "solution" I was able to implement was to include the desired output as a parameter and doing things differently for each, without using CSS classes in the Latex case, and even manually changing the text of cells (which is not ideal).

title: ENH:  df.to_sql lacks a parameter if_not_exist with options [create, fail]

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
#### feature request and related problem 
If a table does not exist pd.to_sql is unconditionnally creating it. There are situations, where this is not acceptable.

There are application strategies where this has to be avoided. Eg. in case failed name matching the ISERT might have to fail and signal, that programcode has to be adapted. Such condition arise because of possible changes in the DB model - the outside of python's data environment.

requested option feature for pd.to_sql:
If the table  expected by python is not there, it should not be created but the attempted INSERT should fail.

Presently a  a certain amount of boilerplate is needed to do such fail-safe handling. 

```python
tableName = '...'
schemaName = '...'
dbEngine = ....
# dataframe df is holding the data for target table named in [tableName]
# currently quote some boilerplate is needed to fail safe, if database table does not exist to avoid creating one
if tableExists(tableName):
    df.to_sql(tableName,  schema=schemaName, con=dbEngine,  index=True, if_exists='append')**
    print(f"INSERT-I-done ")
else
    print(f"INSERT-I-failed: table with expected name [{schemaName}].[{tableName}] does not yet or nomore exist")

```
This missing feature leads to another level of encapsulation in a wrapper class. It would be better to integrate this as a option directly to PANDAS. 

#### Describe the proposed solution
Integrate this checking of the outside DB environment into Dataframe.to_sql

Suggested new parameter: 

if_not_exists{‘fail’, ‘create’}, default 'fail'


#### API breaking implications

Dataframe.to_sql fails if the table specified by name does not exist in the schema. This should be the default, thus avoiding that dead phantom tables are created, resulting in dead ends off the track of the DB model,  once the nomenklatura of the DB model has moved on. Coevolutive and agile development of applications python code and the datamodel and its naming thus should be supported, by failsafe handling of naming assumptions.

present processing still is possible with parameter if_no_exist='create'

Possible the default 'create' might be preferred, as thus it does not break existing code, even though in a greenfield approach I consider 'fail' to be the better choice.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered

Handling outside of Pandas is possible, as shown above. Anyway this results in widespread boilder-plate code and violates the idea of code centralisation and functional encapsulation.

#### Additional context

title: BUG: `factorize(use_na_sentinel=True)` ignores `use_na_sentinel` for pre-encoded PyArrow `DictionaryArray`s

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

for null_encoding in ["mask", "encode"]:
    arr = pa.array([*"abc", None]).dictionary_encode(null_encoding=null_encoding)
    s = pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type))
    print(
        f' {null_encoding = } '.center(80, '='),
        s.factorize(use_na_sentinel=True),
        sep="\n",
        end="\n\n",
    )



============================ null_encoding = 'mask' ============================
(array([ 0,  1,  2, -1]), Index(['a', 'b', 'c'],
      dtype='dictionary<values=string, indices=int32, ordered=0>[pyarrow]'))

=========================== null_encoding = 'encode' ===========================
(array([0, 1, 2, 3]), Index(['a', 'b', 'c', <NA>],
      dtype='dictionary<values=string, indices=int32, ordered=0>[pyarrow]'))
```

### Issue Description

`pandas.factorize` produces inconsistent results for PyArrow dictionary-encoded
arrays depending on how the input `DictionaryArray` was is structured.

Specifically, when the array is created with:

- `.dictionary_encode(null_encoding="mask")`
- `.dictionary_encode(null_encoding="encode")`

calling `factorize(use_na_sentinel=True)` produces different outputs, even though both arrays represent the same logical data.

The unexpected case arises from production a `pyarrow.DictionaryArray` via `dictionary_encode(null_encoding="encode") then factorizing with `pandas.factorize(..., use_na_sentinel=True)`

In this case, factorize behaves as though `use_na_sentinel=False`: the missing
value is assigned a regular code (`3`) and `<NA>` is included in the returned
uniques.

The bug seems to arise from within the [`factorize` implementation for arrow backed arrays in pandas](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py#L1869-L1874). Where already dictionary-encoded arrays are only re-encoded when `use_na_sentinel=False`. However, when `use_na_sentinel=True` (null_encoding="mask"), the existing `DictionaryArray` is returned unchanged, preserving whatever null encoding it originally had. As a result, a `DictionaryArray` created with null_encoding="encode" bypasses the requested `use_na_sentinel=True` behavior and continues to treat null as a regular dictionary value.

### Expected Behavior

I would expect the MRE code to produce the following output, where the code `-1` is used to refer to the location of Null values in the input provided that `use_na_sentinel=True` was used in the `pandas.factorize` call:

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Documentation correction

The previous report incorrectly treated an all-scalar call to `PeriodIndex.from_fields` as supported. At least one field must be array-like; scalar fields are broadcast to the array-like field's length. Pull request #66334 clarifies this in the docstring.

### Open question

The documentation describes fields as array-like, but `range`, `Index`, and nullable pandas arrays are rejected. Should those inputs be supported? Pull request #66334 leaves their behavior unchanged pending guidance.

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.PeriodIndex.from_fields(year=range(2020, 2022), month=range(1, 3), freq="M")
```

title: BUG: read_csv fails to finalize index when engine='pyarrow' and dtype is scalar (or dict without an index specified)
body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python from io import StringIO test=""" col1,col2 10,1 20,2 """ f=StringIO(test) import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa # For AttributeError df = pd.read_csv( f, dtype='int64[pyarrow]', dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow', # Removing either engine or index_col avoids the error index_col='col1', ) # For IndexError df = pd.read_csv( f, dtype={'col2': 'int64[pyarrow]'}, dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow', # Removing either engine or index_col avoids the error index_col='col1', ) print(df.info()) # Simplified example here; see below for more complete testing results ``` ### Issue Description Using `read_csv` raises an `AttributeError` if... - `index_col` is specified, and - `engine='pyarrow'` is specified, and - `dtype` is specified as a scalar or a `dict` that doesn't include the index column ### Scenario A: Scalar dtype raises AttributeError The AttributeError occurs in `ArrowParserWrapper._finalize_index` ([3.0.5](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032/pandas/io/parsers/arrow_parser_wrapper.py#L202) | [main](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/795cd84559d9147679bfe8461853569727a5ee69/pandas/io/parsers/arrow_parser_wrapper.py#L390)) when it tries to call `self.dtype.get(item)` on a scalar dtype (e.g., 'int64[pyarrow]' or pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64())) instead of a dictionary.
Simplified traceback of AttributeError ``` File "deleteme.py", line 10, in df = pd.read_csv( f, ...<3 lines>... index_col='col1', # Works fine if removed ) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 873, in read_csv return _read(filepath_or_buffer, kwds) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 306, in _read return parser.read(nrows) ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 1935, in read df = self._engine.read() # type: ignore[attr-defined] File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 328, in read return self._finalize_pandas_output(frame, multi_index_named) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 253, in _finalize_pandas_output frame = self._finalize_index(frame, multi_index_named) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 202, in _finalize_index if self.dtype.get(item) is not None ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get' ```
### Scenario B: Dictionary dtype missing the index column raises IndexError If a dictionary is passed to `dtype` but the index column is omitted from the keys, it looks like the wrapper engine incorrectly handles the remaining columns during `_finalize_dtype`, leading to an `IndexError` down the line.
Simplified traceback of IndexError ``` File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 873, in read_csv return _read(filepath_or_buffer, kwds) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 306, in _read return parser.read(nrows) ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 1935, in read df = self._engine.read() # type: ignore[attr-defined] File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 328, in read return self._finalize_pandas_output(frame, multi_index_named) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 253, in _finalize_pandas_output frame = self._finalize_index(frame, multi_index_named) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 203, in _finalize_index else (frame.columns[item], self.dtype.get(frame.columns[item])) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\core\indexes\base.py", line 5425, in __getitem__ result = getitem(key) File "....\site-packages\pandas\core\arrays\arrow\array.py", line 780, in __getitem__ raise IndexError( ...<2 lines>... ) IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices ```
## Reproducible testing code I tested several different combinations of `dtype`, `engine`, and `index_col` in a local environment and in Google Colab. The results are summarized below.
```python import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa f = 'deleteme.csv' pd.DataFrame({'col1':[10, 20], 'col2':[1, 2]}).to_csv(f, index=False) pd_arrow_int64 = pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64()) # Any of the following dtype specifications have the same test results py_int64 = pd_arrow_int64 py_int64 = 'int64[pyarrow]' py_int64 = {'col1': pd_arrow_int64, 'col2': pd_arrow_int64} def works_as_expected_no_index(py_int64): """Can specify what you want if index_col is omitted""" # Specify dtype df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64) df2 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, engine='pyarrow') df3 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') # No dtype; infer with dtype_backend, with or without engine df4 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype_backend='pyarrow') df5 = pd.read_csv(f, engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.equals(df2) and df2.equals(df3) assert df1.dtypes.eq(pd_arrow_int64).all() assert df1.equals(df4) and df4.equals(df5) def works_as_expected_with_index_no_engine(py_int64): """Can specify dtype or engine, but not both, unless dtype is a dict""" # Omit engine; specify dtype df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, index_col='col1') df2 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, index_col='col1', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.equals(df2) assert df1.dtypes.eq(pd_arrow_int64).all() assert df1.index.dtype == pd_arrow_int64 # Omit dtype; specify engine df3 = pd.read_csv(f, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.equals(df3) def raises_error_with_index_and_both_dtype_and_engine(py_int64): try: df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') except AttributeError as e: print(f"AttributeError: {e}") #################################### # AttributeError related #################################### works_as_expected_no_index(py_int64) works_as_expected_with_index_no_engine(py_int64) # Raises ➡️ 'ArrowDtype' object has no attribute 'get' raises_error_with_index_and_both_dtype_and_engine(pd_arrow_int64) # Raises ➡️ 'str' object has no attribute 'get' raises_error_with_index_and_both_dtype_and_engine('int64[pyarrow]') #################################### # IndexError related #################################### # Mostly works as expected if dtype is a dict, but it triggers if index dtype not specfied def works_with_engine_if_dtype_specified_for_index(py_int64): """Works if specifying the dtype for the index using a dict. Other column detype is optional""" dd = {'col1':pd_arrow_int64, 'col2':pd_arrow_int64} df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=dd, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') dd = {'col1':pd_arrow_int64} df2 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=dd, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.dtypes.eq(pd_arrow_int64).all() assert df1.index.dtype == pd_arrow_int64 assert df1.equals(df2) try: dd = {'col2': pd_arrow_int64} df3 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=dd, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') except IndexError as e: print(f"IndexError: {e}") # Raises ➡️ only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices works_with_engine_if_dtype_specified_for_index(pd_arrow_int64) ```

```python
df.sort_index(axis=1, level="B", key=lambda x: np.argsort(index_natsorted(x)))
# KeyError: 'Level B not found'
```

`level=1` works, as does a key that returns a named `Index`. `_ensure_key_mapped_multiindex` applies the key to each level and rebuilds the `MultiIndex` with `from_arrays(mapped)`, which takes the names from the mapped arrays. A key that returns an ndarray gives an unnamed level, so `sortlevel("B")` can't find it.

As @rhshadrach suggested in the issue, the name is now set internally rather than requiring the key to return a named `Index`: the rebuilt `MultiIndex` gets `names=index.names`. `ensure_key_mapped` already wraps the key's result in an `Index`, so no other change is needed. This only affects `MultiIndex`, since `level` is a no-op on a flat index.

The test sorts by level name with a key returning an ndarray, on both axes, and fails on main. The sort tests in `tests/frame/methods`, `tests/series/methods`, `tests/indexes/multi/test_sorting.py`, `tests/test_sorting.py` and `tests/indexes/test_base.py` pass (2078 passed).

### Problem
With `MultiIndex` columns, `to_excel` wrote a NaN column label as the last value of that level (in the report, the NaN bin from `pd.cut` became `(0.0, inf]`).

### Cause
`_format_header_mi` calls `levels.take(level_codes)` without `allow_fill=True`, so the `-1` code of a NaN label wraps around to the last element. The row-index path already passes `allow_fill=True`.

### Fix
Pass `allow_fill=True`; the NaN is then written as `na_rep` (an empty cell), same as NaN row-index labels.

### Test
`test_to_excel_multiindex_nan_column_label` runs for all engines and `merge_cells` values and reads the header rows back with `header=None`, because `read_excel` with `header=[0, 1]` forward-fills empty header cells (which is why the test in #62576 passed on `main`). Fails on `main`, passes with this change.

title: BUG: retain DatetimeIndex freq in concat regardless of input order (GH#64253)

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
- [x] closes #64253
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit).
- [x] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

### Problem

`union_indexes` combines `DatetimeIndex` inputs pairwise. When an intermediate union is not contiguous (e.g. `s1 ∪ s3` before `s2` is added), `DatetimeIndex._union` falls back to the generic set path and `_with_freq("infer")`. Inference cannot recover an offset such as `CustomBusinessDay(holidays=...)` from the values, so `freq` becomes `None` and stays `None`, making the result depend on the order of the inputs. The same path is hit by `pd.DataFrame({dict of Series})`.

The bug still reproduces on current `main`; the earlier "not replicable" comment on the issue mistook the `Pandas4Warning` about the default `sort` for the assertion failing.

### Fix

Following the review on the previous attempt (#66295): do not try to preserve `freq` at every pairwise step; validate once at the end. A private helper `_maybe_restore_freq` is called at the two points where the combined index is final (`union_indexes` "special" branch, and after `safe_sort_index` in `_get_combined_index`). It is a no-op unless the result is a monotonic `DatetimeIndex` with `freq is None` and *all* inputs are `DatetimeIndex` sharing the same non-None `freq`; in that case it runs `_validate_frequency` against the final values and re-attaches the `freq` only if they conform. Nothing is inferred, and non-conforming results (e.g. the tz-aware `America/Santiago` DST case from the issue, which has a real gap) keep `freq=None`.

### Test

`test_concat_datetimeindex_freq_order_independent` is parametrized over `sort=True/False/None` (the `None` case also asserts the existing `Pandas4Warning`). Without the fix the `True` and `None` cases fail; with it all three pass. `pandas/tests/indexes`, `frame`, `series`, `reshape`, `resample`, `tseries`, `window`, `groupby` pass locally.

title: BUG: Fix .to_latex() ValueError when table exceeds max_elements

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

body:
Fixes #68310

When a DataFrame exceeds the `max_elements` budget (default 262144), the Styler renderer trims rows and adds a "..." trim row. However, `_translate_latex` used `concatenated_visible_rows()` to get row indices for ctx lookups, which returned all visible rows (untrimmed). This caused a length mismatch with the trimmed `d["body"]` and raised `ValueError: zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1`.

**Changes:**
- Modified `_translate_body` to return `body_row_indices` (original row indices for regular rows, -1 for trim row)
- Stored `body_row_indices` in the render dict `d`
- In `_translate_latex`, use `d["body_row_indices"]` instead of `concatenated_visible_rows()`
- For trim row (r == -1), skip ctx lookups since no ctx entry exists
- Properly handle concatenated stylers by applying the same ctx offset to their body_row_indices

**Testing:**
- All 880 style tests pass
- All 156 to_latex tests pass
- All 96 format to_latex tests pass
- Verified fix works for:
  - Large frames exceeding max_elements (45211 x 6, 45211 x 17)
  - max_rows/max_columns options
  - Concatenated stylers with hidden rows and styling
  - MultiIndex, hidden rows, etc.

title: BUG: factorize ignored use_na_sentinel on dictionary-encoded arrow arrays (#66490)

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

body:
- [x] closes #66490
- [x] tests added / passed
- [ ] passes `pre-commit run --all-files`
- [ ] whatsnew entry

Closes #66490.

`factorize` with default `use_na_sentinel=True` on an `ArrowDtype`-backed `pandas` object whose underlying `pyarrow.dictionary` array stored nulls as a dictionary value (`null_encoding="encode"`) returned the null inside `uniques` instead of using the `-1` sentinel. This made `use_na_sentinel` a no-op whenever the pre-encoded dictionary contained a null entry, e.g.

```python
>>> import pandas as pd, pyarrow as pa
>>> arr = pa.array(["a", "b", "c", None]).dictionary_encode(null_encoding="encode")
>>> pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type)).factorize()
(array([0, 1, 2, 3]), Index(['a', 'b', 'c', <NA>], dtype='...'))
```

With this fix, `factorize` casts such dictionary arrays back to their value type and re-encodes with the requested null encoding so the result matches what a non-dictionary-encoded array of the same values would produce:

```python
>>> pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type)).factorize()
(array([0, 1, 2, -1]), Index(['a', 'b', 'c'], dtype='...'))
```

title: BUG: clip with missing datetime/timedelta threshold raises TypeError
body:
Closes #44785

`Series.clip` / `DataFrame.clip` with a datetime or timedelta threshold
that contains missing values raises:

```
TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'
```

because GH#40420 fills the missing thresholds with `±np.inf` before
comparing, and `±np.inf` cannot be compared against Timestamp or
timedelta values.

This change treats the missing positions explicitly: for datetime-like
thresholds the missing positions are tracked with a mask and the
original values are kept there (matching the documented behavior that
"a missing threshold will not clip the value"), while numeric
thresholds keep the existing `±np.inf` fill path untouched.

- Series threshold (lower/upper bound)
- DataFrame with a Series threshold along `axis=0` (rows) or `axis=1`
  (columns)
- DataFrame with a datetime-like DataFrame threshold

Regression tests added in `test_clip.py` for both Series and
DataFrame, plus a whatsnew entry.

<details>
<summary>Copy-pasteable example from the issue</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([1.0, 1.0], dtype="datetime64[ns]").clip(
    pd.Series([None, 1.0], dtype="datetime64[ns]")
)
```

- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)

## Summary

Implements `RangeIndex.isin` directly (GH#66263). When the query `values` are smaller than the index, the new fast path allocates only the boolean result array and checks membership with O(1) `range.__contains__`, computing the target location via `(val - start) // step`. This avoids materializing the full integer array (`self._values`, e.g. an 80MB array for a 10M-entry range) that the generic `algos.isin` path allocates.

- For `len(values) < len(self)`, use the O(1) `range.__contains__` fast path.
- For `len(values) >= len(self)`, delegate to `super().isin` as before.
- Non-sized iterables (e.g. generators) are delegated to the base implementation, preserving `Index.isin` behavior.

## Tests

Added coverage in `pandas/tests/indexes/ranges/test_range.py`:
- Correctness of the fast path across positive/negative steps, negative starts, missing values, and empty queries.
- Agreement with the materialized `Index.isin` for mixed-value queries.
- The fast path does not touch `_values` (via a monkeypatched property that raises).
- Set / non-numeric / generator inputs and the `level` kwarg.
- Fallback to the generic implementation for large queries and TypeError for non-list-like values.

title: API: getting the "densified" values of a Categorical (preserving categories dtype) ?
body:
Assume we have a Categorical, and want to convert to a dense array (not encoded). We have `np.asarray(..)` and the `to_dense()` method (which uses asarray under the hood):

```
In [1]: cat = pd.Categorical(['a', 'b', 'a'])

In [2]: np.asarray(cat) 
Out[2]: array(['a', 'b', 'a'], dtype=object)

In [3]: cat.to_dense() 
Out[3]: array(['a', 'b', 'a'], dtype=object)
```

In addition, we also have `get_values`:
```
In [4]: cat.get_values() 
Out[4]: array(['a', 'b', 'a'], dtype=object)
```

`get_values` is mostly the same, with the exception that returns an Index for datetime/period/timedelta, and an object array for integers if there are missing values instead of float array:

```
In [10]: cat = pd.Categorical(pd.date_range("2012", periods=3))

In [11]: cat.to_dense()
Out[11]: 
array(['2012-01-01T00:00:00.000000000', '2012-01-02T00:00:00.000000000',
       '2012-01-03T00:00:00.000000000'], dtype='datetime64[ns]')

In [12]: cat.get_values()
Out[12]: DatetimeIndex(['2012-01-01', '2012-01-02', '2012-01-03'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='D')
```

With the result that it preserves somewhat more the dtype (although only specifically for datetime-like, it will not do it for any EA)

While looking into the deprecation of `get_values` (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/26409), I was wondering: do we want some method to actually get a "dense" version of the array, but with the exact same dtype? (so returning an EA in case the categories have an extension dtype)

And should we deprecate `to_dense()` ?

title: PERF: out-of-band pickling of a sliced DataFrame (GH#55781)

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
closes #55781

numpy serializes an ndarray out of band (PEP 574) only when it is C- or F-contiguous, so a sliced `DataFrame` — whose block values are a strided view of the parent — had its data copied into the pickle stream rather than shared with the consumer. `Block.__reduce_ex__` now makes such a block contiguous when the protocol can actually use a buffer.

The gate is `protocol >= 5` on a non-contiguous, non-object ndarray. Below protocol 5 the copy is waste: numpy copies again via `tobytes` and peak memory doubles. Object dtype numpy refuses out of band whatever the layout, as it does `datetime64`/`timedelta64` — which is why extending this to the EA-backed blocks would buy nothing. At protocol 5 peak memory is unchanged, since main already paid a `tobytes` copy on the same block, while an out-of-band consumer goes from 0 buffers to 1.

Two things worth flagging for review. The issue's own reproducer no longer shows the bug — block layout has changed since it was filed, so a column slice is already contiguous; the surviving case is the row slice, which is also the one that matters to the frameworks in the report, since they partition by rows. And the win is confined to out-of-band consumers: `pickle.dumps` defaults to protocol 4, and `to_pickle` passes no `buffer_callback`, so neither changes.

Only block values are covered. A step-sliced frame's `Index` and a `Series`' values reach the pickler by other routes and still go in band.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the change and its tests, ran a main-vs-branch differential over dtypes, slicings and protocols, and reviewed the branch across five rounds before this PR.

title: BUG: read_csv silently wrapped out-of-range integers (GH#55232)

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
closes #55232

Since 2.0, `read_csv` silently wrapped a value the requested integer `dtype` could not hold — `read_csv(StringIO("x\n-1\n257"), dtype={"x": "UInt8"})` returned `[255, 1]` — where the `Series` and `array` constructors raise.

Three cast sites reached the wraparound:

- `_coerce_to_data_and_mask`'s `isinstance` fastpath raw-astyped instead of calling `_safe_cast`. This is the nullable half, and the actual 2.0 regression; both engines route nullable dtypes through it. Masked slots are filled before the check, since the data behind the mask is meaningless.
- the c engine's int branch in `TextReader._convert_with_dtype`. The check is gated on `user_dtype` rather than skipped for `int64`, so a column that only fits `uint64` now raises for `dtype={"x": "int64"}` instead of coming back as `uint64` with the requested dtype ignored. Inference is unaffected — it passes `user_dtype=0` and keeps the `uint64` fallback result.
- `PythonParser._cast_types`, in both branches an integer cast can reach: the plain ndarray one, and the `ExtensionArray` one that `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` lands in, because `_infer_types` applies the backend before the cast runs.

Nullable dtypes raise `TypeError`, restoring the pre-2.0 message; numpy dtypes raise `ValueError`, reusing the message the parser already produces from the fallback safe-cast block in `_convert_tokens`.

With the fastpath fixed, `BaseMaskedArray._coerce_same_family` (added in GH-66332) is redundant — both call sites fall through to the identical `_coerce_to_array(..., dtype=self.dtype)` — so it is removed. That also drops its one remaining difference, which was a bug: it checked `value._data` at masked positions, so assigning an NA whose stale payload did not fit the target dtype raised.

Deliberately unchanged: `engine="pyarrow"`, which casts the parsed frame in `_finalize_dtype` (the new parser test is `@xfail_pyarrow`); `astype`, which keeps numpy semantics and belongs to GH-45588 — note `Series`/`DataFrame` construction from an existing masked array delegates to `astype`, so only `pd.array` changes there; and float-to-integer *truncation* on the python engine, which `test_read_fwf.py::test_dtype` asserts — floats are compared truncated so only wraparound raises.

Routing the nullable path through `_safe_cast` put `IntegerDtype._safe_cast` on a hot path — it answered "is this cast safe?" by raising and catching a `TypeError`, a fixed ~5µs per call that `read_csv` pays per column per chunk. It now asks `np.can_cast(..., casting="safe")` first, which is behaviour-identical on everything that reaches it and measures 5.30µs → 1.61µs at N=10, unchanged at N=1e6 where the compare dominates.

One divergence this leaves in place, for review: on an *index* column the two engines now report an out-of-range numpy dtype differently — the c engine hits the new check (`ValueError`), while the python engine still raises `OverflowError` from `_agg_index`, which the diff does not touch. The nullable case agrees (`TypeError` on both).

This does not depend on GH-45588, which was raised on the issue as a possible prerequisite.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which reproduced the issue, wrote the fix and tests, and ran the review loop that produced them.

body:
Setting a tz-aware `Timestamp` into a tz-naive `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]` column stored the value's UTC epoch under a naive target, so it came back shifted by the UTC offset; the reverse direction did the same. Every `datetime64`/`DatetimeTZDtype` equivalent raises `TypeError`.

```python
arr = pd.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="timestamp[ns][pyarrow]")   # tz-naive
arr[0] = pd.Timestamp("2016-01-01 00:00", tz="US/Eastern")
arr[0]   # Timestamp('2016-01-01 05:00:00')   <- the UTC epoch stored as naive
```

`_box_pa_scalar` now raises `TypeError` when the value and the target disagree about being timezone-aware. The guard keys on `datetime`, so the `Timestamp` and plain `datetime.datetime` spellings behave alike, and there is a second guard at the trailing cast, which is where an already-boxed `pa.Scalar` reaches the boundary. Only setitem, `fillna`, `where`/`mask`, `replace` and `reindex`'s fill pass a target `pa_type`, so comparison, arithmetic and `isin` are untouched.

`ArrowDtype._get_common_dtype` stops routing a tz-aware timestamp through `numpy_dtype`, which drops the tz. This is load-bearing rather than a separate fix: without it, `Index.where`/`putmask` answer the new `TypeError` by widening through the common dtype, which collapses the index to tz-naive and silently relabels entries the caller never selected. It independently fixes `concat` and `combine_first`, which were shifting tz-aware values with no setitem involved, and the same path is what `Index.union`/`append`/`join` use — two tz-aware arrow indexes differing only in unit came back relabelled tz-naive and shifted. It also lets an unresolvable pyarrow tz label yield no common dtype rather than raising.

Deliberately out of scope: the array-valued spelling in `_box_pa_array` still crosses the boundary, since the check belongs in `_validate_setitem_value` and that reroute is GH-68419; `merge`'s key casting, `insert`/`shift(fill_value=)` via `_from_sequence`, and the lossy-unit rounding are likewise separate.

title: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations

labels.name: IO Data
labels.description: IO issues that don't fit into a more specific label

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination.

Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed.

It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution.

For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows.

This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as API requests, machine learning inference, LLM calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations.

The goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. Instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards.

### Feature Description

result = df[“column”].apply(
expensive_function,
checkpoint=“apply_checkpoint.pkl”,
checkpoint_every=10,
)

### Alternative Solutions

for i, value in df["column"].items():
    df.at[i, "result"] = expensive_function(value)

    if i % 10 == 0:
        df.to_pickle("checkpoint.pkl")

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: ENH: Add convenience API to summarize null counts grouped by dtype (e.g. df.dtype_nulls.summary())

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

labels.name: Describe/info/etc
labels.description: obj.describe, obj.info, requests for methods that look similar

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Add a small convenience API to provide a quick, per-dtype view of missing values in a DataFrame. The utility should list columns grouped by dtype with null counts and optional null percentages, and return both a one-row-per-dtype summary and a per-dtype detail table (columns + null counts).

This is a diagnostic convenience (similar in spirit to df.info(show_counts=True) but grouped by dtype and returning programmatic output).

### Feature Description

Add a DataFrame accessor that provides a compact, programmatic summary of missing values grouped by column dtype.

@pd.api.extensions.register_dataframe_accessor("dtype_nulls")
class DtypeNullsAccessor:
    def __init__(self, df):
        self._df = df

    def summary(self, include_pct: bool = True, sort_desc: bool = True):
        """
        Return (summary_df, detail_dict)

        Parameters
        ----------
        include_pct : bool, default True
            Include null_pct columns (percentage of nulls relative to len(df)).
        sort_desc : bool, default True
            Sort per-dtype detail tables by null_count descending when True.

        Returns
        -------
        summary_df : pd.DataFrame
            One row per dtype with columns:
              - dtype : str (dtype string, e.g., 'float64', 'object')
              - n_columns : int
              - cols_with_nulls : int
              - total_nulls : int
              - avg_null_pct : float (if include_pct)
        detail_dict : dict[str, pd.DataFrame]
            Mapping dtype string -> DataFrame listing columns of that dtype with
            columns ['column','null_count','null_pct'?] (null_pct present if include_pct).
        """

Implementation sketch / pseudocode:

nrows = len(df)
per_col = DataFrame({
    "column": df.columns,
    "dtype": df.dtypes.astype(str),
    "null_count": df.isna().sum().values
})
if include_pct:
    per_col["null_pct"] = per_col["null_count"] / (nrows if nrows else 1) * 100

detail = { dtype: g.sort_values("null_count", ascending=not sort_desc).reset_index(drop=True)
           for dtype, g in per_col.groupby("dtype") }

agg = per_col.groupby("dtype").agg(
    n_columns=("column","count"),
    cols_with_nulls=("null_count", lambda s: (s>0).sum()),
    total_nulls=("null_count","sum")
).reset_index()

if include_pct:
    agg["avg_null_pct"] = per_col.groupby("dtype")["null_pct"].mean().values

return agg, detail


Expected behaviour / examples:

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "a": [1, None, 3],
    "b": [None, None, 2.0],
    "c": ["x","y", None],
    "d": [True, False, True]
})
summary, detail = df.dtype_nulls.summary()
### summary: rows for 'float64', 'object', 'bool' with counts and percentages
### detail['float64'] lists columns 'b' and 'a' with null_count and null_pct


### Alternative Solutions

One-liner / ad-hoc: Users can already compute this with a short snippet:

(pd.DataFrame({'dtype': df.dtypes.astype(str), 'nulls': df.isna().sum()})
   .reset_index()
   .groupby('dtype')[['index','nulls']])


### Additional Context

Related design rationale:

This feature is a convenience diagnostic that complements df.info() and profiling packages; it returns programmatic data structures (DataFrames and dict) so downstream tooling and tests can consume results.

title: API/BUG: support for operations with custom objects / object dtype
body:
Consider the following dummy example of a custom Python object that supports some arithmetic operations:

```python
class MyObject:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
    def __add__(self, other):
        if hasattr(other, "dtype"):
            return NotImplemented
        return MyObject(self.val + other)
    def __radd__(self, other):
        if hasattr(other, "dtype"):
            return NotImplemented
        return MyObject(other + self.val)
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"<MyObject({self.val})>"
```

Working with such objects in pandas containers generally works, i.e. we defer to the scalar operation and assemble the results:

```python
# operation of scalar/arr/series with numeric other
arr = np.array([MyObject(1), MyObject(2)])
ser = pd.Series([1, 2])

print(ser + arr[0])
print(ser + arr)
print(ser + pd.Series(arr))
print(arr[0] + ser)
print(arr + ser)
print(pd.Series(arr) + ser)
```

When the other operand were strings, this worked in pandas 2.x as well:

```python
# operation of scalar/arr/series with string (object) other
arr = np.array([MyObject("a"), MyObject("b")])
ser = pd.Series(["1", "2"])

print(ser + arr[0])
print(ser + arr)
print(ser + pd.Series(arr))
print(arr[0] + ser)
print(arr + ser)
print(pd.Series(arr) + ser)
```

However, this case no longer works in pandas 3.0 with the default `str` dtype.

We specifically fixed this for `pathlib.Path` objects for the scalar case (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/61940 / https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62229), but then got a report for such objects in a Series (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63832). But in the end, while we can "fix" this again specifically for Path objects, this is a more general issue with any generic Python object. 

I think in general pandas has always been quite flexible in supporting custom objects, and IMO we should continue to do that (yes, you can define ExtensionDtypes for full control over handling of custom objects, but that is often overkill). Once we detect something we cannot infer to a non-object dtype, we can use a slower element-wise code path. And IMO we should keep doing that also for newer dtypes (such as now `str` dtype).

```python
import numpy as np
```

title: BUG: Inconsistent NaN detection based on Series dtype, to_numeric dtype_backend, None vs np.nan, strings in orig list

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
# Create 'float' Series with numeric and np.nan (or None)
ser = pd.Series([1, np.nan], dtype=np.float64)
# Passing either dtype_backend results in failure to find nulls
for backend in ['numpy_nullable', 'pyarrow']:
    s = pd.to_numeric(ser, dtype_backend=backend)
    assert 0 == s.isna().sum() # should be 1
    assert 2 == s.dropna().size # should be 1

# See 54 different in df_failures under the Full Testing section
```

### Issue Description

The `.isna()` and `.dropna()` methods do not always find nulls in float and float-like Series. This includes Series that have been passed to `pd.to_numeric`. The behavior depends on...  
- The `dtype_backend` of `to_numeric`  
- Whether the original data were numbers, strings, or mixed  
- The `dtype` of the Series when it was created    

Please, see the **Full testing** section below for combinations.

This is tagged with `to_numeric`, but given some of the behavior happens even before `to_numeric` is called, it may be more of a general pandas issue.

# Reproduction  steps 
There are several variations that will reproduce the issue as shown in the Full Testing section; this is just one example:  

1. Create a list that has only numbers and `np.nan` values
2. Create a pandas Series from the list with `dtype=np.float64`
3. Use `pd.to_numeric()` on that Series with one of the `dtype_backend` options
    - You must pass either `'numpy_nullable'` or `'pyarrow'`
4. Check the number of nulls with `pd.isna().sum()` and see it returns `0`
    - Or use `.dropna()` and see that all values are still in the Series

# Other notes  

## NaN != null, so what is actually "expected"?  
I read some of the discussion about whether `np.nan` should be treated as the result of a failed mathematical calculation rather than as a `null` value. I assume decisions about that are partly responsible for some of the behavior documented here, so it's possible some of what I see as "unexpected" behavior is actually "expected" and I just don't understand the inner mechanics.

However, that doesn't explain everything I found in testing, particularly not after running `to_numeric`.

## Cases where `isna` fails before we run `to_numeric`  
Putting aside `to_numeric` for a moment, simply creating a Series with `dtype=pd.Float64Dtype()` causes `isna` to not find nulls if the original list...  
- Included any string values  
- Had nulls as `np.nan`, not `None`  

It *always* finds nulls if the Series is created with `None`. That's because `pd.Float64Dtype()` converts `None` to `pd.NA`, but it doesn't always convert `np.nan`.

## Conditions where `isna` works as expected every time  

Using `isna` works as expected every time...

1. If the initial `dtype` used when creating the Series is... 
    - `'object'`
    - `pd.ArrowDtype(pa.float64())`
    - `'Int64'` (when the input list has only ints, ints as str, or nulls)

2. If the nulls are `pd.NA` (as opposed to `np.nan` or `None`).

3. If `isna` is applied element-wise (e.g., `ser.apply(pd.isna).sum()`)


## Other documentation of issue  

I looked through the issues and didn't find much. After posting this on [r/learnpython](https://www.reddit.com/r/learnpython/comments/1qdum99/pdto_numeric_and_dtype_backend_seemingly/), a user reproduced this on 3.0.0rc2 and found something that might be related in the release notes ([Changed treatment of NaN values in pyarrow and numpy-nullable floating dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/3.0/whatsnew/v3.0.0.html#changed-treatment-of-nan-values-in-pyarrow-and-numpy-nullable-floating-dtypes)).

# Full testing  

Below are the results of my testing with various combinations. I found it helpful to put the output df into a Pivot Table to look for patterns, but I added a `FindPatterns` class here if you want to get a quick overview while in python.

This looks at each combination of...  
- Base list type (floats, ints, strings, mixed, etc.)
- Null value type (`None` and `np.nan`; `pd.NA` was tested but always worked as expected)
- Dtype used when creating the Series (`np.float64`, `pd.Float64Dtype()`, etc.); there were others, but I commented out ones that always worked as expected
- `dtype_backend` methods of `to_numeric`  

<details>

```python  

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
from itertools import product, combinations
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

pd.options.future.infer_string = True
pd.options.mode.copy_on_write = True

BASE_LIST = {
    'floats': [1.0, 2.0],
    'ints': [1, 2],
    'nums': [1.0, 2],
    'floats_as_str': ['1.0', '2.0'],
    'ints_as_str': ['1', '2'],
    'nums_as_str': ['1.0', '2'],
    'mixed_str_float': [1.0, '2'],
    'mixed_str_int': [1, '2'],
    'mixed_str_float_int': [1.0, 2, '3.0', '4']
}

NULL_VALUES = {
    'None': None,
    'np.nan': np.nan,
    # 'pd.NA': pd.NA,
}
""" 
If the null value is pd.NA,
`to_numeric` works as expected every time
"""

DTYPES = {
    'dtype_np_float64': np.float64,
    'dtype_pd_Float64': pd.Float64Dtype(),
    # 'dtype_object': 'object',
    # 'dtype_pa_float64': pd.ArrowDtype(pa.float64()),
    # 'dtype_float': 'float',
    # 'dtype_float64': 'float64',
    # 'dtype_Int64': 'Int64',
}
""" 
Removed dtypes that always worked as expected  

Passing `np.float64`, `'float'`, or `'float64'` had unexpected results,
but they all produced identical results to each other,
so I kept only `np.float64` for simplicity.
"""

CONVERSIONS = {
    'no_args': lambda s: pd.to_numeric(s),
    'numpy_nullable': lambda s: pd.to_numeric(s, dtype_backend='numpy_nullable'),
    'pyarrow': lambda s: pd.to_numeric(s, dtype_backend='pyarrow'),
}

CARTESIAN = product(
    BASE_LIST.items(),
    NULL_VALUES.items(),
    DTYPES.items(),
    CONVERSIONS.items()
)

type TBaseList = tuple[str, list]
type TNullValue = tuple[str, Any]
type TDtype = tuple[str, str | type]
type TConversion = tuple[str, Callable]

class Trial:

    def __init__(self, trial_vars: tuple[TBaseList, TNullValue, TDtype, TConversion]):
        self.lst_name, self.lst_vals = trial_vars[0]
        self.null_name, self.null_val = trial_vars[1]
        self.dtype_name, self.dtype_passed_to_ser_constructor = trial_vars[2]
        self.conv_name, self.conv_func = trial_vars[3]

        self.list_values = self.lst_vals + [self.null_val]
        self.ser_orig = self._create_series()
        self.ser_converted = self._apply_conversion()

    @property
    def trial_result(self) -> str:
        if self.ser_converted is None:
            return "Ignore"
        sum_isna = self._sum_isna(self.ser_converted)
        sum_elementwise = self._sum_elementwise()
        if (sum_isna is None) or (sum_elementwise is None):
            return "ERROR SUMMING"
        if np.isclose(sum_isna, sum_elementwise):
            return "AsExpected"
        else:
            return "Failure"

    def _create_series(self) -> pd.Series | None:
        try:
            return pd.Series(self.list_values, dtype=self.dtype_passed_to_ser_constructor)
        except Exception:
            return None

    def _apply_conversion(self) -> pd.Series | None:
        if self.ser_orig is None:
            return None
        try:
            return self.conv_func(self.ser_orig)
        except Exception:
            return None

    def _sum_isna(sel, ser: pd.Series) -> float | None:
        if ser is not None:
            return ser.isna().sum()

    def _sum_elementwise(self) -> float | None:
        if self.ser_converted is not None:
            return self.ser_converted.apply(pd.isna).sum()

    def _get_unique_types_in_ser_elements(self, s: pd.Series) -> set[str] | None:
        if s is None:
            return None
        return set(type(x) for x in s)

    def _format_dtype_for_display(self, dtype_to_format) -> str:
        if dtype_to_format == np.float64:
            return 'np.float64'
        elif dtype_to_format == pd.Float64Dtype():
            return 'pd.Float64Dtype()'
        elif dtype_to_format == pd.ArrowDtype(pa.float64()):
            return 'pd.ArrowDtype(pa.float64())'
        else:
            return f"'{dtype_to_format}'"

    def _get_str_to_reproduce(self) -> str:
        """Generate code string to reproduce the trial."""
        dtype_backend = '' if 'dtype_backend' not in self.conv_name else ', dtype_backend='
        dtype_display = self._format_dtype_for_display(self.dtype_passed_to_ser_constructor)
        str_ser = f"pd.Series({self.lst_vals + [self.null_val]}, dtype=" + dtype_display + ")"
        str_ser = str_ser.replace("nan", "np.nan").replace("NA", "pd.NA")
        return f"pd.to_numeric({str_ser}{dtype_backend}).isna().sum()"    

    def as_dict(self) -> dict:

        def display_dtype_of_series(s: pd.Series) -> str | None:
            if s is None:
                return None
            return self._format_dtype_for_display(s.dtype).replace("'", "")

        return {
            'result': self.trial_result,
            'conversion': self.conv_name,
            'list_name': self.lst_name,
            'null_type': self.null_name,
            'dtype_passed_to_ser_constructor': self._format_dtype_for_display(self.dtype_passed_to_ser_constructor).replace("'", ""),
            'dtype_of_ser_orig': display_dtype_of_series(self.ser_orig),
            'dtype_of_ser_conv': display_dtype_of_series(self.ser_converted),
            'dtypes_of_ser_orig_elements': self._get_unique_types_in_ser_elements(self.ser_orig),
            'dtypes_of_ser_conv_elements': self._get_unique_types_in_ser_elements(self.ser_converted),
            'sum_isna_orig': self._sum_isna(self.ser_orig),
            'sum_isna': self._sum_isna(self.ser_converted),
            'sum_elementwise': self._sum_elementwise(),
            'base_list': self.lst_vals,
            'str_to_reproduce': self._get_str_to_reproduce()
        }

class RunTrials:

    def __init__(self, cartesian_product):
        self.objs_trials = []
        self.results = []
        for situation in cartesian_product:
            self.obj = Trial(situation)
            self.objs_trials.append(self.obj)
            self.results.append(self.obj.as_dict())
    
    def to_df_all(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        df = pd.DataFrame(self.results)
        df.index.name = 'TrialNum'
        return df

    def to_df(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        df_all = self.to_df_all()
        return df_all.query('result != "Ignore"')
    def to_df_failures(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        df_all = self.to_df_all()
        return df_all.query('result == "Failure"')


class FindPatterns:
    def __init__(self, df_results: pd.DataFrame):
        self.df_results = df_results
        self.group_vars = ['conversion', 'list_name', 'null_type', 'dtype_passed_to_ser_constructor']
        self.all_combos = self._get_all_combinations()

    def _get_all_combinations(self) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]:
        all_combos = {}
        for idx_group_vars in range(1, len(self.group_vars) + 1):
            for variable_combo in combinations(self.group_vars, idx_group_vars):
                pattern = (
                    self.df_results
                    .groupby(list(variable_combo))['result']
                    .agg([
                        ('total_count', 'count'),
                        ('failure_count', lambda x: (x == 'Failure').sum()),
                        ('failure_rate', lambda x: (x == 'Failure').sum() / len(x))
                    ])
                    .sort_values('failure_rate', ascending=False)
                )
                combo_name = ' + '.join(variable_combo)
                all_combos[combo_name] = pattern
        return all_combos

    def _get_txt_combos_at_specific_failure_rate(self, failure_rate: float) -> list[str | pd.DataFrame]:
        msg_parts = []
        for combo_name, pattern in self.all_combos.items():
            meets_fail_rate = pattern[pattern['failure_rate'] == failure_rate]
            if len(meets_fail_rate) > 0:
                msg_parts.append(f"\n{combo_name}:\n")
                msg_parts.append(meets_fail_rate)
        return msg_parts

    def _get_text_always_header(self, text: str) -> list[str]:
        hr = '\n' + ('=' * 80) + '\n'
        return [hr, text, hr]

    def show_summary(self) -> None:

        # Find combinations that always fail (100% failure rate)
        hdr_always_fail = self._get_text_always_header('PATTERNS THAT ALWAYS FAIL')
        txt_always_fail = self._get_txt_combos_at_specific_failure_rate(1.0)
        
        # Find combinations that always succeed (0% failure rate)
        hdr_always_succeed = self._get_text_always_header('PATTERNS THAT ALWAYS SUCCEED')
        txt_always_succeed = self._get_txt_combos_at_specific_failure_rate(0.0)

        for content in hdr_always_fail + txt_always_fail + hdr_always_succeed + txt_always_succeed:
            print(content)

obj_run = RunTrials(CARTESIAN)
df_results = obj_run.to_df()
df_failures = obj_run.to_df_failures()
# df_results.to_clipboard()

obj_patterns = FindPatterns(df_results)
# obj_patterns.show_summary()

```

</details>

### Expected Behavior

Using `isna` and `dropna` should consistently find null-like values.  
```python  
ser = pd.Series([1, np.nan], dtype=np.float64) # 1 na value
pd.to_numeric(ser, dtype_backend='numpy_nullable').isna().sum() # Should return 1
pd.to_numeric(ser, dtype_backend='pyarrow').isna().sum() # Should return 1
```

See `df_results.query('result == "AsExpected"')` from the *Full Details* section for 54 examples of the expected behavior.

- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)
- [x] If I used AI to develop this pull request, I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`.

`merge_asof` accepts `tolerance=0` — an exact-match-only merge, a meaningful asof semantic — but the `MergeError` raised for a negative `tolerance` claimed the value `must be positive`. All three type-specific guards reject only strictly-negative values (`self.tolerance < 0` / `< Timedelta(0)`), so `0` passes and the "positive" wording is inconsistent with the actual constraint.

The three messages now say `tolerance must be non-negative`. A new regression test (`test_tolerance_zero`) asserts that `tolerance=0` performs an exact-match merge (a row with no exact counterpart gets no match), pinning the accepted behavior so the wording can't drift back.

title: BUG: suppress tz .values deprecation raised by pyarrow in internal conversions

labels.name: Compat
labels.description: pandas objects compatability with Numpy or Python functions

body:
Resolves part of #68426

pyarrow reads `.values` when converting tz-aware Series/Index data, which triggers the unreleased `.values` deprecation from GH-64613. Users can't act on it when pandas itself makes the call. This PR suppresses that specific warning around pandas' own pyarrow conversions: `Series`/`DataFrame.__arrow_c_stream__`, `to_parquet`, `to_feather`, `to_orc`, `to_iceberg` and ADBC `to_sql`. Direct user calls such as `pa.array(ser)` still warn; those need the pyarrow-side fix (apache/arrow#51302). The helper should be removed once the minimum pyarrow includes that fix.

This also drops the `filterwarnings` marks that were hiding the warning in the pyarrow-engine parquet/feather tests, and adds tz-aware tests for the arrow C stream interface and ORC.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5 (high)`), used for investigation, implementation and tests.

title: BUG: `sort_index` failing on MultiIndex with label name when key is used
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from natsort import index_natsorted

df = pd.DataFrame(
    [[1, 2], [3, 4]],
    columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["a"], ["top10", "top2"]], names=("A", "B")),
)
df.sort_index(axis=1, level=1)  # Passes
df.sort_index(axis=1, level="B")  # Passes
df.sort_index(axis=1, level=1, key=lambda x: np.argsort(index_natsorted(x)))  # Passes
```

### Issue Description

When sorting over a multi-index with level name and key being set, an error is raised.

Early investigations:
* in the sort process the name of the level is dropped, due to key

* when `sort_level` is called from `get_indexer_indexer`, the sort is attempted on the level name, which has been dropped already

`sort_index` should support both level id or level name

## Summary

- Deprecate `.values` returning lossy/object-dtype results for `DatetimeTZDtype` (drops timezone), `PeriodDtype` (returns object ndarray), and `IntervalDtype` (returns object ndarray)

Affects both Series (via `external_values()` in `blocks.py`) and Index (via overrides in `period.py` and `datetimelike.py`). IntervalIndex already returns the ExtensionArray from `.values` so only the Series path needs deprecation for IntervalDtype.

title: BUG: DataFrame.replace/Series.replace silently stored a callable value

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
`NDFrame.replace` validates `to_replace` up front but never checks `value`. A callable `value` passes straight through, so `s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True)` stores the function object in the result instead of applying it or raising, and later operations on that object-dtype data fail far from the actual mistake.

```python
s = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"])
s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True)
# 0    <function <lambda> at 0x...>
# 1    <function <lambda> at 0x...>
```

This adds the same kind of check that already exists for `to_replace`: `replace` now raises `TypeError` when `value` is callable, matching the error already raised for a callable `to_replace` (GH-18634). The check is recursive so it also catches a callable hiding inside a list-like or dict-like `value` (`replace([...], [callable])`, `replace({...: callable})`, `replace(regex={...: callable})`), not just a bare callable passed directly. Covered for `Series` and `DataFrame`, across all of those spellings.

Fixes #68199

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude sonnet 5 (low)`), which found the missing validation and wrote the fix and the regression tests.

title: BUG: Preserve sequence name during fancy indexing for Series subclasses with custom _metadata (#61491)

body:
- [x] closes #61491

This PR fixes a bug where list-indexing (and methods like `drop_duplicates`) on a `Series` subclass would lose the sequence `name` if the subclass explicitly defined its own `_metadata`.
The root cause is that subclassing with custom `_metadata` completely overwrites `Series._metadata = ["_name"]`, causing `__finalize__` to skip propagating the `_name` attribute. This PR unconditionally propagates `_name` for 1-dimensional Series-like objects during `__finalize__` to prevent this.
