*[original issue body]*

With PDEP-10 (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/52711/, https://pandas.pydata.org/pdeps/0010-required-pyarrow-dependency.html), we decided to start using pyarrow for the default string data type in pandas 3.0.

For pandas 2.1, an option was added to already enable this future default data type, and then the various ways to construct a DataFrame (type inference in the constructor, IO methods) will use the new string dtype as default:

```python
>>> pd.options.future.infer_string = True

>>> pd.Series(["a", "b", None])
0      a
1      b
2    NaN
dtype: string

>>> pd.Series(["a", "b", None]).dtype
string[pyarrow_numpy]
```

This is documented at https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/whatsnew/v2.1.0.html#whatsnew-210-enhancements-infer-strings

One aspect that was discussed after the PDEP (mostly at the sprint, I think; creating this issue for a better public record of it), is that for a data type that would become the default in pandas 3.0 (which for the rest still uses all numpy dtypes with numpy NaN missing value semantics), should probably also still use the same default semantics and result in numpy data types when doing operations on the string column that result in a boolean or numeric data type (eg `.str.startswith(..)`, `.str.len(..)`, `.str.count()`, etc, or comparison operators like `==`). 
(this way, a user only gets an ArrowDtype column when explicitly asking for those, and not by default through using a the default string dtype)

To achieve this, @phofl has done several PRs to refactor the current pyarrow-based string dtypes, to add another variant which uses `StringDtype(storage="pyarrow_numpy")` instead of `ArrowDtype("string")`. From the updated whatsnew: *"This is a new string dtype implementation that follows NumPy semantics in comparison operations and will return ``np.nan`` as the missing value indicator"*. Main PR:

* https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/54533

plus some follow-ups (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/54720, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/54585, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/54591).

cc @pandas-dev/pandas-core

title: API: default to microseconds for Timestamp/Timedelta creation from numeric input
body:
After the recent PRs for defaulting to microseconds when possible in `date_range`/`Timestamp`/`to_datetime` etc (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/58989), there is one main type of input to those functions that still result in nanoseconds, which is numeric input.

For example:

```
>>> pd.to_datetime([1, 2, 3], unit="s")
DatetimeIndex(['1970-01-01 00:00:01', '1970-01-01 00:00:02',
               '1970-01-01 00:00:03'],
              dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
```

(there is the, separate, confusing part that the `unit` keyword here is define how to interpret the input, and not to specify the unit of the return value)

As a starter, I think there is no reason (apart from that it is currently implemented like that) to return nanoseconds here (unless the input are nanoseconds). 
So I would at least default to microseconds when possible. 

But then another option would also be to do as minimal conversion as possible, and for example if the input is seconds (or minutes, hours, etc) also return seconds, etc. This gives more variation in the resulting dtype, but causes less conversion.

(I have a slight preference to as much as possible return the same dtype)

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

print( pd.Timedelta( 1, 's' ) / 2, "Result should be '0 days 00:00:00.500000'" )
print( pd.Timedelta( 1, 'day' ) * 0.1111, "Result should be '0 days 02:39:59.040000'" )

```

### Issue Description

Timedeltas smaller than 1 second are truncated to 0 in some situations and larger Timedeltas are truncated to the nearest second. Similarly, dividing a 1 ms Timedelta by 2 is truncated to 0. This is distinct from the behavior reported in #65389, but they could be related. 

This bug occurs in 3.0.3 and 3.0.2, but not in pandas 2.2.

import pandas as pd

```

Thanks for all the work that you do to make pandas so excellent!

title: DOC/WEB: Move not versioned docs to the web

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
The reason we have a separate website and docs is that the docs are specific to a version (e.g. pandas 1.5.3), while the website is global to all versions and updated in real time.

For historic reasons, we have several things that are not version specific in the docs, which IMHO doesn't add any value and brings confusion and extra work backporting and keeping things sync. To be specific, what's in the docs that is not version dependent is:

- Development documentation
- Release notes
- Installation instructions (just a small section in the Getting started docs)

The change is not trivial for two reasons:

- The docs use restructured text, and the website uses markdown
- The website doesn't provide automatic references (we can't use things like `:meth:'Series.isin'`)

For the development documentation I think the second point is not a big problem, but for the release notes we do use references to the API a lot. Not sure if it's worth the migration, but creating an issue anyway for visibility of the problem, and in case anyone has comments.

title: PDEP-8 inplace keyword deprecation - implementation tracker issue

labels.name: Master Tracker
labels.description: High level tracker for similar issues

labels.name: inplace
labels.description: Relating to inplace parameter or equivalent

body:
Issue to track the progress of implementing the accepted PDEP-8: https://pandas.pydata.org/pdeps/0008-inplace-methods-in-pandas.html

Summary of the PDEP proposed changes:

- The ``inplace`` parameter will be removed from any method which can never update the
  underlying values of a pandas object inplace or which alters the shape of the object,
  and where the `inplace=True` option is only syntactic sugar for reassigning the result
  to the calling DataFrame/Series.
  - In practice, this are the methods `drop`, `rename`, `rename_axis`, ``reset_index``,  ``set_index``, `dropna` `drop_duplicates`, `sort_values`, `sort_index`, `eval`, `query`
- The `inplace` parameter is kept for those methods that can
  modify the underlying values of a pandas object inplace, such as `fillna` or `replace`, and those methods will return the calling object (`self`), instead of the current `None`.
- With the introduction of Copy-on-Write ([PDEP-7](https://pandas.pydata.org/pdeps/0007-copy-on-write.html)), users don't need the `inplace` keyword to avoid a copy of the data.

---

List of TODO items:

title: BUG: defer the blocked-numexpr warning to first use (GH#66956)

labels.name: Warnings
labels.description: Warnings that appear or should be added to pandas

body:
Follow-up to GH-66956, addressing @jorisvandenbossche's review comment there: that PR warned about the refused numexpr 2.14.1 at `import pandas`, which reaches users who never evaluate anything through numexpr — including the many who have it transitively, since PyTables hard-depends on it.

The warning now fires at most once per process, at the first operation that would actually have been offloaded: arithmetic and comparisons large enough and of the right dtype for numexpr, `where`/`mask`, and `eval`/`query` on the default engine. A small `df + df` stays silent, and so does everything when `compute.use_numexpr` is False. `expressions.py` gains `_evaluate_blocked`/`_where_blocked`, chosen by `set_use_numexpr` only when the option is on and the installed numexpr is blocked; they gate on the same `_can_use_numexpr` predicate the numexpr path uses, so "would have used numexpr" cannot drift from the real decision.

An explicit `engine="numexpr"` still raises `ImportError` rather than warning. Since that path no longer has a warning alongside it, the message now names the refused version instead of telling a user who does have numexpr installed that it "is not installed".

HDF5 `where=` queries remain uncovered, as the whatsnew already states, because PyTables imports numexpr itself. The warning is deliberately not raised there: its text says numexpr "will not be used by pandas", which is false on that path, and making it accurate would need a second message and a second one-shot flag.

The GH-66956 whatsnew bullet is amended in place rather than given its own entry, since 3.1 is unreleased.

title: ENH: DataFrame.filter and Series.filter to take a boolean masks
body:
Initially written by Claude Fable 5, heavily refined by me.

Closes https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/23541 (as "no")

Enhances `DataFrame.filter` and `Series.filter` to accept a boolean mask by adding a new keyword argument `cond`. Users specifying `items=...` will not see any changes. Users passing without a keyword (e.g. `df.filter(items)`) will see a warning to specify either `items=` or `cond=` when the argument appears to be a boolean mask.

API Decisions:
- Users can control NA behavior via an added `na` argument. Defaults to `na=False` to agree with `DataFrame.__getitem__` behavior. Allows to raise on NA values because they can accidentally sneak into masks.
- A Series mask aligns.
- `items`, `like`, and `regex` arguments are not deprecated yet, but we plan to in the future.

title: BUG: iloc setitem wrote the wrong cells on a Copy-on-Write referenced frame (GH#65446)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
Repairs a regression from GH-65864, which is in 3.0.4 and later.

When another object references a `DataFrame`'s values, `BlockManager.setitem` splits the block so only the targeted columns get copied, then re-expresses the caller's column indexer in the new block's coordinates. GH-65864 collapsed any increasing column selection to `slice(None)` and compensated for reordered ones with an array of positions, plus a reshape of the row indexer to `(n, 1)`. Both substitutions change what numpy does: a slice takes the cross product with the row indexer, an array broadcasts against it. So the referenced path could disagree with the unreferenced one in either direction — writing a cross product where the caller asked for an elementwise pairing, or the other way round.

The column indexer now keeps the kind the caller used: an integer stays an integer, a slice stays a slice (reversed if the selection was), `Ellipsis` normalizes to `slice(None)` since it also selects the axis in full, and anything else stays an array of positions. The row-indexer reshape goes with it — it was independently wrong, turning an intended broadcast into a cross product whenever `np.ix_` had not already run — and so does the `np.squeeze`, which is only correct for `np.ix_` output; a user-supplied 2-D row key still reaches that spot, and not squeezing it is what makes it match the unreferenced path.

Symptoms fixed, all only when another object holds a reference:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(12.0).reshape(4, 3), columns=list("abc"))
ref = df[["a", "b", "c"]]

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::-1] = np.array([100.0, 101.0, 102.0])
# IndexError: shape mismatch: indexing arrays could not be broadcast
#   together with shapes (2,) (3,)

df.iloc[np.array([1, 0]), range(1, -1, -1)] = 99.0
# silently writes 4 cells; without the reference it writes 2

df.loc[np.array([True, False, True, False]), "c":"a":-1] = 99.0
# IndexError: too many indices for array: array is 2-dimensional, but 3 were indexed
```

For the `managers.py` split path the unreferenced path is the oracle: it never enters this code, so referenced-vs-unreferenced is a differential with no shared failure mode. Over 35,728 cases (4 dtypes x 4 frame shapes x 20 row-key spellings x 14 column-key spellings x 7 value shapes, `iloc` and `loc`) `main` diverges in 3,621. The branch's residual divergences are the empty-indexer family, where an early return skips value validation; that predates GH-65864 and is left alone here.

`EABackedBlock.setitem` needed a second change, and it is not covered by that oracle. Keeping the column indexer as an array walks 2-D EA blocks into the `indexer[::-1]` + `value.T` pair, which `slice(None)` had been keeping them out of. Two advanced indices broadcast against each other, and their order does not change the result's orientation, so the `value.T` is spurious there; it is now gated accordingly. Because the unreferenced path always reached that pair through `np.ix_`, the gate also changes **unreferenced** all-`datetime64`/`timedelta64` frames: `df.iloc[[2, 0], [0, 2]] = value` with a 2-D value silently wrote the transposed cells, and a non-square selection raised `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. There the oracle is the float64 peer, which both now match. Hence the second whatsnew entry.

Note for the backport decision: GH-65864 shipped in 3.0.4, so the `IndexError`/`ValueError` families here are live for 3.0.x users. The datetimelike entry is *not* a GH-65864 regression — `value = value.T` came in with GH-64620 (2026-03-15), and the unreferenced path never enters the block GH-65864 changed — so a backport necessarily carries that older fix too. The entry is in `v3.1.0.rst` as there is no open 3.0.x file (3.0.6 released 2026-09-17).

Overlap with GH-68521: that PR rewrites the same `EABackedBlock.setitem` hunk, and its second whatsnew entry describes the same 2-D-value transposition fixed here, with a more general `transposed` flag that also handles a 1-D value. Whichever lands first, the other should drop the duplicate entry and rebase onto it.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and ran the differential sweeps; reviewed by me.

title: BUG: read_sql no longer works simply with SqlAlchemy selectables and a quick fix

labels.name: Needs Tests
labels.description: Unit test(s) needed to prevent regressions

body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [x] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

---

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

Hey--I noticed while running [siuba's](https://github.com/machow/siuba) SQL unit tests that queries using the modulo operator are failing.

The issue is due to a recent change for issue #34211 in pandas setting the [no_parameters](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blame/5507452c4a675ad5453bc5f02cd68b65fe3977df/pandas/io/sql.py#L1161) argument before executing via a sqlalchemy engine. This was done to allow queries like `SELECT 1 % 2`, but causes SqlAlchemy expressions handling `%` to not always work with `read_sql`.

**Solution**. Rather than executing in a special way (`no_parameters`), I think you want to wrap a string query in SqlAlchemy.sql.text ([see here](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/13/core/tutorial.html#using-textual-sql)). This will allow both queries with `%` and the full range of SqlAlchemy expressions. WDYT?

```python
from sqlalchemy import sql, create_engine
import pandas as pd

engine = create_engine('postgresql://postgres:@localhost:5433/postgres', echo=False)
#engine = create_engine('postgresql://USERNAME:PASSWORD@localhost:PORT/DBNAME', echo=False)

# doesn't work, original issue in pandas: 'dict' object does not support indexing
engine.execute("SELECT 1 % 2")

# works, ideal solution
engine.execute(sql.text("SELECT 1 % 2" ))

# queries below broken by no_parameters change ----
pd.read_sql(sql.text("SELECT 1 % 2"), engine)

pd.read_sql(sql.select([sql.literal(1) % sql.literal(2)]), engine)
```

Here's a gist of the error for the last two queries...

```
ProgrammingError: (psycopg2.errors.UndefinedFunction) operator does not exist: integer %% integer
LINE 1: SELECT 1 %% 2
                 ^
HINT:  No operator matches the given name and argument types. You might need to add explicit type casts.

[SQL: SELECT 1 %% 2]
(Background on this error at: http://sqlalche.me/e/13/f405)
```

title: BUG: GroupBy.agg with as_index=False and MultiIndex column grouping key raises ValueError

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

body:
---
Closes GH-39103

---

### Reproduction

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({("col0", "l0"): [0, 0, 1], ("col1", "l1"): [10, 20, 30]})
df.groupby(("col0", "l0"), as_index=False).agg({("col1", "l1"): ["min", "max"]})
```

```text
ValueError: Item must have length equal to number of levels.
```

### Root cause

`_insert_inaxis_grouper` in `pandas/core/groupby/groupby.py` decides whether the `as_index=False` group key has already been inserted by the aggregation itself. For a `MultiIndex` columns frame, the str-name path pads the key to the columns' `nlevels` (`("key", "", ...)`, per GH-17024 / GH-28549), but a tuple name of fewer levels than `result.columns.nlevels` was returned unchanged, and `result.insert(0, name, lev)` then failed with the "Item must have length equal to number of levels" `ValueError`.

### Fix

`full_key()` now also pads tuple names when `len(name) < result.columns.nlevels`, and the membership check uses `full_key(name)` so it looks up the exact key that will be inserted (previously a partial-tuple lookup which additionally raised `PerformanceWarning` on un-lex-sorted `MultiIndex` columns, surfaced as an error under CI's `filterwarnings`).

The inserted grouper column now exactly matches the canonical `groupby(..., as_index=True).agg(...).reset_index()` output.

### Verification

- Issue repro now returns the expected padded columns `[("col0", "l0", ""), ("col1", "l1", "min"), ("col1", "l1", "max")]`, byte-identical to the `as_index=True` + `reset_index()` form for `agg`, `describe`, and multi-tuple-grouper cases
- New tests: `test_groupby_agg_as_index_false_multiindex_column` (padded columns, existing column order, empty input) and `test_groupby_as_index_false_multiindex_column_matches_reset_index` (agg/describe/multi-tuple equivalence)
- `pandas/tests/groupby/`: 24447 passed, 866 skipped, 43 xfailed
- Sweep of `pandas/tests/resample/`, `pandas/tests/apply/`, `pandas/tests/reshape/`: green (2 unrelated pre-existing tzdata DST failures, confirmed identical on `main`)
- `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean (repo-pinned ruff 0.16.6); `aggregate/` suite green under `-W error`

body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [ ] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

---

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas

# Could be any data with MultiIndex columns
data = {(f"col{i}", f"level-{i % 2}"): np.arange(5) for i in range(5)}
df = pandas.DataFrame(data)

by = df.columns[0]
agg_col = df.columns[1]

agg_dict = {agg_col: ["min", "max"]}
df.groupby(by, as_index=False).agg(func=agg_dict)  # ValueError

```

    self._mgr.insert(loc, column, value, allow_duplicates=allow_duplicates)

    raise ValueError("Item must have length equal to number of levels.")
ValueError: Item must have length equal to number of levels.
```

</details>

#### Problem description

When we specify an aggregation function via list, pandas adds a new level with function name to the columns of the resulted frame:
```python
>>> df
   col0  col1
0     0     0
>>> df.groupby("col0").agg({"col1": ["max"]})

      max
col0
0       0
```
In the result, the number of levels in the index which represents grouper and columns is different, which causes some problems in [`_insert_inaxis_grouper_inplace`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3bd3d1ec253a8a18ac951511820eb970f62baaed/pandas/core/groupby/generic.py#L1610-L1621). When we're trying to insert MultiIndex grouper inside the resulted frame, but their `nlevels` is different, `pandas.DataFrame.insert` raises a `ValueError` because of it. 

Filling mismatched levels with an empty string (like pandas already does when inserted value don't have MultiIndex columns) will probably solve this issue

MultiIndex([('col0',    ''),

With `include_lowest=True` (which `qcut` always uses), `_format_labels` rounds every break with `formatter` and then subtracts `10**-precision` from the first one, so the first label picks up float noise, e.g. `(0.057999999999999996, 0.5]`. title: BUG: Value-dependent formatting when casting from datetime to string

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

assert pd.__version__ == "3.0.5"
assert np.__version__ == "2.5.1"

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:01"],  # <- value dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:01.000"],  # <- unit dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
```

### Issue Description

The string formatting of datetimes depends on the values rather than the time unit of the data type. The analogous operation in NumPy only depends on the unit.

I was not able to find a definitive answer on the matter that clarified whether this is intended behavior. I can see that this may have been intended in pandas 1.x where the one and only unit was `ns` which would lead to very long strings in all cases, despite most users probably never working on a ns resolution. 

### Expected Behavior

My understanding is that value-dependent semantics are not desired in pandas these days(?). Given that pandas allows users to define their desired units these days, it seems reasonable to me to make the formatting depend only on the unit rather than the values. 

Alternatively, it may be nice to document the intended formatting semantics (unless I missed them and that is already the case).

body:
#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example if possible

```
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> mydf = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(dict(dt=[pd.Timestamp('2000-01-01'),pd.Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00.000000001')]))
>>> print(mydf.to_csv(index=False))
dt
2000-01-01 00:00:00.000000000
2000-01-01 00:00:00.000000001
>>> print(mydf.to_csv(index=False,date_format='%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f'))
dt
2000-01-01T00:00:00.000000
2000-01-01T00:00:00.000000
```
#### Problem description

ISO-8601 specifies that the 'T' separator is optional in contexts where there is no ambiguity with other 8601 date or time formats. I'm trying to make some CSV files and am trying to be very strict with what I emit because I don't know how they'll be consumed.

It'd be *really* nice to be able to preserve full precision in the data but still have that separator character present and as far as I am aware, there is no Python Datetime format string which displays nanoseconds.

The shortest alternative I can come up with for this is the following (and I am not 100% sure this will work correctly):

```
tmp_df = mydf
dt_cols = mydf.select_dtypes(include='datetime64').columns
tmp_df[dt_cols] = tmp_df[dt_cols].applymap(lambda x:str(x.to_datetime64()))
tmp_df.to_csv(index=False)
```

#### Expected Output

dt
2000-01-01T00:00:00.000000000
2000-01-01T00:00:00.000000001

labels.name: Missing-data

body:
#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example if possible

```python
import datetime as dt
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
data = [
    ['one', 1.0, pd.NaT],
    ['two', np.nan, dt.datetime(2019, 2, 2)],
    [None, 3.0, dt.datetime(2019, 3, 3)]
    ]
df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=["Name", "Value", "Event_date"])
```
```pycon
>>> df
   Name  Value Event_date
0   one    1.0        NaT
1   two    NaN 2019-02-02
2  None    3.0 2019-03-03

>>> df.replace({pd.NaT: None})
   Name Value           Event_date
0   one     1                 None
1   two  None  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None     3  2019-03-03 00:00:00
>>> df.replace({np.nan: None})
   Name Value           Event_date
0   one     1                 None
1   two  None  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None     3  2019-03-03 00:00:00

>>> df.replace({np.nan: None}).replace({np.nan: None})
   Name  Value           Event_date
0   one    1.0                 None
1   two    NaN  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None    3.0  2019-03-03 00:00:00

>>> df.replace({np.nan: None}).replace({np.nan: None}).replace({np.nan: None})
   Name Value           Event_date
0   one     1                 None
1   two  None  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None     3  2019-03-03 00:00:00

>>> df.replace({pd.NaT: None, np.nan: None})
   Name  Value           Event_date
0   one    1.0                 None
1   two    NaN  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None    3.0  2019-03-03 00:00:00
```
#### Problem description

This might seem somewhat related to #17494. Here I am using a dict to replace (which is the recommended way to do it in the related issue) but I suspect the function calls itself and passes `None` (replacement value) to the `value` arg, hitting the default arg value.

When calling `df.replace()` to replace NaN or NaT with None, I found several behaviours which don't seem right to me :
- Replacing NaT with None (only) also replaces NaN with None.
- Replacing NaN with None also replaces NaT with None
- Replacing NaT and NaN with None, replaces NaT but leaves the NaN
- Linked to previous, calling several times a replacement of NaN or NaT with None, switched between NaN and None for the float columns. An even number of calls will leave NaN, an odd number of calls will leave None.

This is a problem because I'm unable to replace only NaT or only NaN. This is also a problem because if I want to replace both, I intuitively call replace with the dict `{pd.NaT: None, np.NaN: None}` but end up with NaNs.

I suspect two problems here : NaN, NaT and None being all considered as equals, and replace() calling itself with None as value argument.

```pycon
>>> df.replace({pd.NaT: None, np.NaN: None})
   Name  Value           Event_date
0   one    1.0                 None
1   two    None  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None    3.0  2019-03-03 00:00:00

>>> df.replace({pd.NaT: None})
   Name Value           Event_date
0   one     1                 None
1   two   NaN  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None     3  2019-03-03 00:00:00

>>> df.replace({np.NaN: None})
   Name Value           Event_date
0   one     1                  NaT
1   two  None  2019-02-02 00:00:00
2  None     3  2019-03-03 00:00:00
```

title: ENH: use the option framework to opt-out of auto-alignment

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: New Option Request
labels.description: Request for something to be configurable by pd.set_option

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

As far as I know, auto-alignment of DataFrames and Series (e.g. with arithmetic operations) cannot be disabled. To work in "strict" mode, the user must first check alignment and then make a computation:
```
a = pd.DataFrame(...)
b = pd.DataFrame(...)

c = pd.Series(...)
d = pd.Series(...)

if not a.index.equals(b.index) or not a.columns.equals(b.columns):
    raise ...
k = a + b

if not c.index.equals(d.index):
    raise ...
m = c + d
```
Since alignment must also be checked internally by pandas, this is not only cumbersome but inefficient.


### Feature Description

Use the pandas option framework to opt-out of auto-alignment. One could even go one step further to allow deactivation of alignment check altogether for data that is known to be aligned (to gain some computation time). So the option would look like: ``mode.on_misaligned``:
* ``coerce``: default and current behaviour
* ``raise``: strict mode, raise an error if indices are not aligned
* ``ignore``: skip alignment checking and proceed with the computation assuming data is already aligned
The user would then set the option as he sees fit, e.g. with a context manager:
```
with pd.option_context("mode.on_misaligned", "raise"):
    k = a + b
    m = c + d
```

### Alternative Solutions

The alternative solution is the problem

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: BUG: setitem/getitem inconsistency with dict_values

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
- [X] I have searched the [[pandas] tag](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/pandas) on StackOverflow for similar questions.

- [X] I have discussed my usage related question on [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com).

---
@kristiancanler came across different behavior between assignment and look-ups when using a `dictionary.values()` view object as slice, as documented in his [StackOverflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66961614/why-does-pandas-recognize-dictionary-values-as-a-list-of-column-names-when-used/67001369#67001369).
We do know how to work around this - as is documented in the question, as well as answers - we just want to know if it is intended.

Creating a DataFrame + dictionary, using `dictionary.values()` as slice in `print()` simply prints the correct column:

```python
import pandas as pd

cols_dict = {'X': 'col1'}

df = pd.DataFrame({'col1': range(2),
                   'col2': range(3, 5)})

print(df[cols_dict.values()])
   col1 
0     0
1     1
```
however using dictionary.values() on assignment yielded unexpected results:
```python

df[cols_dict.values()] = df[cols_dict.values()]

print(df)
   col1  col2  (col1)
0     0     3       0
1     1     4       1
```
Is this expected behavior?
If not, is the reason for this behavior the difference in this part of frame's [`__setitem__()`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/822db7a53fdcf8d860aaa8b51da4b767b3f56fad/pandas/core/frame.py#L3528-L3536) and [`__getitem__()`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/822db7a53fdcf8d860aaa8b51da4b767b3f56fad/pandas/core/frame.py#L3368-L3388)?

```python
        # Do we have a slicer (on rows)?
        indexer = convert_to_index_sliceable(self, key)
        if indexer is not None:                                    #!
            if isinstance(indexer, np.ndarray):                    #!
                indexer = lib.maybe_indices_to_slice(              #!
                    indexer.astype(np.intp, copy=False), len(self) #!
                )                                                  #!
            # either we have a slice or we have a string that can be converted
            #  to a slice for partial-string date indexing
            return self._slice(indexer, axis=0)
```

The part with #! is only in `__getitem__()`, not in `__setitem__()`, even though both parts of code start with `indexer = convert_to_index_sliceable(self, key)` and the pre-return comments come to the exact same conclusion as to what indexer could be.

title: PERF: avoid temporary allocations in multi-block DataFrame axis=1 reductions
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


## Reproducible Example

Multi-block `DataFrame` reductions along `axis=1` use the `_reduce_axis1` fast path for operations such as `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. For eligible NumPy-backed blocks, the current implementation still creates a per-block `middle` vector and then allocates another result while combining it with the accumulated reduction.

These intermediate allocations become significant for DataFrames with many rows and several blocks. For a guarded subset of compatible NumPy blocks, the reduction and combine steps can avoid these temporaries while retaining the existing fallback for other block types and configurations.

```python
from timeit import repeat

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


nrows = 1_000_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
df = pd.DataFrame(index=range(nrows))
for i in range(8):
    values = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1, nrows)
    values[i::1000] = np.nan
    df[f"column-{i}"] = values

assert len(df._mgr.blocks) == 8


def best_ms(func):
    return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000


for name in ("sum", "prod", "min", "max"):
    value = best_ms(lambda name=name: getattr(df, name)(axis=1))
    print(f"{name}: {value:.3f} ms")
```

```text
pandas 3.0.5:
sum: 141.387 ms
prod: 147.783 ms
min: 181.131 ms
max: 185.854 ms

upstream main (ebcf0ed7):
sum: 39.205 ms
prod: 37.257 ms
min: 18.315 ms
max: 18.293 ms

optimized branch (40817a6d):
sum: 26.450 ms
prod: 26.643 ms
min: 5.681 ms
max: 5.696 ms
```

Compared with upstream main, the optimized implementation reduced runtime by approximately:

* 32.5% for `sum`
* 28.5% for `prod`
* 69.0% for `min`
* 68.9% for `max`

A matched ASV comparison covered 72 cases across:

* `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`
* 2,048, 32,768, and 100,000 rows
* 2 and 8 blocks
* `float64`, mixed `float32`/`float64`, and `int64` blocks

At a significance factor of 1.05, 38 cases improved, 34 were unchanged, and none regressed. Statistically significant improvements ranged from approximately 8% to 60%.

Representative ASV results:

```text
sum, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 2.15 ms -> 1.71 ms
prod, 100,000 rows, 8 int64 blocks: 1.36 ms -> 0.547 ms
min, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 1.04 ms -> 0.487 ms
max, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 1.02 ms -> 0.498 ms
```

Matched ASV peak-memory measurements for 1,000,000 rows and eight `float64` blocks also improved:

```text
sum: 188 MB -> 175 MB
min: 174 MB -> 158 MB
```

This is related to #51474 , the broader request to use `_reduce_axis1` for these reductions, and #65105, which implemented the multi-block fast path.

The issue described here is narrower: that fast path is already present, but it still materializes a per-block `middle` vector and an allocating combine result. The proposed optimization avoids those allocations for an explicitly guarded subset of NumPy-backed blocks.

title: API: require scalar result from the scalar .at indexer

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
The `.at` indexer is documented as the fast, restricted version of `loc` to "access a scalar value"  (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/indexing.html#fast-scalar-value-getting-and-setting).

However, currently, there is not always a guarantee that the result will actually be a scalar. For example, with a Series with duplicate index values:

```
In [3]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=['a', 'b', 'a'])  

In [4]: s.at['a'] 
Out[4]: 
a    1
a    3
dtype: int64
```

There are some other possible cases that could give a non-scalar value as well:

- MultiIndex if not all levels are indexed (#26989)
- DataFrame with duplicate index labels in index and/or columns (#33041)

However, those cases currently all fail (error or produce wrong result, see below for examples). 
So a question that can be posed: **should we consider those cases as bugs, or should we rather actually require a scalar result** and thus see the series behaviour above as too liberal?

Since those linked issues have open PRs to "fix" them, I think we should first decide on what guarantees on the `.at` API we want to provide. And personally, I think taking the documented intention of accessing a scalar would be a plus (it gives a certainty about the type of the result, i.e. always a scalar, and not sometimes a series or dataframe depening on the value of the label passed to `at`).

If we prefer the more strict scalar result requirement, we can deprecate the Series case (but only if accessing a duplicated label) and provide better error messages for the error cases.

---

Examples of the failing behaviours (on pandas 1.0.1):

```python
# duplicated row label -> you get a numpy array (which I would say is always wrong)
>>> df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(3, 2), index=['a', 'b', 'a'], columns=['A', 'B'])  
>>> df.at['a', 'A'] 
array([-0.02914828,  0.2856617 ])

# duplicated column label -> error
>>> df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(3, 2), index=['a', 'b', 'c'], columns=['A', 'A'])  
>>> df.at['a', 'A']  
...
AttributeError: 'BlockManager' object has no attribute 'T'

# Selecting one level of a MultiIndex -> error
>>> s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(4), index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([['A', 'B'], [1, 2]]))  
>>> s.at['A']  
...
KeyError: 'A'
During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:
...
AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute '_values'

# selecting all MultiIndex levels -> this should actually work (#26989)
>>> s.at['A', 1] 
...
TypeError: _get_value() got multiple values for argument 'takeable'

# DataFrame with all MultiIndex levels specified works OK
>>>s.to_frame('col').at[('A', 1), 'col']
1.341421652269149
```

title: IntervalIndex: outer intervals closed 'both' should be possible

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
#### The following ipython session demonstrates the issue

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# a simple population of integer events
population = np.array([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])

# let's make a histogram of the population
hist, edges = np.histogram(population, 4)

# lets turn the histogram into a dataframe using the edges as IntervalIndex
df = pd.DataFrame(data=hist, index=pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks(edges))

# The 3 events are indexable properly
print(df.loc[3]) # Works

# To see the event at 1 you need to apply some offset
print(df.loc[1+1e-6]) # Works but ugly

print(df.loc[1]) # fails
```
#### Problem description

The current behavior of `IntervalIndex` is that all the intervals have the same closing. It is however desireable to have an `IntervalIndex` like `[[0, 1], (1, 2], (2, 3]]` including the lower and the upper limit. 

`cut()` solves this by adding an arbitrary offset to the lower limit to make it loo like `[(-0.002, 1], (1, 2], (2, 3]]`. Then the lower interval is left open but the value 0.0 is still contained by the interval. 

This however results in the fact that the intervals contains also values like -0.001 which might be undesired as due to semantics negative values might be impossible. Histograms that allow events in the closed range `[0,1]`, forbidding negative values are impossible to model with a `pandas.IntervalIndex`.

#### Expected behavior.

I'd like to be able to do something like
```
idx = pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks(np.arange(10))
idx[0].set_closed('both')

title: .infer_objects() behavior is unintuitive when used with schemaless inputs

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example if possible

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

df = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({'a': ['a', 'b']}),
    pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 'c']}),
    pd.DataFrame({'a': [2, 3]})
]).reset_index(drop=True)

#int64
print(df.loc[[2,4,5]].infer_objects().dtypes)

#object
df2 = pd.read_html(StringIO(df.to_html(index=False)))[0]
print(df2.loc[[2,4,5]].infer_objects().dtypes)

#object
df3 = pd.read_csv(StringIO(df.to_csv(None, index=False)))
print(df3.loc[[2,4,5]].infer_objects().dtypes)

#int64
df4 = pd.read_csv(StringIO(df.loc[[2,4,5]].to_csv(None, index=False)))
print(df4.dtypes)
```
#### Problem description

`.infer_objects()` attempts only a soft conversion of columns classified as objects. When you read from a file type that doesn't come with any schema information like HTML tables or CSVs, the type inference system will read numbers in a mixed format column as strings. As a result, even after you filter to just the numeric rows, `.infer_objects()` will leave them as `object` instead of `int64`/`float64`, whereas dumping/rereading them will convert them to numbers.

It would be nice if `.infer_objects()` did something more like rerunning the standard type inference that happens in `pd.read_csv()` or `pd.read_html()` on the DataFrame since the read/write feels hacky, and having to do a whole lot of `pd.to_numeric()` on a wide frame is cumbersome, particularly if it's just a subset of the columns.

#### Expected Output

```
a    int64
dtype: object
```
for all above.

title: BUG: rolling skew/kurt returned NaN after a window emptied

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
- [x] closes #69037
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

`remove_skew` and `remove_kurt` decrement `nobs` and then immediately divide by it:

```cython
nobs[0] -= 1
n = <float64_t>(nobs[0])
delta = val - mean[0]
delta_n = delta / n
```

When the observation being removed is the last one in the window, `n` is `0.0`, so `delta_n` is `inf` or `nan` and the running `mean`, `m2`, `m3` (and `m4` for kurt) are poisoned for every window after it. That is why the reported series return `NaN` even where the final window itself has no missing values.

There is already a recompute path for exactly this kind of damage, but **it cannot fire here**. The guard is

```cython
if (fabs(m3_update) + fabs(m3[0])) * InvCondTol > fabs(new_m3):
    numerically_unstable[0] = True
```

and once `m3_update` is `NaN` that comparison is `NaN > NaN`, which is `False`. So the one case the guard exists to catch is the single case that slips past it silently.

The fix zeroes the moments when `nobs` reaches zero, since an empty window has no moments to carry forward. That addresses the root cause rather than widening the instability check.

This is the same shape as the already-fixed `.Rolling.corr`/`.Rolling.cov` bug in #65739 ("returning NaN for all later windows once a window contained no valid pairs").

Verified by rebuilding both ways. Before the change, both reproducers return `nan`; after, they match a fresh computation over the final window, and independently match scipy:

| | pandas | scipy |
|---|---|---|
| `skew` | `0.0` | `0.0` |
| `kurt` | `-0.41610621014935756` | `-0.41610621014935845` |

Added a parametrised regression test covering both functions. `pandas/tests/window/` is 9003 passed, 45 skipped, 1 xfailed.


This supersedes #69122, which the bot closed because I had commented `take` rather than `/take` on #69037. The issue is now assigned to me. The two CI failures there were an artefact of that closure, not of this change: the log shows `fatal: couldn't find remote ref refs/pull/69122/merge`, because the merge ref disappeared when the PR was closed mid-run.

title: BUG: preserve line breaks in ODS cells in to_excel/read_excel
body:
Hello Team!!!

The ODS writer put a newline character straight into the paragraph text of a cell.
XML collapses that to a space, so a multi-line cell written by pandas shows up as
one line in LibreOffice or Excel. Each line break is now written as a
`<text:line-break/>` element instead.

The reader had the matching gap: it ignored `<text:line-break/>` elements, and
joined the several `<text:p>` paragraphs that other spreadsheet applications use
for a multi-line cell without any separator. Both now yield `"\n"`, so a frame
round-trips through `to_excel`/`read_excel`, and a file written elsewhere reads
back with its line breaks intact.

This picks up #66237, which was closed as stale. The three review points there are
addressed: the qualified names in the reader are plain tuples rather than odf
element instances (that ran once per cell), the paragraph tracking is a boolean
rather than a counter, and the reader test builds its `.ods` file at runtime
instead of adding a binary fixture to the repo.

closes #55728

The reader half also covers what was reported in #53924, which was closed at the time as an upstream issue, so that one is referenced rather than closed here.

title: Surprising type conversion when iterating

labels.name: python_scalars

body:
#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example if possible

```python
>>> df = pandas.DataFrame({'ints': range(5)})
>>> type(df.iloc[:, 0][0])
<class 'numpy.int64'>
>>> type(list(df.iloc[:, 0])[0])
<class 'int'>
```
#### Problem description

When iterating over a series, values are being converted to closest Python type and not left as an original type. This is problematic because it is a surprising change and leads to data manipulation one does not expect. One would hope that you can easily get what you stored into a dataframe out when iterating and not a variation of it.

The issue is that iterating uses internally numpy's [`tolist`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy-1.14.0/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.tolist.html) which has this behavior. This is problematic for two reasons: it constructs the whole list first in memory (#20783) and converts to "closest Python type".

>>> type(df.iloc[:, 0][0])

body:
Currently there is some inconsistency around the scalar type returned from a `Series` aggregation, both in terms of whether it is a numpy or python type, as well as different behavior for an empty `Series` - see table below. Normally this isn't a big deal as the numpy types mostly behave like the python type, but can be an issue with serialization, which is where I ran into this. Is the desired behavior to make all of these python types?
function type type_empty
sum <class 'float'> <class 'int'>
mean <class 'float'> <class 'float'>
median <class 'float'> <class 'float'>
count <class 'numpy.int32'> <class 'numpy.int32'>
var <class 'float'> <class 'float'>
std <class 'float'> <class 'float'>
sem <class 'numpy.float64'> <class 'numpy.float64'>
nunique <class 'int'> <class 'int'>
prod <class 'numpy.float64'> <class 'float'>
min <class 'numpy.float64'> <class 'float'>
max <class 'numpy.float64'> <class 'float'>
Code for table ```python fxs = ['sum', 'mean', 'median', 'count', 'var', 'std', 'sem', 'nunique', 'prod', 'min', 'max'] s = pd.Series([1., 2., 3.]) s_empty = pd.Series([], dtype='f8') data = [] for f in fxs: row = dict(function=f) res = getattr(s, f)() row['type'] = type(res) res = getattr(s_empty, f)() row['type_empty'] = type(res) data.append(row) pd.DataFrame(data).to_html(index=False) ```

body:
Follow-up on https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/22762 which added `_reduce` to the ExtensionArray interface and added an implementation for IntegerArray.

Currently, for that IntegerArray we special case 'sum', 'min', 'max' to make sure they return ints (because the underlying implementation can be based on a float array, depending whether there are missing values). 

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/08e27520eb56927f96cf9b0f0f3fb11eca480abe/pandas/core/arrays/integer.py#L549-L554

That basic check has the following "problem": 

- Some reductions with return python integers, others will return numpy scalars. Accessing single elements also gives numpy scalars.


```
In [3]: pd.Series(pd.core.arrays.integer_array([1, None, 3])).mean()
Out[3]: 2.0

In [4]: type(_)
Out[4]: numpy.float64

In [5]: pd.Series(pd.core.arrays.integer_array([1, None, 3])).sum()
Out[5]: 4

In [6]: type(_)
Out[6]: int

In [7]: type(pd.Series(pd.core.arrays.integer_array([1, None, 3]))[0])
Out[7]: numpy.int64
```

title: QST: Subject: User Experience Issue - NumPy Types in DataFrame Results Breaking Readability

labels.name: python_scalars
labels.description: Python scalars vs numpy scalars in results

body:
### Research

- [x] I have searched the [[pandas] tag](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/pandas) on StackOverflow for similar questions.

- [x] I have asked my usage related question on [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com).


### Link to question on StackOverflow

None

### Question about pandas

ssue Description
TL;DR: Since pandas 2.0+, .tolist() and similar methods return NumPy types instead of native Python types, severely impacting user experience and data readability.
Problem Example
Before (pandas 1.x):
```
pythondf.index.tolist()
# Returns: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # Clean, readable
```

Now (pandas 2.x):

```
pythondf.index.tolist()
# Returns: [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(2), np.int64(3), np.int64(4)]  # Verbose, confusing
```

Impact on User Experience

Poor Readability: Results are cluttered with np.int64(), np.float64() wrappers
Debugging Nightmare: Harder to quickly scan and understand data
Display Issues: When printing or logging, output is unnecessarily verbose
User Confusion: Many users don't understand why they're seeing NumPy types
Breaking Change: Existing code expectations broken without clear migration path

Current Workarounds Are Painful
Users now need to write additional code for basic operations:
python# Instead of simple:
indices = df.index.tolist()

# We need:
indices = [int(x) for x in df.index.tolist()]
The Core Problem
DataFrames are meant for data analysis and exploration. The primary use case is human-readable data inspection, not performance-critical numerical computation at the .tolist() level.
Suggested Solutions

Add a parameter: .tolist(native_types=True) (default True for user-facing methods)
Separate methods: Keep .tolist() for NumPy types, add .tolist_clean() for Python types
Configuration option: Allow users to set pandas behavior globally
Revert the change: Prioritize user experience over marginal performance gains

Why This Matters
Pandas' strength has always been its ease of use and intuitive behavior. This change sacrifices user experience for performance gains that most users don't need when calling .tolist().
The goal of data analysis is insight, not fighting with data types.
Request
Please consider reverting this behavior or providing a simple, built-in solution. The current situation forces every pandas user to write boilerplate code for basic data inspection.
Thank you for maintaining this incredible library. I hope we can find a solution that balances performance with the user-friendly experience that makes pandas great.

Environment:

pandas: 2.2.3
numpy: 1.26.4
Impact: All DataFrame operations returning lists

title: BUG: DataFrame.to_dict(orient="records") does not return native types with frame constructed from pyarrow Scalars

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

labels.name: python_scalars
labels.description: Python scalars vs numpy scalars in results

body:
On 1.2 master:
```python
In [15]: import pandas as pd
    ...: import pyarrow as pa
    ...: 
    ...: df = pd.DataFrame({'a': pa.scalar(7)}, index=['a'])
    ...: print(type(df.to_dict(orient="records")[0]['a']))
    ...: 
<class 'pyarrow.lib.Int64Scalar'>
```
This is inconsistent with the corresponding op for NumPy backed types (xref #37571)
```
In [13]: import pandas as pd
    ...: import numpy as np
    ...: 
    ...: df = pd.DataFrame({'a': np.int(7)}, index=['a'])
    ...: print(type(df.to_dict(orient="records")[0]['a']))
    ...: 
<class 'int'>
```

In general we'd like `to_dict` to return Python native types if possible.

title: BUG: keep left/right index dtype in Index.join on mismatched dtypes (GH#63371)

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
closes #63371

When the two indexes have different dtypes, `Index.join` casts both to a common dtype and returned the result in that dtype even for `how="left"`/`"right"`, where every value comes from one side. The join still runs in the common dtype; the result is now rebuilt from the kept side via its indexer, so it keeps that side's dtype (including 1-to-many joins). `inner`/`outer` are unchanged.

This follows the thread's consensus to fix left joins generally rather than special-casing `str.cat`, and carries through `align`, `DataFrame.join`, `merge` and `str.cat`. It also removes an asymmetry where `ser1.align(ser2, join="left")` gave a `str` index on one result and `object` on the other. The empty-index path already kept the left dtype.

Behavior change: 14 existing tests asserted the old cast and are updated.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5 (high)`), used to investigate the issue, write the fix and tests, and draft this description.

Part of #64266.

Follow-up to #68461 for `Index.__getitem__`. This is the one remaining place where index-derived values leaked NumPy scalars. It also covers:

title: BUG: merge_asof says "tolerance must be positive" but accepts tolerance=0

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

left = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 5, 10], "left_val": ["a", "b", "c"]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 6, 10], "right_val": ["A", "B", "C"]})

# tolerance=0 is accepted and meaningful: exact-match-only
print(pd.merge_asof(left, right, on="a", tolerance=0))
#     a left_val right_val
# 0   1        a         A
# 1   5        b       NaN   <- no exact match within 0
# 2  10        c         C

# but a negative tolerance is rejected with a message that claims 0 is invalid too:
pd.merge_asof(left, right, on="a", tolerance=-1)
# MergeError: tolerance must be positive
```

### Issue Description

`merge_asof` accepts `tolerance=0` (which means exact-match-only, a meaningful asof semantic), but the error raised for an invalid `tolerance` says it `must be positive`. The three guards in `_MergeOperation`/`_AsOfMerge` reject only strictly-negative values:

```python
if self.tolerance < Timedelta(0):
    raise MergeError("tolerance must be positive")
...
if self.tolerance < 0:
    raise MergeError("tolerance must be positive")
```

So `0` is accepted, yet "must be positive" (which means `> 0`) excludes it. The message is inconsistent with the guard.

### Expected Behavior

The message should say `tolerance must be non-negative`, matching the values the guard actually accepts.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on `main` and pandas 3.0.3.

</details>

title: BUG: MultiIndex.set_levels/set_codes give self-contradictory "must be list-like" error for a nested value with a scalar level

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", 1), ("b", 2)], names=["l", "n"])
mi.set_levels([["x", "y"]], level=0)
```

### Issue Description

`MultiIndex.set_levels` (and `set_codes`) raise a self-contradictory message when a **single, scalar** `level` is paired with a **nested** (list-of-lists) value:

```
TypeError: Levels must be list-like
```

The value `[["x", "y"]]` *is* list-like — that's precisely why control reaches this branch. In `_require_listlike` (`pandas/core/indexes/multi.py`), the scalar-level branch first rejects a non-list-like `arr` with `"must be list-like"`, and then rejects a *nested* `arr` (a list of lists) with the **same** string, which is a copy-paste of the first message:

```python
if level is not None and not is_list_like(level):
    if not is_list_like(arr):
        raise TypeError(f"{arrname} must be list-like")          # arr is not list-like — message correct
    if len(arr) > 0 and is_list_like(arr[0]):
        raise TypeError(f"{arrname} must be list-like")          # arr IS list-like (nested) — message wrong
```

For a scalar level the value must be a *flat* list-like, so the second message should say that, not repeat "must be list-like".

### Expected Behavior

The nested-value case should raise a message that names the real constraint, e.g.:

```
TypeError: Levels must be list-like, not a list of lists-like
```

which mirrors the existing `"must be list of lists-like"` message used for the list-valued `level` branch.

It seems that the `PandasArray.__array_ufunc__` implementation assumes the results of the ufunc will go into the same type of array as the input, in this case a `StringArray`, which produces an error when the results are not a string. (Credit to @jorisvandenbossche in a comment on pygeos/pygeos#338.)

#### Expected Output

If we pass a numpy array into `pygeos.from_wkt` it works fine and produces an output array of geometries.

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.array(["POINT (0 0)"])
array(['POINT (0 0)'], dtype='<U11')
>>> pygeos.from_wkt(np.array(["POINT (0 0)"]))
array([<pygeos.Geometry POINT (0 0)>], dtype=object)
```

I would expect the same output using a `StringArray`.

```python
>>> pygeos.from_wkt(pd.array(["POINT (0 0)"]))
array([<pygeos.Geometry POINT (0 0)>], dtype=object)
```

title: API: with CoW, should every new Series/DataFrame object also have its own new Index objects?

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
Related to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/53529, about index labels still being shared after an indexing operation.

Currently, a shallow copy of a DataFrame/Series only creates a new DataFrame/Series object, while pointing to the same data and index objects under the hood. Quoting the docstring:

> When ``deep=False``, a new object will be created without copying
        the calling object's data or index (only references to the data
        and index are copied).

and one of the examples in the docstring:

```python
>>> s = pd.Series([1, 2], index=["a", "b"])
>>> deep = s.copy()
>>> shallow = s.copy(deep=False)

# Shallow copy shares data and index with original.
>>> s is shallow
False
>>> s.values is shallow.values and s.index is shallow.index
True
```

So apart from being the long-standing behaviour, it's also clearly documentation that the Index objects (for row index and columns) are identical in the returned shallow copy. 

However, under Copy-on-Write, we now updated the behaviour of a shallow copy to no longer propagate mutations to the _values_ of the Series/DataFrame, but still returning a new Series/DataFrame with the shared memory, but protected with a reference track to ensure we will copy later on if needed. 
So the question is, for shallow copies like this, **when CoW is enabled, should we also protect from sharing mutable state in the index/columns attributes** of the Series/DataFrame?

Current behaviour:

```python
>>> s = pd.Series([1, 2], index=["a", "b"])
>>> shallow = s.copy(deep=False)
>>> shallow.index.name = "some_new_name"
>>> s
some_new_name      # <-- modifying shallow copy also modified the parent series
a    1
b    2
dtype: int64
```

My proposal would be to extend the notion of "changing one object never updates another object" under CoW that we currently apply to the data values, to also apply this to the Index mutable state.

This can easily be achieved by also shallow copying the Index objects when shallow copying a DataFrame/Series. 

**How to shallow copy an Index?**
While the Index class also has a copy method with a `deep` argument, and thus one can do `idx.copy(deep=False)` to get a new Index object sharing the same data (and this option is actually the default for Index), there is also a `idx.view()` method, which essentially does the same, but also sets the `_id` attribute of the Index, ensuring equality testing still pass the fast path check for identity (`idx1.is_(idx2) is True`). 
We can probably use a view instead of an actual shallow copy with `copy(deep=False)`, which will ensure we keep a faster path in several places where we check for Index equality between objects.

**Consequence beyond the copy method?**
It seems we actually have quite some places that are currently returning identical index objects shared by multiple objects, beyond just the typical shallow copy case. Those could / should all change with the proposal above. Some examples:

* Any method that currently returns a new Series/DataFrame that preserves the shape. Those that return a shallow copy with CoW will automatically get updated by changing the behaviour of `copy(deep=False)`, such as:

    ```python
    >>> s = pd.Series([1, 2])
    >>> s2 = s.infer_objects()
    >>> s2.index is s.index    # current behaviour, would become False
    True
    ```

  but also any object that returns new data (and currently doesn't care about CoW) but preserves the shape currently typically reuses the index object and should probably be updated?

    ```python
    >>> s = pd.Series([1, 2])
    >>> s2 = s.diff()
    >>> s2.index is s.index    # current behaviour, would become False
    True
    ```

* Binary / unary operations preserve the index in the result:

    ```python
    >>> s = pd.Series([1, 2])
    >>> s2= s + 1
    >>> s2.index is s.index   # current behaviour, would become False
    True
    ```
* Reindexing with an index also would end up with not exactly that index object but with a shallow copy of it:

    ```python
    >>> s = pd.Series([1, 2])
    >>> idx = pd.Index([0, 1, 2])
    >>> s2 = s.reindex(idx)
    >>> s2.index is idx   # current behaviour, would become False
    True
    ```

* Maybe more controversially or more surprising for users if we would do this, but what about constructors where you pass an Index object? 

    ```python
    >>> idx = pd.Index([0, 1, 2])
    >>> s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c"], index=idx)
    >>> s.index is idx    # should this be False as well?
    True
    ```

  Here it might be more logical to use _exactly_ that object (and not create a shallow copy of it)? (but that will mean propagating changes if you passed the index object of an existing Series/DataFrame)

title: BUG: allow timezone-aware subtypes in IntervalArray arrow conversion
body:
- [x] closes #67753
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

Following up on the suggestion in the issue to take the subtype from `storage_type` rather than from the serialized metadata.

There were three places that had to change before a timezone-aware interval could make the trip out to arrow and back.

**Writing.** `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` resolved the arrow type with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype`, which only understands numpy dtypes, so any `ExtensionDtype` subtype was rejected outright. It now uses the existing `to_pyarrow_type` helper, which already maps `DatetimeTZDtype` to `pyarrow.timestamp(unit, tz)`. The `TypeError` message is unchanged for subtypes that genuinely cannot be converted.

**Reconstructing the extension type.** `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_deserialize__` rebuilt the subtype by feeding the serialized string to `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for a parametrized type, so a file written with a tz subtype failed on read with `ValueError: No type alias for timestamp[us, tz=europe/brussels]`. It now reads the subtype off `storage_type.field("left").type`.

I left `__arrow_ext_serialize__` writing the subtype string unchanged. It is no longer read, but keeping it means files written by this version still deserialize on older pandas for every subtype that already worked, so this is only additive on the metadata side.

**Reading.** `IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` passed the subtype to `np.asarray`, which cannot interpret an `ExtensionDtype`:

```
TypeError: Cannot interpret 'datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]' as a data type
```

It now defers to the subtype's own `__from_arrow__` when the subtype is not a numpy dtype.

One thing worth flagging, since it is the least obvious part of the diff. Handing a tz-aware `DatetimeArray` to `pyarrow.array` makes pyarrow fall back on `Series.values`, which drops the timezone and emits `Pandas4Warning`. That warning is an error under the test suite's filters, so it had to be dealt with rather than left. The backing values are converted and cast to the parametrized arrow type instead, which is valid because `_ndarray` holds UTC for tz-aware data, exactly what a cast to a tz-aware timestamp expects. I checked the values round-trip identically rather than relying on that reasoning alone. This is only on the `ExtensionDtype` branch, so the numpy path is untouched.

Testing:

`test_arrow_array_tz_subtype` is new and covers the write plus a serialize/deserialize cycle of the extension type. The two existing round-trip tests gain a `datetime64[ns, tz]` parametrisation; `test_arrow_table_roundtrip_without_metadata` is the interesting one, since stripping the schema metadata forces reconstruction through `__arrow_ext_deserialize__`, which is the path that was broken.

All three fail on main and pass with this change.

```
pytest pandas/tests/arrays/interval/test_interval_pyarrow.py     ->  12 passed
   (on main: 3 failed, 9 passed)
pytest pandas/tests/arrays/interval/ pandas/tests/extension/test_interval.py pandas/tests/dtypes/
                                                                 ->  6304 passed, 71 skipped, 11 xfailed
pytest pandas/tests/io/test_parquet.py                           ->  86 passed, 46 skipped, 1 xfailed
ruff check / ruff format --check (0.16.1)                        ->  All checks passed
```

The one error in `test_parquet.py` is `test_parquet_read_from_url`, which needs network access I do not have.

I also confirmed end to end that a tz-aware interval column now survives an actual parquet write and read with its dtype intact, and that `int64`, `float64` and naive `datetime64` intervals still round-trip unchanged.

Written with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5); I reviewed the change and ran the tests above.

title: BUG: IntervalArray.__arrow_array__ rejects ExtensionDtype subtypes, and ArrowIntervalType metadata cannot round-trip them
body:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

ser = pd.Series(pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks(pd.date_range("2012", periods=5, tz="Europe/Brussels")))
pa.array(ser)
# TypeError: Conversion to arrow with subtype 'datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]' is not supported
```

### Issue Description

`IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` computes the arrow subtype with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype(self.dtype.subtype)`, which raises for any `ExtensionDtype` subtype — including `DatetimeTZDtype`, which `IntervalArray` otherwise supports.

GH-64297 fixed only the read side (`IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__`), so an interval-with-tz column can now be read from arrow but still cannot be written.

Lifting the restriction is not just a subtype-lookup change: `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_serialize__` stores `str(self.subtype)` and deserializes with `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for `timestamp[us, tz=Europe/Brussels]`. Simply allowing the write produces parquet that fails to read back:

```
ValueError: No type alias for timestamp[us, tz=europe/brussels]
```

So a fix needs a metadata-format change on the registered `pandas.interval` extension type, which has cross-implementation compatibility implications and seems worth its own discussion.

### Expected Behavior

`pa.array(ser)` succeeds for a tz-aware interval subtype, and the result round-trips through parquet back to the same `IntervalDtype`.

title: DOC: Clarify rolling window behavior with negative offset strings and froward rolling windows
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.rolling.html
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rolling.html

### Documentation problem

There is no documentation on a forward-looking rolling windows with offset strings.
I often need to make a forward-looking rolling window on datetime data. To do so, I've tried different ways and the only one I found was using two `.iloc[::-1]` (reverse the series order) with the rolling occurring in the middle. 

nb: Because the data has irregular DateTimeIndex (not every 2 hours for example), I can not use the `pd.api.indexers.FixedForwardWindowIndexer` 

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

fake_data = [1, 5, 4, 6, 7, 65, 21, 5, np.nan, 56, 1]
random_index = pd.to_datetime([
    '2025-01-01 00:22:00', '2025-01-01 02:31:00',
    '2025-01-01 05:00:00', '2025-01-01 07:18:00',
    '2025-01-01 09:42:00', '2025-01-01 12:29:00',
    '2025-01-01 14:38:00', '2025-01-01 16:59:00',
    '2025-01-01 19:32:00', '2025-01-01 22:03:00',
    '2025-01-02 00:25:00'
])
ser = pd.Series(fake_data, index=random_index)

out = pd.DataFrame({
    "raw": ser,
    "5h": ser.rolling("5h").max(),
    "-5h": ser.rolling("-5h").max(),
    "5h_inv": ser.iloc[::-1].rolling("5h").max().iloc[::-1],
    "-5h_inv": ser.iloc[::-1].rolling("-5h").max().iloc[::-1],
})
print(out)
```
```
                      raw    5h   -5h  5h_inv  -5h_inv
2025-01-01 00:22:00   1.0   1.0   1.0     5.0      1.0
2025-01-01 02:31:00   5.0   5.0   5.0     6.0      5.0
2025-01-01 05:00:00   4.0   5.0   4.0     7.0      4.0
2025-01-01 07:18:00   6.0   6.0   6.0     7.0      6.0
2025-01-01 09:42:00   7.0   7.0   7.0    65.0      7.0
2025-01-01 12:29:00  65.0  65.0  65.0    65.0     65.0
2025-01-01 14:38:00  21.0  65.0  21.0    21.0     21.0
2025-01-01 16:59:00   5.0  65.0   5.0     5.0      5.0
2025-01-01 19:32:00   NaN  21.0   NaN    56.0      NaN
2025-01-01 22:03:00  56.0  56.0  56.0    56.0     56.0
2025-01-02 00:25:00   1.0  56.0   1.0     1.0      1.0
```

This is what this shows :
- The behavior of negative offset strings (e.g., "-5h") in Series.rolling() and DataFrame.rolling() is not documented and produces counterintuitive results. They don't inverse the rolling window, the window just collaps into 1 element windows. The negative int values are actually prohibited by the function (`ValueError: window must be an integer 0 or greater`) so I would expect the same to be for offset stings. > Maybe a bug ?

- Using .iloc[::-1] to invert the series before performing the rolling window (suggested by https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51740121/pandas-rolling-how-to-roll-from-left-to-right-or-from-up-to-down) works. But, you still have to use a positive offset even if your dataset is anticrhonological order when the rolling occurs.


### Suggested fix for documentation

For me, adding something like the following text on the examples (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/v3.0.2/pandas/core/generic.py#L12058-L12109) would do the tricks:

        Rolling sum with forward-looking windows with 3 seconds

        >>> df_time.iloc[::-1].rolling("3s").sum().iloc[::-1]
                       B
        2013-01-01 09:00:00  1.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:02  3.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:03  2.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:05  4.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:06  4.0

        Note: Negative offset strings (e.g., ``"-5h"``) do not create forward-looking
        windows and should be avoided. They collapse to single-element windows.

import pandas as pd

title: BUG: DataFrame axis=1 reductions accumulated in each block's own dtype (GH#51474)
body:
Repairs a silent-wrong-answer defect in the block-wise `axis=1` reduction fast path added by GH-65105 (for GH-51474). That PR is unreleased, so the wrong answers never reached users and there is no *Bug fixes* whatsnew entry.

`DataFrame._reduce_axis1` reduced each block in that block's **own** dtype and combined the per-block partials with a numpy ufunc, where the transpose path it replaced reduced in the common dtype of all blocks. On current `main`:

| frame | `axis=1` | `df.T` (correct) |
|---|---|---|
| int64 + float `sum` | `-9.22e18` | `9.22e18` |
| uint64 + float `sum` | `0.5` | `1.84e19` |
| int64 + uint8 `sum` | `4.6e18` (float64) | `4611686018427387906` (int64) |
| float32 + float `sum` | `inf` | `6.0e38` |
| bool + complex64 `mean` | `1.0` | `1+1j` |

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [2**62], "b": [2**62], "c": [0.5]})
df.sum(axis=1)  # -9.223372036854776e+18
df.T.sum()      #  9.223372036854776e+18
```

Compute one cross-block accumulation dtype with `np.result_type` and `astype` each block to it before reducing. For `mean` the accumulator mirrors `nanmean`: float and complex accumulate in their own dtype and widen only at the division, everything else accumulates in float64. `mean` also stops unconditionally casting the combined result to float64, which is what discarded the imaginary part.

Two places then widen the combined result before writing a missing value into it — the `mean` division and the `min_count` null-out. Both now go through one helper that reproduces what `nanops` produces there (float64 for an integer or bool result, complex128 for complex64), and the `min_count` row count is gated on `skipna` so it matches the mask `_maybe_get_mask` actually builds. Without that gate a `complex64` frame reduced with `min_count` and `skipna=False` came back as `complex128` where `df.T` gives `complex64`.

`find_common_type` cannot serve as the accumulation dtype here: it returns `object` as soon as a bool block is present, which would switch the fix off for exactly the bool+numeric frames that reach this path.

There **is** an *Other API changes* entry, for a behavior change GH-65105 itself introduced and did not document: these reductions on a bool + NumPy-numeric mix no longer reduce through `object`, so an integer `sum` or `prod` can overflow and a float result can lose precision where Python's arbitrary-precision arithmetic was exact, and `min`/`max` on a bool + complex mix return a complex result where they previously raised `TypeError`.

Verified against the transpose oracle, the `axis=0` result on the transposed frame, and the single-block frame `df.astype(np.result_type(*dtypes))`, over roughly 260k dtype × block-layout × method × `skipna` × `min_count` cells, with no value or dtype divergence introduced against `main`. Each of the five families above fails if the fix is reverted, and 18 of the 20 new test cells fail on `main`. The residual divergences are two pre-existing families: `min`/`max` still combine per-block partials and so can land on a different dtype than the transpose, and bool-mixed pairs where the transpose itself gives `object`.

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow) deletes a pre-existing file it cannot open
body:
`DataFrame.to_parquet` (pyarrow engine) raised `PermissionError` and *deleted* the pre-existing file when the local destination was one pandas could not open for writing — a `0o444` file, or one owned by another user in a writable directory.

`pyarrow.parquet.write_table` does `except Exception: os.remove(where)` whenever `where` is path-like, and that fires even when the write never got past *opening* the destination. GH-65811 dropped the pandas-side `get_handle()` open for local paths (completing GH-64590), so pyarrow began opening the path itself; before that, `get_handle` raised first and the file was untouched.

The fix hands pyarrow a `pa.OSFile` that pandas opened, so `where` is not path-like and the cleanup cannot fire. `pa.OSFile` opens in C++ rather than through `builtins.open`, so both properties GH-65811 bought are preserved — no `get_handle`, and a single native open of the destination — and its tests pass unchanged. This also brings `to_parquet` back in line with `to_csv`, `to_feather` and `to_orc`, which all leave the file intact here.

No whatsnew entry: GH-64590 and GH-65811 are both unreleased, so the data loss never shipped.
