title: BUG: MultiIndex reports the wrong problem for an over-long key (GH#45762)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
closes #45762

A MultiIndex key with more entries than the index has levels was reported as an unsorted index — `df.loc[pd.IndexSlice[2:4, 8:10, 15:19], :]` on a 2-level index asked the user to lexsort an index that was already sorted. Other spellings of the same over-long key leaked a raw `IndexError: list index out of range`.

All three sites that can be handed such a key now raise the `KeyError` that `MultiIndex.get_loc` already uses for an over-long tuple:

- `get_locs`, reached by `.loc` with a nested tuple (the reported repro);
- `_get_loc_level`, reached by `get_loc_level` and `xs`, which leaked the `IndexError` when the key held a slice;
- `_partial_tup_index`, reached by `slice_locs`, `get_slice_bound` and `df.loc[tuple:tuple]`, which gave the same misleading lexsort-depth message even on a fully lexsorted index.

`get_locs`' pre-existing Ellipsis check moves above the new guard so that more specific message is not shadowed.

Trailing entries that consume no level are discounted from the length, because `.loc` passes the column selector down: `df.loc[:, key, :]` reaches `get_locs` and `df.loc["a", :, :]` reaches `_get_loc_level` with more entries than the index has levels. The rule differs per site, which the comments explain — `get_locs` also discounts a trailing bool indexer, since its body resolves one positionally, while `_get_loc_level` resolves a bool indexer against its level and so cannot.

The lexsort-depth message keeps its real job: a key the index genuinely is too unsorted for still reports the depth, covered by a new test alongside the existing ones.

Found while investigating, not fixed here: `df.loc[[("a", 1, 4)]]` silently reads *and writes* row `("a", 1)` rather than raising, because `MultiIndex.get_indexer` truncates an over-long tuple to the index's depth. That is a silent-wrong-data bug in a different mechanism and wants its own issue.

title: BUG: the logical ufuncs were not rejected against datetimelike data (GH#68524)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
`np.logical_and`, `np.logical_or`, `np.logical_xor` and `np.logical_not` returned a result for
datetime-like data, where `&`, `|` and `^` raise `TypeError`:

```python
pi = pd.period_range("2016-01-01", periods=2, freq="D")

np.logical_and(pd.Series([True, False]), pd.Series(pi))
# 0    2016-01-01
# 1         False
# dtype: object          <- a Period in a logical result

pd.Series([True, False]) & pd.Series(pi)
# TypeError: operation 'and_' not supported for dtype 'bool' with dtype 'period[D]'
```

Values NumPy converts to `object` — `PeriodDtype`, timezone-aware `datetime64`, and several
temporal `ArrowDtype`s — came back in the result themselves; the rest were truth-tested on their
integer representation, which made the epoch falsy and `NaT` truthy. `np.logical_or.reduce` and
datetime-like scalar operands leaked the same way.

GH-68452 made the operator spelling raise for every datetime-like operand and added
`disallow_datetimelike_logical_op` with its `_is_datetimelike_array` predicate. The logical
ufuncs were missed by it because they are not in `UFUNC_ALIASES` — they are deliberately not
aliased, since for integer data `np.logical_and` and `&` genuinely differ. This is the ufunc half
of that change: it adds `disallow_datetimelike_logical_ufunc` beside the existing helper, reusing
its dtype predicate, and calls it from the seven `__array_ufunc__` implementations that can reach
datetime-like values — `arraylike.array_ufunc`, `ExtensionArray`, `Index`, `SparseArray`,
`BaseMaskedArray`, `NumpyExtensionArray`, and `ArrowExtensionArray`'s GH-62506 numeric fast path.
Four of those never reach `ExtensionArray.__array_ufunc__` at all and the arrow fast path returns
before it does, so a guard on the base class alone does not cover them.

Note this makes plain `datetime64`/`timedelta64` raise where they previously returned bools.
That is the same trade GH-68452 already made for `&`/`|`/`^` in this release, and it is what
makes timezone-naive and timezone-aware data agree.

Two cases deliberately do *not* match `&`. Arrow boxes any NA-like scalar as a typed null, so
`pd.Series([True, False], dtype="bool[pyarrow]") & pd.NaT` returns `[<NA>, False]` where every
other backend raises; the ufunc rejects it, which is also what fixes the `np.datetime64("NaT")`
spelling of the same null — that one was truth-tested on its int64 and came back `True`. A
datetime-like scalar against an `object`-dtype operand also raises, where `&` truth-tests it; the
ufunc never gave the `&` answer there either, it broadcast the scalar into a `datetime64` result.
The whatsnew names the arrow divergence; the `&` side of it is left for its own change.

The guard steps aside for the whole call whenever any operand is one pandas hands the ufunc off
to. That holds in both directions: a third-party array carrying a real NumPy `M8`/`m8` dtype is
not rejected on its behalf, and a datetime-like *pandas* operand does not take the call back from
such an operand. Deferral is of the whole operation, not of the deferring operand's share of it,
so anything narrower would make the result depend on argument order. An `__array_ufunc__` of its
own is not enough to qualify, though: every `_HANDLED_TYPES` contains `np.ndarray`, so pandas
computes against an `ndarray` subclass rather than deferring to it, and `Index` and the bare
arrays compute against `pd.NA` as well — both stay guarded. The test is `issubclass` on the
operand's type rather than `isinstance`, so that deciding this never reads an attribute off an
operand that answers every attribute, such as a `pd.col` expression.

`_is_datetimelike_dtype` also stops reading `.kind` unconditionally, so an operand whose dtype is
neither a NumPy nor a pandas dtype — a polars `Series`, say — no longer crashes inside pandas,
whether that dtype has no `kind` or one that is not a string. That reached `&`/`|`/`^` as merged
in GH-68452 too, not just the ufuncs added here.

title: BUG: Index.insert silently truncating a value into a sparse subtype

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
`pd.Index(SparseArray([1, 2, 3])).insert(0, 1.5)` returned `Index([1, 1, 2, 3], dtype='Sparse[int64, 0]')`, where the dense control widens to `float64`. `SparseArray` has no `insert` override, so it falls through to `ExtensionArray.insert`, which relies on `_from_sequence` raising for an item the dtype cannot hold — `SparseArray._from_sequence` coerces instead. Every subtype was affected: `2**63` wrapped to `INT64_MIN`, a `Timestamp` was stored as an integer, and a bool subtype turned `1.5`, `"x"` and a `Timestamp` alike into `True`.

`SparseArray.insert` now validates the item against the subtype and raises, so `Index.insert`'s existing widening arm runs. Two supporting fixes are needed for that arm to return a usable result, and each fixes a user-visible bug of its own:

- `SparseDtype._get_common_dtype` resolves the widened subtype with `find_common_type` rather than `np_find_common_type`. Otherwise `insert(0, True)` raises, because numpy resolves bool + int64 to int64 and `SparseDtype` rejects the bool fill value for it — as it already did for `concat`, `Index.union`, `Index.append` and `DataFrame.combine_first` on that pair.
- `SparseArray._concat_same_type` builds its result with `_simple_new` rather than the constructor, whose `sanitize_array` re-infers an object array of datetimelikes back to `M8`. Otherwise an all-fill-value index (empty `sp_values`) hit the same `ValueError`.

Missing-value inserts are out of scope: a sparse subtype that cannot hold NA still raises or coerces, which needs `ensure_dtype_can_hold_na` to become sparse-aware.

title: BUG: read_csv with integer `names` treats integer `dtype` keys as both label and position

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
Copying from my comment at https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62242#issuecomment-5424056917

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

data = "01,02\n02,03"

# reading by default parses as numbers
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=["a", "b"]).dtypes
a    int64
b    int64
dtype: object
# but with dtype dict we can override this to stay as string
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=["a", "b"], dtype={"a": str}).dtypes
a      str
b    int64
dtype: object
# however when using integer key, both columns stay as string
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=[1, 2], dtype={1: str}).dtypes
1    str
2    str
dtype: object
```

It looks like the `1` is both applied as a label and positionally?


---

When column names (manually specified `names=`) are integers, `dtype={...}` dict keys are incorrectly applied both as column labels and as positional indices, so a single item in the dict can cause a conversion of multiple columns.

As a sidenote, with the python engine, this works correctly:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=[1, 2], dtype={1: str}, engine="python").dtypes
1      str
2    int64
dtype: object
```
---

This is caused by the code here:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4e54dd017d57ae524f74cee9445750c649633809/pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx#L1742-L1751

where for `i=0, name=1` we find a match by name, and the for column `i=1, name=2` we find a match by position, regardless that the key has a match by name as well

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

branches = pd.DataFrame(
    data={
        "name": ["river_1", "river_2", "river_3", "river_4", "river_4-1", "pipe_51_E11", "pipe_51_E12", "pipe_52_E0"],
        "branchtype": [0,0,0,0,0,2,2,2],
        "sourceCompartmentName": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, "manhole_987_generated", "manhole_988_generated", "manhole_989_generated"],
        "targetCompartmentName": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, "manhole_988_generated",
                                  "manhole_967_generated", "manhole_990_generated"],
    },
index=[0,1,2,3,4,1002,1003,1004],
)

# print the dtype, str in pandas 2 (?) and <StringDtype(na_value=nan)> in pandas 3
# using repr since StringDtype is also printed as str otherwise
print(branches["sourceCompartmentName"].dtype.__repr__())

# does not work in pandas 3, since None is interpreted as the dype na_value
branches = branches.replace(np.nan, None)
# a useful workaround that does work
# branches = branches.replace([np.nan], [None])

print(branches.to_dict("records"))
```

### Issue Description

Context: Originally reported in https://github.com/Deltares/HYDROLIB-core/issues/1107. In our code, we would regularly initiating an object of some class (hydrolib-core BranchModel) with some parameters set to `None`. These are then considered empty/notset, consistent with many other class/method argument defaults.

This is why we need to have `None` values in our dataframes with string dtype columns (and not np.nan values). Pandas 2 supports both these values, pandas 3 implemented stringdtype to be more robust. This has a na_value argument/property, which is set to np.nan per default. This na_value cannot be set to `None` since it is considered an empty argument (which sort of makes sense to me).

However, we noticed that in pandas 3 it is actually possible to convert `np.nan` to `None`  by adding square brackets:
- `branches.replace(np.nan, None)` does not replace the np.nan values
- `branches.replace([np.nan], [None])` replaces the np.nan values with None

This is quite nice for our usecase, since we can use this as a workaround. However, this seems inconsistent and might be considered as a bug. If this is intended behaviour, that is also fine since we can then trust that the behaviour will not change in the future.

### Expected Behavior

One of these two:
- consistent behaviour between the two methods
- confirmation that this is intended and will not change in the forseeable future. Or any other suggestion to avoid the need for a workaround.

labels.name: Awaiting Review

body:
Fixes #66080

When `to_html(render_links=True, escape=True)` is used, the visible cell text is HTML-escaped but the generated `href` attribute uses the raw unescaped URL. This breaks the HTML when the URL contains double quotes or ampersands.

This escapes the URL value before placing it in `href`, matching the escaping applied to visible cell text.

title: BUG: setting SparseDtype integers into an integer Series raised AttributeError

labels.name: Awaiting Review

body:
Setting sparse integer values into a plain integer Series raised before anything was written:

```python
ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
ser[:] = pd.arrays.SparseArray([4, 0, 6])
# AttributeError: 'SparseDtype' object has no attribute 'itemsize'
```

`.loc`/`.iloc`, `Series.where`/`mask`/`update` and `Index.putmask`/`where` hit the same line. Sparse integers then take the same path as `Int64` values, including the `TypeError` when they do not fit a narrower dtype. The new tests fail on main with the `AttributeError` and pass with the fix. The float case (`TypeError: Invalid value` with a sparse `NaN`) is a question of intended behaviour, so I left it for a separate issue.

- [ ] I did **not** use AI to develop this pull request.
- [x] I used AI to develop this pull request. I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`, I have reviewed and understood every change, and I have described above how I used it and exactly which tool, model version, and effort setting — e.g. `claude opus 4.8 (xhigh)`, not just `claude`.

## What happened

As reported in #66593: for an arrow-backed string `Index`, `_get_engine_target()` returns `vals.astype(object)` — a distinct object-dtype copy that the cached lookup engine retains for its lifetime — and `memory_usage(deep=True)` accounted for neither that array nor its `PyUnicode` payloads. On the reporter's 500k-row repro only the hashtable growth (~16.9 MB) was reported where ~61 MB was actually allocated (3.6x under-report).

## What I did

`Index.memory_usage` now adds, when `deep=True` and the engine's mapping is populated:

- `engine.values.nbytes` — the retained pointer array, and
- `lib.memory_usage_of_objects(engine.values)` — its boxed strings,

**only** when the engine's array is an object-dtype copy that was not already counted, i.e. the Index's own array is an `ArrowExtensionArray` and the engine's array is neither `self._values` nor `self._values._ndarray`. This keeps the shared-array cases exactly as before:

- `object` dtype: engine array *is* `self._values` → unchanged
- `string[python]`: engine array *is* `StringArray._ndarray` → unchanged
- arrow-backed `str`/`string`: engine owns an exclusive copy → now counted

This is the shape the issue itself suggested (count the engine's retained values plus `lib.memory_usage_of_objects` when deep and not shared). Accounting was placed in `Index.memory_usage` rather than in `IndexEngine.sizeof`/`HashTable.sizeof` because the engine cannot tell whether its array is shared with the Index — only the Index knows that — so doing it in the engine risks double-counting the `object`/`string[python]` cases.

Note on exactness: as in the existing deep accounting for object dtype, this uses `sys.getsizeof` sums (`memory_usage_of_objects`), so the number is an accounting estimate, not RSS. On the repro it now lands at 61,408 kB growth vs the ~61.4 MB the reporter measured.

### Repro numbers (Linux x86_64, built from this branch)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| reported growth (500k × 40-byte str, `str` dtype / arrow storage) | 16,908 kB | **61,408 kB** |
| engine object array | 4,000 kB (unaccounted) | counted |
| its PyUnicodes | 40,500 kB (unaccounted) | counted |
| object-dtype growth (must not change) | 16,908 kB | 16,908 kB |
| `string[python]` growth (shares `_ndarray`; must not change) | 16,908 kB | 16,908 kB |

The propagation to `DataFrame.memory_usage(deep=True)` (one `.loc` on a string-indexed frame) is fixed transitively since it sums `Index.memory_usage(deep=True)`.

## Tests

- `tests/indexes/test_old_base.py`: two new regression tests — the arrow-backed case asserts the engine-build growth covers `held.nbytes + Σ sys.getsizeof`; the object-dtype case pins the no-double-count invariant (`after - before == engine.sizeof(deep=True)`). The first fails on main, passes here.
- `tests/base/test_misc.py::test_memory_usage`: the shared module-level fixture objects can carry a *populated* nested engine (categorical categories / MultiIndex levels) left over from earlier tests; since deep now correctly counts those engines' retained copies, the fixture setup clears nested engines recursively so each parametrization starts pristine. (Without this, `res == res_deep` fails for `categorical`/`tuples`/`multi` purely due to test-order cross-contamination, not the fix.)
- Ran: `pandas/tests/indexes` (17,906 passed; the single `tzlocal` failure reproduces on unmodified main in this environment), `pandas/tests/base` (all pass), plus `frame/methods/test_info.py`, `series/methods/test_info.py`, `arrays/categorical/test_analytics.py`, `arrays/string_/test_string.py`, `extension/base`, `apply/test_frame_apply.py`, `frame/test_subclass.py`, `arrays/sparse/test_array.py` — all pass. `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean on the touched files.

Developed with AI assistance: Hermes Agent (Nous Research), model `qwen3.8-flash`, running an interactive session against the repo per `AGENTS.md` (default effort). The AI reproduced the issue on a locally built editable install before and after the change, ran the test suites listed above, and drafted this description; every diff hunk was reviewed line-by-line.

title: BUG: fix read_excel crash when index_col consumes all columns with list-valued header
body:
Closes #66372

## Problem

```python
df1 = pd.read_csv('test.csv', header=[0,1], index_col=0)
df2 = pd.read_excel('test.xlsx', header=[0,1], index_col=0, engine='openpyxl')
```

`read_csv` returns an empty `DataFrame` for a single-column sheet where `index_col` consumes the only column. `read_excel` on the equivalent file raises:

```
ValueError: Length of new names must be 1, got 2 (sheet: 0)
```

## Root cause

`BaseExcelReader._parse_sheet` (`pandas/io/excel/_base.py`) pops one "header name" per header row from the `index_col` position, building `header_names` (length == number of header rows, e.g. 2 for `header=[0, 1]`). It then unconditionally applies these to the parsed result's `.columns` via `.set_names(header_names)`.

When `index_col` consumes every data column, the resulting `.columns` is a plain (non-`Multi`) empty `Index` — only 1 level, not 2 — so `set_names` raises. `read_csv` has no equivalent post-hoc "reapply names" step, so it doesn't hit this.

## Fix

Guard the `set_names` call on `output[asheetname].columns.nlevels == len(header_names)`, so it only applies when the level counts actually match (i.e. when there are data columns left to form a matching MultiIndex).

## Testing

- Reproduced with the exact files attached to #66372: `df1.equals(df2)` now passes (was previously raising).
- Added `test_read_excel_multiindex_header_index_col_consumes_all_columns` to `pandas/tests/io/excel/test_readers.py`, parametrized across all excel engines via the existing `engine`/`read_ext`/`tmp_excel` fixtures.
- Verified this is a true regression guard: fails with `ValueError: Length of new names must be 1, got 2` without the fix, passes with it.
- Re-ran the existing fixture-based multi-header regression tests (`mi_column`, `mi_column_name` from `testmultiindex.xlsx`, `header_with_index_col` from `df_equals.xlsx`, `test_read_excel_header_index_out_of_range` from `df_header_oob.xlsx`) to confirm the normal (non-degenerate) MultiIndex-naming path is unaffected.
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check`: clean.
- Added a whatsnew entry under `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` I/O bug fixes.

Note: building pandas' Cython/C extensions from source wasn't needed for this pure-Python fix — verification above was done by applying the identical diff to an installed pandas 3.0.3 wheel and running the reporter's exact repro plus the existing fixture-based tests against it, then mirroring the same test into this branch's `test_readers.py`.

title: PERF: High overhead in DataFrame.apply(raw=True) due to np.apply_along_axis
body:
- [x] Closes #66203 

### Description
This PR optimizes `apply_raw` in `pandas/core/apply.py` for default Python execution path by replacing `numpy.apply_along_axis` with an optimized list comprehension path over the 2D values.

Specifically:
- Accesses `values.T` for `axis=0` and `values` for `axis=1`.
- Preserves the dtype returned by the first row/column calculation using `np.asanyarray(first_res).dtype`.
- Unpacks 0D numpy arrays (returned by wrapper to avoid truncation) back to scalars using `.item()`.
- Raises correct ValueErrors for empty iteration dimensions matching NumPy's original behavior.

### Performance Benchmarks
Tested on a local environment using `time.perf_counter` (average of multiple runs):

|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Row-wise (`axis=1`)** | 20k x 10 | `0.043715` seconds | `0.030654` seconds | **1.43x** |
| **Column-wise (`axis=0`)** | 20 x 10k | `0.056720` seconds | `0.026032` seconds | **2.18x** |

All tests inside `pandas/tests/apply/test_frame_apply.py` pass without regression.

title: BUG: stacked bar subplots raise IndexError when a single-column group comes first
body:
- [x] closes #67726
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

Reopening the earlier PR was not possible once the bot had closed it, so this replaces it. The issue is now assigned to me.

Still reproduces on `main` as of `5c91b22f0a`:

```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": [1, 2, 3, 4], "c": [1, 1, 1, 1]})

df.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, subplots=[["b", "c"], ["a"]], sharex=True)  # works
df.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, subplots=[["a"], ["b", "c"]], sharex=True)  # IndexError
```

```
IndexError: list index out of range
```

## Cause

`BarPlot._make_plot` keeps two structures for stacked subplots:

- `_stacked_subplots_ind` maps a column position to a slot in the offsets list
- `_stacked_subplots_offsets` holds the running positive/negative stack heights

The offsets list only gains an entry for groups that hold more than one column, since a single-column group has nothing to stack onto. The index stored in `_stacked_subplots_ind`, though, came from `enumerate(self.subplots)`, which keeps counting through the groups that were skipped:

```python
for i, sub_plot in enumerate(self.subplots):
    if len(sub_plot) <= 1:
        continue
    for plot in sub_plot:
        _stacked_subplots_ind[int(plot)] = i          # position in self.subplots
    _stacked_subplots_offsets.append((pos_prior, neg_prior))   # appended at a different index
```

So the two indices agree only while no single-column group has been skipped yet, which is why the failure depends on ordering:

| `subplots` | stored index | offsets slot | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[["b", "c"], ["a"]]` | 0 | 0 | happens to line up |
| `[["a"], ["b", "c"]]` | 1 | 0 | `IndexError` |

The later `_stacked_subplots_offsets[offset_index]` lookup then runs off the end of the list.

## Fix

Store the index into `_stacked_subplots_offsets` itself rather than the position within `self.subplots`, so the mapping holds for any group ordering:

```python
offset_index = len(_stacked_subplots_offsets)
for plot in sub_plot:
    _stacked_subplots_ind[int(plot)] = offset_index
_stacked_subplots_offsets.append((pos_prior, neg_prior))
```

## Testing

`test_bar_2_subplot_single_column_first_stacked` mirrors the existing `test_bar_2_subplot_1_double_stacked` with the single-column group moved to the front, and reuses the same `_df_bar_subplot_checker` helper, so it verifies the resulting bar heights and stacking offsets rather than only the absence of an exception.

It fails on `main` for all three parametrisations with the `IndexError` above, and passes with the fix.

```
pytest pandas/tests/plotting/test_misc.py -k single_column_first   ->  3 passed
   (with the fix reverted:                                              3 failed)
pytest pandas/tests/plotting/                                      ->  1502 passed, 11 skipped, 10 xfailed
ruff check / ruff format --check                                   ->  clean
```

I also checked #67727, filed alongside this one by the same reporter: that is a separate problem in the non-stacked grouping path and is not addressed here.

Everything in this PR was reviewed manually by me. Claude Opus 5, via Claude Code, was used to draft the change, the test and this description.

title: API: return "correct" missing value scalar from Categorical?

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

labels.name: PDEP missing values
labels.description: Issues that would be addressed by the Ice Cream Agreement from the Aug 2023 sprint

body:
From https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/27929#discussion_r350469472. In `__getitem__` or  `Categorical.min(..)`, we always return `np.nan` as scalar missing value, regardless of the dtype:

```
In [7]: cat = pd.Categorical([pd.Timestamp("2012"), None], ordered=True)

In [8]: cat  
Out[8]: 
[2012-01-01, NaT]
Categories (1, datetime64[ns]): [2012-01-01]

In [9]: cat[1]   
Out[9]: nan

In [10]: cat.min(skipna=False) 
Out[10]: nan

```

In the above, this could also be `pd.NaT` instead? 
(similar issue will come up once we can use the EAs that use the new NA scalar in categoricals)

However, `CategoricalDtype.na_value` now also returns `np.nan` (which should be consistent with what we return in the cases above):

```
In [13]: cat.dtype.na_value 
Out[13]: nan
```

We can of course let the `CategoricalDtype.na_value` be dependent on the `na_value` of the dtype of the categories. But I am not fully sure we want such values-dependent behaviour?

title: BUG: arrow and StringDtype ops with 2D or mismatched-length operands (GH#62682)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
Part of GH-62682 — this slice does not close it; the `_box_pa` error leakage in the issue's own repro is handled separately.

Arithmetic, comparison and logical ops between PyArrow-backed data and a two-dimensional operand raised assorted internal errors (`ArrowInvalid: only handle 1-dimensional arrays`, `ValueError: Mask must be 1D array`, `IndexError: too many indices`) or silently returned a wrong result — a `(2, 2)` ndarray for `&`/`|`/`^` against a boolean ndarray, and a correctly-shaped all-`False` comparison against a 2-D datetimelike ExtensionArray. They now raise `NotImplementedError("can only perform ops with 1-d structures")`, the guard `BaseMaskedArray` already uses.

`StringDtype("python")` has the same exposure — a silent `(2, 2)` result from the shared string-vs-bool arm, `IndexError: too many indices` for a square operand, and a misleading `Lengths of operands do not match: 3 != 1` for arithmetic — so the guard lives in `pandas.core.ops.common` and is applied from `StringArray` as well. Otherwise the two storages of one dtype would answer the same call differently, which `test_add_2d` would have had to branch on.

Separately, comparison against a differently-sized array or list raised `ArrowInvalid: Array arguments must all be the same length`, and now raises `ValueError("Lengths must match to compare")`; the range-only length check from GH-67979 is generalized to the other list-like arms of the same `isinstance` tuple. `ArrowInvalid` already subclasses `ValueError`, so this is a clearer message rather than a newly-catchable type.

title: BUG: read_csv c engine ignored na_values on a converters column (GH#13302)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
closes #13302

When a column has a `converters` entry, the default `c` engine silently ignored `na_values` *and* the default NA strings for that column, where the `python` engine applies them: `_convert_column_data` returned from the converter branch before any NA handling ran. This matches them against the converter's output, as the `python` engine does.

The `converters` docstring for `read_csv`/`read_table` and the matching text in `io.rst` documented the old `c`-engine behavior as the spec ("`na_values` and `keep_default_na` have no effect on a column that has a converter"), so they are updated too. The sharpest user-visible change is that an empty field under `converters={"a": str}` now reads as `NaN` rather than `""` — which is what the `python` engine already returned.

Two deliberate limits, both left for separate PRs:

- A converter that *raises* on the NA token (`converters={"a": float}` with a blank field) still raises here; the `python` engine retries with those rows masked. That is the other half of GH-13302, and the whatsnew and docstring claim only output-matching. `test_converters_raising_on_empty_field` asserts the `c` engine's raise and strict-xfails the `python` engine, so a later fix surfaces as an XPASS.
- GH-13302's discussion favored applying `na_values` to the raw token *before* the converter. That is a semantics change for both engines and would need a deprecation; this PR only reconciles the engines, one of the open items on the GH-12686 tracker.

One consequence worth flagging: under the default `low_memory=True`, a converter column whose leading internal chunk is now entirely NA draws the `Columns (N) have mixed types` warning, because that chunk infers `float64` while a later text chunk infers str. The resulting dtype is correct. This is a pre-existing `_concatenate_chunks` bug — it reproduces with no converter at all, on any column whose first chunk is all-NA — and this PR only routes a new kind of input into it. Fixing it means not counting an all-NA chunk as type evidence, which is general enough to want its own PR.

Note `True == 1`, so a bool returned by a converter matches a numeric `na_values` entry. That is intentional on the `c` side — it agrees with the same read without a converter and with `Series.isin`. The `python` engine computes the same mask but `np.putmask` writes the NaN into a bool array, where it reads as `True`; `test_converters_na_values_bool_output` strict-xfails that engine so a later fix surfaces as an XPASS.

title: Inconsistent Handling of na_values and converters in read_csv
body: On `master` (commit 40b4bb4): ``` python >>> data = """A 1 CAT 3""" >>> f = lambda x: x >>> read_csv(StringIO(data), na_values='CAT', converters={'A': f}, engine='c') A 0 1 1 CAT 2 3 >>> read_csv(StringIO(data), na_values='CAT', converters={'A': f}, engine='python') A 0 1 1 NaN 2 3 ``` I expect both to give the same output, though I believe the Python output is more correct because it respects `na_values` unlike the C engine. I thought the simple fix would be to remove the `continue` statement here, but that causes test failures, so probably a more involved refactoring might be needed to align the order of converter application, `NaN` value conversion, and `dtype` conversion. IMO this should be added to #12686, as this is a difference in behaviour between the two engines. xref #5232

title: BUG: DataFrame.duplicated self-triggering the .values deprecation

labels.name: Warnings
labels.description: Warnings that appear or should be added to pandas

body:
The multi-column path of `DataFrame.duplicated` read `col.values`, which for `DatetimeTZDtype`, `PeriodDtype` and `IntervalDtype` emits the `Pandas4Warning` added by GH-64613. So `duplicated`, `drop_duplicates` and `wide_to_long` with a list `i` each warned from pandas' own code, attributed to the user's own line — and warnings-as-errors suites hard-fail on it. `col._values` is what GH-64613 already did for the ujson helper and `core/computation/align.py`; this is the one internal caller it missed.

No whatsnew bug-fix entry: that deprecation is itself unreleased, so the spurious warning has never shipped.

The switch also skips an object-dtype round trip for `PeriodDtype`, which is a large speedup (roughly 50x at n=1e5 and more at larger sizes) and does have a whatsnew entry. `DatetimeTZDtype` is unchanged at 1.0x. `IntervalDtype` is ~1.1x slower at the cardinalities where duplicates actually exist, because `ExtensionArray.factorize` rebuilds a uniques array that `duplicated` discards; that is a pre-existing inefficiency, not introduced here.

Behavior is unchanged: results were compared against the pre-fix expression across every dtype family the path serves, crossed with `keep`, `subset` spelling, duplicate column labels, MultiIndex columns, NA placement, and empty/length-1 frames.

body:
Follow-up to GH-63961, which fixed the wrong-groups symptom of GH-63920 but left the cause in place: in the arm of `BaseGrouper.result_index_and_ids` that combines observed and unobserved groupings, `ids = len(unob_index) * ob_ids + unob_ids` maps the `-1` marking a dropped NA key onto an arbitrary position — negative, or a valid one belonging to another group — and both branches below used `ids` as positions before that PR restored the `-1`s at the end of the function.

title: BUG: to_datetime returned category dtype for categorical input when the cache fired (GH#28629)
body:
closes #28629

`to_datetime`'s internal date cache is applied with `Series.map`, and `map` can hand back the input's own container — `Categorical.map` maps the categories and rebuilds a `Categorical` — or, on its slow path, an object-dtype `Index`. So once the input was long and repetitive enough for `should_cache` to fire, categorical input came back as `category` (or, when every category coerced to `NaT`, `object`) instead of `datetime64`, while the same values just under the threshold came back as a `DatetimeIndex`.

The cache lookup now casts to `cache_array.dtype`, which is by construction the dtype the uncached `convert_listlike` produces, so the cache can no longer be observed in the result.

title: API: select_dtypes raises on a partly specified IntervalDtype/CategoricalDtype (GH#40234)
body:
During 3.1 development `select_dtypes` grew partial-dtype matching: an instance naming only some of its attributes selected the family those attributes describe. This reverts that in favour of one rule — an instance that names an attribute names one exact dtype — while none of it has shipped. Adding the support back later is cheap; removing it after 3.1 would take a deprecation cycle.

Now raising, since no column can have any of these dtypes:

- `pd.IntervalDtype("int64")` / `"interval[int64]"` — no `closed`
- `pd.IntervalDtype(closed="left")` — no subtype
- `pd.IntervalDtype("datetime64", "left")` — subtype has no resolution
- `pd.CategoricalDtype(ordered=True)` — no categories

An instance that names *no* attribute keeps its 3.0 behaviour of selecting the whole family: `pd.IntervalDtype()`, `pd.CategoricalDtype()`, and `pd.CategoricalDtype(ordered=False)`, which is indistinguishable from the bare one since `ordered=False` is the constructor default. The class and the bare string select the family as before — `pd.IntervalDtype`/`"interval"`, `pd.CategoricalDtype`/`"category"` — as do fully specified instances, every other spec form, and the unitless `np.dtype("datetime64")`.

One thing this settles beyond the line count: the helper that existed only to work around `IntervalDtype` hashing as plain `"interval"` once its subtype is `None` goes away, so `select_dtypes` no longer carries its own notion of interval-dtype identity.

Reverts GH-68491, GH-68450, GH-68444, GH-66325 and the partial-matching half of GH-66120, all unreleased. Context in GH-40234.

title: BUG: ArrowDtype setitem reinterpreted values through their integer storage

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
`ArrowExtensionArray` setitem and `fillna` handed the value straight to `_box_pa`, and pyarrow will convert a temporal array into an integer array without complaint. So a mismatched assignment was silently reinterpreted rather than rejected:

```python
arr = pd.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]")
arr[:] = pd.date_range("2016-01-01", periods=3)._data
arr   # [1451606400000000, 1451692800000000, 1451779200000000]
```

numpy `int64`, masked `Int64`, `Categorical` and `string` all raise `TypeError` for the same assignment — only the Arrow path accepted it. The reverse direction (an integer array into `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]`/`duration[ns][pyarrow]`) reads back as timestamps, and a scalar `Timestamp` in the same position raised a raw `AttributeError` from inside `_box_pa`.

Adds a three-state predicate — temporal / non-temporal / *unsettled* — consulted by `_validate_setitem_value` before boxing. Unsettled means the value's type does not decide the question (`object` dtype, strings, plain lists); those fall through to the existing behavior, so nothing that worked before starts raising. An all-NA value is likewise exempt, which keeps `where`/`fillna` working against an alignment-produced all-NaN column. That exemption returns typed nulls rather than deferring to `_box_pa`, which has no `double`->`timestamp` cast kernel: an all-NA masked or Arrow-backed float, and any all-NA numeric or boolean value into a `date32`/`date64`/`time64` column, used to raise `ArrowNotImplementedError`.

`fillna` held a verbatim copy of the same `_box_pa` + `except pa.ArrowTypeError` block; it now calls `_validate_setitem_value`, which is what carries the fix to `Series.fillna` and also makes its `limit=None` path agree with `limit=1`.

`_box_pa_scalar`'s unit workaround compounded this: it read `pa_type.unit` for every `Timestamp`/`Timedelta` value regardless of the target. A `string`, `binary` or `date32` target has no `.unit`, hence the `AttributeError`; a target that had one but was the wrong flavor (`Timedelta` into `time64`, `Timestamp` into `duration`) reconciled the units and stored the integer. Gating the workaround on the target hands those to `pa.scalar`, which assigns a `Timestamp` into `date32`/`date64` correctly and rejects the rest as `TypeError`.

Deliberately left for follow-ups: values whose dtype settles nothing (a plain `list` of `Timestamp`s) still reinterpret; reinterpretation *between* temporal types is now rejected for scalars across type families, but not within one — a tz or unit mismatch still goes through integer storage — and not for the array spelling; and `insert`/`shift` bypass the guard via `_from_sequence`.

title: API/DEPR: SparseArray constructor usability

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
Currently the constructor includes `sparse_index`, which is not publicly exposed (nor is there a publicly exposed function to make one). Because of this, I'd like to suggest deprecating `sparse_index`.

One related issue is that without `sparse_index` (or a preexisting `SparseArray`), there is no way to use the  constructor to construct a `SparseArray` without using dense data (which seems to defeat the purpose of using a `SparseArray`.

I'd like to replace `sparse_index` with the parameters `indices` and `length` (giving equivalent functionality to what `sparse_index` provided). `indices` would refer to array locations with actual values, `length` would be length of the `SparseArray` (I'm not attached to these names if people prefer others, these just match naming in existing `SparseArray` code).

This would allow constructing something sparse without first constructing a dense array, for example

`arr = SparseArray([1, 2], indices=[5, 11], length=1_000_000)`
or
`arr = SparseArray(1, indices=[1000, 2000, 4000, 9000], length=1_000_000)`
without needing to materialize an array of length `1_000_000`

title: PERF: avoid redundant allocations in StringArray duplicated and value_counts

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

## Summary

Python-backed `StringArray` already stores its values in an object ndarray. However, `duplicated` and `value_counts(dropna=True)` currently perform avoidable allocations before hashing for arrays using `pd.NA`.

The two paths incur this overhead differently:

* `duplicated` already passes the existing backing ndarray through `_ensure_data` (`_ensure_data(arr) is arr._ndarray`), so it does not materialize another object ndarray. Its avoidable allocation is the boolean NA mask created by the generic extension-array path.
* `value_counts(dropna=True)` creates a filtered object-array copy through boolean indexing before hashing.

For Python-backed `StringArray` using `pd.NA`, these allocations can be avoided by operating directly on the existing backing ndarray where the missing-value semantics permit it.

## Proposed change

Use the existing backing ndarray directly when:

* The array is Python-backed.
* Its missing-value sentinel is `pd.NA`.
* For `value_counts`, `dropna=True`.

For `duplicated`, avoid constructing the generic NA mask when the backing ndarray can be hashed directly.

Retain the existing generic paths for other missing-value semantics, `dropna=False`, and other string backends.

This does not change public behavior or results.

## Relation to #14860

This is related to #14860, which tracks improving `value_counts` and `duplicated` performance for string data through string-specific hashing.

This change is narrower. It removes avoidable allocations in the Python-backed `StringArray` dispatch path before hashing:

* A boolean NA mask for `duplicated`.
* A filtered object-array copy for `value_counts(dropna=True)`.

It does not change the underlying hashtable implementation or introduce the general string-specific hashing approach discussed in #14860.

## Benchmarks

ASV benchmarks used arrays containing 500,000 elements. Nullable cases replaced every tenth value with `pd.NA`, giving 10% missing values.

Among statistically significant comparisons:

* `duplicated`: 16/18 cases improved, 2 were unchanged, and none regressed. Significant improvements ranged from approximately 9% to 55%.
* `value_counts`: 5/6 cases improved, 1 was unchanged, and none regressed. One no-null, cardinality-50,000 measurement had high variance and is omitted from the representative results.

Representative ASV results:

* `duplicated`, cardinality 256, no nulls, `keep="first"`:
  **19.4 ± 0.03 ms → 8.76 ± 0.1 ms — 54.9% faster.**
* `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 256, 10% nulls:
  **31.3 ± 0.3 ms → 19.3 ± 0.08 ms — 38.2% faster.**
* `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 50,000, 10% nulls:
  **59.1 ± 0.3 ms → 45.2 ± 0.4 ms — 23.6% faster.**
* `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 500,000, no nulls:
  **322 ± 6 ms → 306 ± 3 ms — 4.7% faster.**

## Reproducible timing example

```python
from timeit import repeat

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def make_array(cardinality, has_nulls):
    values = np.resize(
        np.array([f"value-{i}" for i in range(cardinality)], dtype=object),
        500_000,
    )
    if has_nulls:
        values[::10] = pd.NA
    return pd.array(
        values,
        dtype=pd.StringDtype(storage="python", na_value=pd.NA),
    )


def best_ms(func):
    return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000


no_nulls = make_array(256, False)
nullable_256 = make_array(256, True)
nullable_50k = make_array(50_000, True)

print("duplicated:", best_ms(lambda: no_nulls.duplicated(keep="first")))
print(
    "value_counts 256:",
    best_ms(lambda: nullable_256.value_counts(dropna=True)),
)
print(
    "value_counts 50k:",
    best_ms(lambda: nullable_50k.value_counts(dropna=True)),
)
```

body:
Changed the return type of write_version_info to str and updated its usage in main. Improved handling of MESON_DIST_ROOT environment variable.

`write_version_info()` previously discarded the version string it
resolved internally. When both `--outfile` and `--print` were passed
together, `main()` would re-derive the version a second time via a
fresh call to `versioneer.get_version()` (and, in the `_version_meson`

once.

- `main()` reuses that returned value in the `--print` branch instead
  of re-deriving it, only falling back to a fresh resolution if
  `--outfile` wasn't passed at all.
- `os.environ.get("MESON_DIST_ROOT")` is looked up once into a local
  variable instead of twice.

title: Fix: prefer column over index level in groupby

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
closes #33657

### What does this PR do?

When a label passed to `DataFrame.groupby()` matches both a column label and an index level name, pandas currently raises a `ValueError` because the label is considered ambiguous.

This PR makes `DataFrame.groupby()` prefer the column label in this case.

The `level=` argument remains available when grouping by the index level explicitly.

### Example
Previously:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(
    2,
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
        [range(4), list("abcd")],
        names=["I", "II"],
    ),
    columns=["I"],
)

df.groupby("I")
```
raised: ValueError: 'I' is both an index level and a column label, which is ambiguous.

After this change:
```python
df.groupby("I")
```
groups by the column "I".

Grouping by the index level can still be done explicitly:
```python
df.groupby(level="I")
```
### Changes
- Changed `DataFrame.groupby()` to prefer a column label when the grouping key matches both a column label and an index level name.
- Removed the ambiguity check that previously raised a `ValueError` for this case.
- Added a regression test for the ambiguous column/index-level case.
- Verified that explicit level= grouping continues to use the index level.
- Added a What's New entry for the bug fix.

title: BUG: astype/construction from float to datetime64 is an unchecked narrowing
body:
A ``float`` outside the ``int64`` domain cast to ``M8``/``m8`` was silently converted. Positive overflow saturated to ``INT64_MAX`` and read back as a real-looking timestamp; negative overflow landed on ``INT64_MIN``, which *is* the ``NaT`` sentinel, so ``-inf`` became missing data. The only signal was a numpy ``RuntimeWarning``, which pandas does not promote.

```python
pd.Series([np.inf]).astype("M8[ns]")[0]    # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
pd.Series([-np.inf]).astype("M8[ns]")[0]   # NaT
pd.Series([1e30]).astype("m8[s]")[0]       # Timedelta('106751991167300 days 15:30:07')
pd.DatetimeIndex(np.array([np.inf]))[0]    # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
pd.to_datetime(np.array([np.inf]))[0]      # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
```

The timedelta64 family was already guarded by ``cast_from_unit_vectorized``'s ``_raise_if_outside_int64``; datetime64 was the unguarded member, so ``.astype`` disagreed with ``dtype=``, and ``DatetimeIndex`` disagreed with ``TimedeltaIndex`` on the same input. This adds the same check to the two sites that lacked it — ``_astype_nansafe``'s fall-through cast and ``maybe_convert_dtype`` — reusing the message the timedelta peer already emits so the two agree.

``errors="coerce"`` is preserved: ``to_datetime`` blanks just the out-of-range entries rather than letting the raise escape, matching what ``to_timedelta`` already does (GH-66823).

`is_float_dtype` is true for ``Float64``, so ``maybe_convert_dtype`` fired for masked input while ``_astype_nansafe`` — which only sees ndarrays — did not, leaving ``DatetimeIndex(masked)`` raising and ``.astype``/``dtype=`` on the same array silently wrong. `BaseMaskedArray.astype` gets the guard too, so the three spellings agree. The pyarrow-backed and ``Sparse`` float spellings were silently wrong on all three and are covered by the same two sites.

The guard is skipped for a multiplier dtype such as ``M8[10s]``, which pandas rejects outright whatever the values; without that gate an out-of-range float turned a ``ValueError`` about the dtype into an ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` naming a unit the user never asked for. One known consequence remains: ``Index([inf]).astype("M8[D]")`` now raises ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` where it raised ``TypeError`` before. Deferring to that ``TypeError`` is not reachable without dropping the guard for ``Series.astype("M8[D]")``, which on main silently turns ``-inf`` into ``NaT``; both arms raise either way, so this narrows the data-dependent-exception problem rather than removing it.

In-range values are untouched, including the deliberate ``float(iNaT)`` → ``NaT`` mapping and ``NaN`` → ``NaT``. Not covered here, and tracked locally instead: ``uint64``, ``complex`` and ``Categorical`` sources, each of which needs a different predicate or a separate API decision.

title: BUG: read_csv with engine="pyarrow" ignored skiprows when header is not None (GH#48507)
body:
closes #48507
closes #58048

`read_csv(engine="pyarrow")` built pyarrow's `ReadOptions` with `skip_rows = skiprows if header is None else header`, so `skiprows` was dropped for every `header is not None` spelling — including the default `header=0`. The rows meant to be skipped were read as the header and as data, and `usecols`/`index_col` were then resolved against that wrong header row.

`skip_rows` is now `skiprows + header`, which is the composition the other engines already implement and the user guide already documents ("`header` will be relative to the end of `skiprows`"). A negative `skiprows` is clamped to 0 so that it skips nothing as with the `c` and `python` engines, rather than being passed to pyarrow, which rejects it.

GH-58048 is a duplicate report of the same bug, so both are closed here.

`test_skiprows_infield_quote` (GH-14459) passes on the pyarrow engine with the fix and is un-xfailed.

Two tests pin behavior that the fix makes reachable on the default `header` path: a `skiprows` landing on or past the end of the file raises on the pyarrow engine, where the `c` and `python` engines raise `EmptyDataError` or return an empty frame. Both are existing `pyarrow.csv` `skip_rows` limitations that already apply with `header=None`, not something this PR introduces.

title: BUG: read_csv raising for sep="\n" with a custom lineterminator (GH#51801)
body:
closes #51801

``read_csv(StringIO(...), sep="\n", lineterminator="-")`` raised ``ValueError``, but the C engine parses it fine: a custom line terminator clears ``has_carriage``, which leaves ``"\n"`` and ``"\r"`` as ordinary characters that split fields. The guard now fires only when ``lineterminator`` is absent or equal to the separator, and the message says how to get the parse.

A ``bytes``/``bytearray`` ``lineterminator`` is normalized before that comparison. The C engine accepts those spellings, so without it ``lineterminator=b"\n"`` slipped past the narrowed guard into the same silent mis-parse GH-43528 was filed about.

The ``"\r"`` clause of the existing entry is amended rather than duplicated: that raise arrived with GH-66896 and is unreleased, so only the ``"\n"`` case is a user-visible change against 3.0.

title: BUG: Series from a pre-2.1 pickle lost its name on copy (GH#61819)
body:
closes #61819

`NDFrame.__setstate__` assigned the *pickled* `_metadata` list onto the instance, shadowing the class attribute. pandas 2.1 (GH-51784) renamed the Series entry from `name` to `_name`, so a Series unpickled from an older file carried `_metadata == ["name"]` while the class declared `["_name"]`. `__finalize__` intersects the two lists, got the empty set, and propagated nothing — the name survived the load but vanished on the first `copy`, `reindex`, `astype` or `sort_values`. `__getstate__` then re-emitted the stale list, so re-pickling carried the breakage into the new file.

The restore loop now leaves `_metadata` alone and merges the two lists instead of letting either replace the other. Merging rather than simply dropping the pickled list matters: a stale name and a name a subclass added per instance are indistinguishable from the pickled list alone, and discarding it regressed subclasses that extend `_metadata` in `__init__`. The stale spelling is filtered where it should be — by `__finalize__`'s intersection with the destination's class list.

This is inside the documented support window: `doc/source/user_guide/io.rst` states that pandas 3.x reads pickles back to 2.0.0, and 2.0.x is exactly the affected range. The repo's own `legacy_pickle` fixtures for 1.1.0 through 2.0.3 each contain two named Series that reproduce it.

Tests cover both halves: a synthetic pre-2.1 state (parametrized over name kinds), the shipped 2.0.3 fixture so the emulation cannot silently drift, and a subclass with per-instance `_metadata` guarding against the over-correction.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which diagnosed the root cause, wrote the fix and tests, and reviewed the branch across several blind review rounds.

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

On pandas < 2.1 (e.g. 1.5.3, 2.0.3):

```python3

import pandas as pd
pd.Series(['a'], name='hi').to_pickle('G:/temp/test.pkl')
```

On pandas 2.3.0 and main:

```python3
import pandas as pd
ser = pd.read_pickle('G:/temp/test.pkl')        # appears to work
ser2 = pd.Series(['a'], name='hi')              # works
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(ser, ser2)       # works
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(ser, ser.copy()) # Attribute "name" are different
```

### Issue Description

In doing a migration from 1.5.3 to the 2.x series we hit an issue where copying an unpickled Series drops its name (the actual operation was a `.reindex_like`, which called `.copy` under the hood). The bug begins with the pandas 2.1 series; I believe this may have been introduced in #51784 when the Series metadata was changed from name to _name.

### Expected Behavior

It seems like an unpickled Series and its copy should be equal in all attributes, since that's what .copy does. However anything which does a copy (including implicit copies, such as calling `.reindex()`) currently causes the name to be dropped inadvertently.

Now I'm not sure to what extent `read_pickle` guarantees that all actions on an unpickled legacy object work the same way on a newly-created object. That said, one reason this may be worth fixing is that the problem seems to persist in new versions, i.e. rewriting the pickle with the new version directly doesn't mitigate the problem:

```python3
# using version 2.3.0
# read legacy pickle
ser = pd.read_pickle('G:/temp/test.pkl')
# write out new pickle of the object
ser.to_pickle('G:/temp/ser_copy.pkl')
# read in new pickle
ser_copy = pd.read_pickle('G:/temp/ser_copy.pkl')
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(ser, ser_copy)             # works
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(ser_copy, ser_copy.copy()) # fails, even though ser_copy is read in from a pickle created in 2.3.0)
```

And of course obviously calling ser.copy() to get a new pandas 2.3 object also does not work.

Thus it seems the only workaround to:
1) Read in the legacy pickle
2) Serialize the legacy pickle to some other format
3) Deserialize the other format
4) Serialize the newly-created object as a replacement pickle

title: BUG: to_clipboard blamed sep for any TypeError in excel mode (GH#44120)

labels.name: IO Data
labels.description: IO issues that don't fit into a more specific label

body:
closes #44120

`to_clipboard(excel=True)` wrapped both `to_csv` and `clipboard_set` in a bare `except TypeError` whose handler warned `"to_clipboard in excel mode requires a single character separator."` and then fell through to the `to_string` path. Any `TypeError` was therefore blamed on `sep` — including `to_csv` rejecting a keyword it does not accept, which is the reported case: `df.to_clipboard(index_names=False)` warns about a separator the user never passed, and the clipboard silently receives the `to_string` representation instead of CSV.

Validating `sep` up front instead means only a genuine separator problem warns and falls back; every other `TypeError` propagates with its own message. Behavior for a non-str, empty, or multi-character `sep` is unchanged.

title: BUG: IntervalIndex set ops and astype with RangeIndex raising TypeError
body:
- [x] closes #68343
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed: `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on all changed files
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst`

## What this fixes

Set operations between an ``IntervalIndex`` and a ``RangeIndex`` raised a confusing Cython ``TypeError`` when the ``RangeIndex`` was empty:

```python
iv = pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks([0, 2, 4])
iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(0))
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)
```

Every other empty array-like (``Index([], dtype="int64")``, ``np.array([])``, empty ``Series``, ``[]``) worked. The mirror (``pd.RangeIndex(0).union(iv)``), ``symmetric_difference``, and the direct constructors (``pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(...))``, ``IntervalArray(...)``, ``RangeIndex.astype("interval")``) hit the same error for empty and non-empty ``RangeIndex`` alike.

## Root cause

``_maybe_convert_platform_interval`` only coerces ``values`` to an ndarray when it lacks a ``dtype`` attribute; ``RangeIndex`` has one, so it reaches the Cython ``intervals_to_interval_bounds`` as a non-ndarray. In set ops, an empty ``RangeIndex`` specifically triggers this because ``_find_common_type_compat`` resolves the common dtype to ``interval[int64, right]`` (an empty ``Index`` resolves to ``object`` instead), so ``other.astype(interval_dtype)`` crashes before the empty-``other`` short-circuit.

## Fix

Convert ``RangeIndex`` to an ndarray in ``_maybe_convert_platform_interval``, the same special-casing place that already handles empty lists (GH19016). After the fix:

- ``iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(0))`` / ``iv.symmetric_difference(pd.RangeIndex(0))`` / ``pd.RangeIndex(0).union(iv)`` return the original interval index
- ``pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(0))`` and ``RangeIndex(0).astype("interval[int64, right]")`` build an empty ``IntervalIndex``
- ``pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(2, 4))`` and ``RangeIndex(2, 4).astype("interval[int64, right]")`` raise the regular ``TypeError: ... is not an interval`` message, consistent with ``pd.IntervalIndex([2, 3])``

## Verification

Run against the ``cb13b0e9a4`` build (main at the time of the report):

- ``pandas/tests/indexes/interval/`` + ``pandas/tests/arrays/interval/``: **1992 passed, 26 skipped, 2 xfailed**

title: BUG: account for engine-retained object values in Index.memory_usage(deep=True) for arrow-backed indexes

body:

- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)
Check exactly one of the following, per the [automated contributions policy](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html#automated-contributions-policy):
- [ ] I did **not** use AI to develop this pull request.
- [x] I used AI to develop this pull request. I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`, I have reviewed and understood every change, and I have described above how I used it and exactly which tool, model version, and effort setting — e.g. `claude opus 4.8 (xhigh)`, not just `claude`.

## What happened

As reported in #66593: for an arrow-backed string `Index`, `_get_engine_target()` returns `vals.astype(object)` — a distinct object-dtype copy that the cached lookup engine retains for its lifetime — and `memory_usage(deep=True)` accounted for neither that array nor its `PyUnicode` payloads. On the reporter's 500k-row repro only the hashtable growth (~16.9 MB) was reported where ~61 MB was actually allocated (3.6x under-report).

## What I did

`Index.memory_usage` now adds, when `deep=True` and the engine's mapping is populated:

- `engine.values.nbytes` — the retained pointer array, and
- `lib.memory_usage_of_objects(engine.values)` — its boxed strings,

**only** when the engine's array is an object-dtype copy that was not already counted, i.e. the Index's own array is an `ArrowExtensionArray` and the engine's array is neither `self._values` nor `self._values._ndarray`. This keeps the shared-array cases exactly as before:

- `object` dtype: engine array *is* `self._values` → unchanged
- `string[python]`: engine array *is* `StringArray._ndarray` → unchanged
- arrow-backed `str`/`string`: engine owns an exclusive copy → now counted

This is the shape the issue itself suggested (count the engine's retained values plus `lib.memory_usage_of_objects` when deep and not shared). Accounting was placed in `Index.memory_usage` rather than in `IndexEngine.sizeof`/`HashTable.sizeof` because the engine cannot tell whether its array is shared with the Index — only the Index knows that — so doing it in the engine risks double-counting the `object`/`string[python]` cases.

Note on exactness: as in the existing deep accounting for object dtype, this uses `sys.getsizeof` sums (`memory_usage_of_objects`), so the number is an accounting estimate, not RSS. On the repro it now lands at 61,408 kB growth vs the ~61.4 MB the reporter measured.

### Repro numbers (Linux x86_64, built from this branch)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| reported growth (500k × 40-byte str, `str` dtype / arrow storage) | 16,908 kB | **61,408 kB** |
| engine object array | 4,000 kB (unaccounted) | counted |
| its PyUnicodes | 40,500 kB (unaccounted) | counted |
| object-dtype growth (must not change) | 16,908 kB | 16,908 kB |
| `string[python]` growth (shares `_ndarray`; must not change) | 16,908 kB | 16,908 kB |

The propagation to `DataFrame.memory_usage(deep=True)` (one `.loc` on a string-indexed frame) is fixed transitively since it sums `Index.memory_usage(deep=True)`.

## Tests

- `tests/indexes/test_old_base.py`: two new regression tests — the arrow-backed case asserts the engine-build growth covers `held.nbytes + Σ sys.getsizeof`; the object-dtype case pins the no-double-count invariant (`after - before == engine.sizeof(deep=True)`). The first fails on main, passes here.
- `tests/base/test_misc.py::test_memory_usage`: the shared module-level fixture objects can carry a *populated* nested engine (categorical categories / MultiIndex levels) left over from earlier tests; since deep now correctly counts those engines' retained copies, the fixture setup clears nested engines recursively so each parametrization starts pristine. (Without this, `res == res_deep` fails for `categorical`/`tuples`/`multi` purely due to test-order cross-contamination, not the fix.)
- Ran: `pandas/tests/indexes` (17,906 passed; the single `tzlocal` failure reproduces on unmodified main in this environment), `pandas/tests/base` (all pass), plus `frame/methods/test_info.py`, `series/methods/test_info.py`, `arrays/categorical/test_analytics.py`, `arrays/string_/test_string.py`, `extension/base`, `apply/test_frame_apply.py`, `frame/test_subclass.py`, `arrays/sparse/test_array.py` — all pass. `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean on the touched files.

Developed with AI assistance: Hermes Agent (Nous Research), model `qwen3.8-flash`, running an interactive session against the repo per `AGENTS.md` (default effort). The AI reproduced the issue on a locally built editable install before and after the change, ran the test suites listed above, and drafted this description; every diff hunk was reviewed line-by-line.

title: BUG: memory_usage(deep=True) under-reports by ~4x for arrow-backed string Index once the engine is built

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. (only tested on main, at 5c2fc85c910)

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import sys

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

N = 500_000
vals = np.array([f"{'x' * 32}{i:08d}" for i in range(N)], dtype=object)
idx = pd.Index(vals, dtype="str")

reported_before = idx.memory_usage(deep=True)
idx.get_loc(idx[0])  # builds and caches the engine
reported_after = idx.memory_usage(deep=True)

held = idx._engine.values  # object-dtype copy the engine retains
unaccounted = held.nbytes + sum(sys.getsizeof(s) for s in held)

print("reported growth  :", (reported_after - reported_before) // 1000, "kB")
print("engine object arr:", held.nbytes // 1000, "kB")
print("its PyUnicodes   :", sum(sys.getsizeof(s) for s in held) // 1000, "kB")
print("unaccounted      :", unaccounted // 1000, "kB")
print("held is a copy   :", held is not np.asarray(idx._values))
```

```
reported growth  : 16908 kB
engine object arr: 4000 kB
its PyUnicodes   : 40500 kB
unaccounted      : 44500 kB
held is a copy   : True
```

### Issue Description

For an arrow-backed string Index, building the engine allocates an object-dtype
copy of the entire Index that the cached engine then holds for its lifetime, and
`memory_usage(deep=True)` accounts for none of it. Above, 16.9 MB is reported
where 61.4 MB was actually allocated — a **3.6x under-report**.

This is not just the boxed strings being missed. There are two separate gaps:

1. **`IndexEngine.sizeof()` never counts `self.values`.** For an object-dtype
   Index that is harmless, because the engine's array *is* the Index's own array
   and `_memory_usage` already counted it. But for `str`/`string[pyarrow]`,
   `_get_engine_target()` returns `vals.astype(object)`
   ([base.py#L5394](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/indexes/base.py#L5394)),
   so the engine holds a *distinct* 4 MB pointer array that nothing counts.

2. **`HashTable.sizeof()` ignores its `deep` argument entirely.** Every
   implementation in `hashtable_class_helper.pxi.in` computes
   `overhead + for_flags + for_pairs` and never looks at `deep`, so the 40.5 MB
   of `PyUnicode` objects is never counted at any setting. For object-dtype those
   strings are shared with the Index and counting them would double-count, but
   for arrow-backed string dtypes the engine owns them exclusively.

The docstring says `deep=True` includes "the memory consumption of underlying
objects referencing this Index (e.g., the characters of object-dtype values)",
and `memory_usage` deliberately adds `self._engine.sizeof(deep=deep)`, so the
intent to count the engine is clearly there — it just counts the wrong thing.

Confirmed against RSS (`psutil`), 500k keys x 40 bytes, engine build only:

| dtype | reported delta | actual RSS delta | engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| `object` | 16.9 MB | 16.9 MB | `ObjectEngine` |
| `str` | 16.9 MB | **69.4 MB** | `StringObjectEngine` |
| `string[python]` | 16.9 MB | 8.4 MB | `StringObjectEngine` |

Only the arrow-backed case is wrong: `object` matches exactly, and
`string[python]` shares `_ndarray` with the engine so nothing extra is
allocated (its RSS delta reads low only because the allocator reuses freed
pages).

It also propagates to frames — one `.loc` lookup on a string-indexed
`DataFrame` is enough:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.arange(N)}, index=idx)
df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()  # +16.9 MB reported, +69.2 MB actual
```

Since `str` is the default string dtype in pandas 3.x, this affects any
string-indexed object after its first label lookup.

### Expected Behavior

`memory_usage(deep=True)` should account for the object-dtype array the engine
retains and, for dtypes where the engine exclusively owns the boxed values, for
those values too. Concretely, `IndexEngine.sizeof` could add `self.values.nbytes`
(plus `lib.memory_usage_of_objects` when `deep=True` and the array is not shared
with the Index), or `HashTable.sizeof` could honour `deep`.

counted and `_engine.sizeof(deep=True)` returning nothing useful — but frames it
for `MultiIndex` and as an enhancement. Filing separately because the
arrow-backed string case is a plain under-report on a default dtype rather than

title: BUG cast values before categorical category lookup
body:
- [x] closes https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/66688

Values are now cast to the categories dtype before categorical code lookup. This prevents `Series.astype(CategoricalDtype(...))` from silently converting valid, castable values to missing values when the input and categories have different dtypes.

Missing values are excluded from the cast and retain their `-1` categorical codes.

Tests cover integer values with string categories and object-backed string values with integer categories.

title: BUG: preserve and improve support for UUID extension arrays

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
addresses part of #63511, replaces #64839.

Changes:

- construction.py: `sanitize_array` (and therefore Series ~~and pd.array~~) construction now keeps pyarrow arrays Arrow-backed when their type is a pa.BaseExtensionType (the remaining pyarrow types are already handled by `__array__`)
- dtypes.py: `ArrowDtype(pa.uuid()).type` is now correct
- array.py:
  - `_cmp_method` now compares via .cast(storage_type). see below regarding other pyarrow kernel backed methods
  - `ArrowExtensionArray.to_numpy` now returns a numpy object array of UUIDs (same special-casing as exists for time stamps), which also fixes a uuid-containing Series’ `repr`

pyarrow has no equal kernel for extension dtypes. this PR circumvents that for comparison (`_cmp_method`), but not for other kernel-backed routines like `unique`, `factorize`, `isin`, `value_counts`, `sort_values`, `groupby`, these still raise `ArrowNotImplementedError`. We should think about how to handle this: create an allowlist of pyarrow extension dtypes that can be compared/grouped/… by their storage dtypes, and then treat them like this PR does in `_cmp_method`? 

I used Claude Opus 5 for this

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

time = pd.Series([
    "2015-03-08 01:00:00", "2015-03-08 01:30:00", "2015-03-08 02:00:00",
    "2015-03-08 02:30:00", "2015-03-08 03:00:00", "2015-03-08 02:00:00",
    "2015-03-08 02:30:00", "2015-03-08 03:00:00", "2015-03-08 03:30:00",
    "2015-11-01 00:30:00", "2015-11-01 01:00:00", "2015-11-01 01:30:00",
    "2015-11-01 02:00:00", "2015-11-01 02:30:00", "2015-11-01 01:00:00",
    "2015-11-01 01:30:00", "2015-11-01 02:00:00", "2015-11-01 02:30:00",
    "2015-11-01 03:00:00",
])

# PyArrow-backed index: slicing fails/returns empty
pa_idx = (
    time.astype("timestamp[ns][pyarrow]")
        .dt.tz_localize("UTC")
        .dt.tz_convert("America/Denver")
        .rename("denver_time")
        .to_frame()
        .set_index("denver_time")
        .sort_index()
)
pa_idx.loc["2015":]  # TypeError
```

### Issue Description

When a DataFrame index is a PyArrow-backed timezone-aware timestamp, string-based `.loc` slicing (e.g., `.loc['2015':]`) raises
```
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'str'
```

### Expected Behavior

Works like with numpy backed data: 

```
import pandas as pd

time = pd.Series([
    "2015-03-08 01:00:00", "2015-03-08 01:30:00", "2015-03-08 02:00:00",
    "2015-03-08 02:30:00", "2015-03-08 03:00:00", "2015-03-08 02:00:00",
    "2015-03-08 02:30:00", "2015-03-08 03:00:00", "2015-03-08 03:30:00",
    "2015-11-01 00:30:00", "2015-11-01 01:00:00", "2015-11-01 01:30:00",
    "2015-11-01 02:00:00", "2015-11-01 02:30:00", "2015-11-01 01:00:00",
    "2015-11-01 01:30:00", "2015-11-01 02:00:00", "2015-11-01 02:30:00",
    "2015-11-01 03:00:00",
])

# PyArrow-backed index: slicing fails/returns empty
np_idx = (
    time
    .pipe(pd.to_datetime)
    #.astype("timestamp[ns][pyarrow]")
        .dt.tz_localize("UTC")
        .dt.tz_convert("America/Denver")
        .rename("denver_time")
        .to_frame()
        .set_index("denver_time")
        .sort_index()
)
np_idx.loc["2015":]  # works!
```

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import io

data = '''agency_cd,site_no,datetime,tz_cd,144166_00060,144166_00060_cd,144167_00065,144167_00065_cd
USGS,9333500,2001-05-07 01:00:00,MDT,71.0,A:[91],,

USGS,9333500,2001-05-08 03:00:00,MDT,70.0,A:[91],,'''

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow')

def to_denver_time(df_, time_col, tz_col):
    return (df_
     .assign(**{tz_col: df_[tz_col].replace('MDT', 'MST7MDT')})
     .groupby(tz_col)
     [time_col]
     .transform(lambda s: pd.to_datetime(s)
         .dt.tz_localize(s.name, ambiguous=True)
         .dt.tz_convert('America/Denver'))
     .astype('timestamp[ns, America/Denver][pyarrow]')
    )

def tweak_river(df_):
    return (df_
     .assign(datetime=to_denver_time(df_, 'datetime', 'tz_cd'))
     .rename(columns={'144166_00060': 'cfs'})
     .loc[:, ['datetime', 'cfs']]
     .set_index('datetime')
    )

dd = tweak_river(df)
def convert_to_numpy_datetime64(df):
    df2 = df.copy()
    df2.index = df2.index.astype('datetime64[ns, America/Denver]')
    return df2.sort_index()
np_idx = (dd
.pipe(convert_to_numpy_datetime64)
.index)
pa_idx = dd.index
missing_attrs = set(dir(np_idx)) - set(dir(pa_idx))
missing_attrs
```

### Issue Description

In the past with numpy backed dates in the index I could do something like
```
(df
.groupby(df.index.month)
.some_col
.describe()
)
```

to get summary stats for *some_col* by calendar month.

With pyarrow date types in the index the `.month` attribute and many others are missing.


### Expected Behavior

Consistency between np and pyarrow time index

## Summary

Clarifies the `func` parameter description in `DataFrame.aggregate` and `Series.aggregate` to explain how string function names are dispatched. When `func` is a string, it is looked up via `getattr` on the aggregated object first (so `"mean"` resolves to `DataFrame.mean` / `Series.mean`), with a fallback to the `numpy` namespace when the object supports the buffer protocol (`obj.__array__` exists); e.g. `"sum"` resolves to `numpy.sum`. `AttributeError` is raised if no match is found.

Closes #49528.

## Tooling

The patch was drafted by the contributor with assistance from the Hermes Agent CLI running the `minimax-m3` model in the contributor's local Hermes desktop app. The reasoning-effort setting was chosen by the contributor in the Hermes UI and is not visible to the agent, so it is reported here as **unspecified** rather than guessed. All changes were reviewed line-by-line by the contributor before commit, and `pre-commit run --files` was executed locally on the modified files.

## Implementation notes

The dispatch rules described in the new docstring text match the actual behavior in `pandas/core/apply.py`:

- The `Apply` engine class routes `func` strings through `apply_str()` (`pandas/core/apply.py:1031`, also `:330`, `:1347`, `:1690`).
- `apply_str` resolves the name using `getattr(obj, func)` first (`pandas/core/apply.py:741`), then falls back to `getattr(np, func)` only when `hasattr(obj, "__array__")` is true (`pandas/core/apply.py:842-846`).

This matches what the issue reporter (`arnaudlegout`) described, with two corrections:

- "numpy MRO fallback" is more accurately phrased as "fallback to the numpy namespace"; Python's `hasattr(np, func)` is a namespace lookup, not an MRO walk.
- The `axis=0` / `axis=1` description of column-vs-row argument shape was omitted because the reporter's wording mis-characterized it: `aggregate` transposes `axis=1` to `axis=0` internally (`pandas/core/frame.py:15168` and `pandas/core/apply.py:1068`) before calling `apply_str`, so from the function's perspective the argument is always a Series.

title: BUG: DateOffset silently truncated non-integer date components

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
Supersedes #69125, which the automation closed because #55909 was not assigned to me yet. The issue is assigned now, and the change is unchanged.

Applying a `DateOffset` multiplies its `relativedelta` by `n`, and dateutil's
`relativedelta.__mul__` casts every component through `int()`, so a fractional
value was discarded without warning:

```python
>>> datetime(2020, 1, 1) + pd.DateOffset(days=1.5)
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2, 0, 0)     # a whole day, not a day and a half
>>> datetime(2020, 1, 1) + pd.DateOffset(hours=1.5)
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 1, 30)    # correct
```

The second is correct because a lone sub-daily keyword is handled by `timedelta`,
which represents fractions exactly. Adding any date component switches to the
relativedelta path, so `DateOffset(days=1, hours=1.5)` lost the half hour too.

This raises `ValueError` on the relativedelta path instead, per @jbrockmendel's
comment on the issue. The timedelta path is unchanged, and a float that is a whole
number, such as `days=2.0`, is still accepted.
