Passing non-bool values to `numeric_only` in DataFrame reduction methods (`sum`, `prod`, `mean`, `median`, `min`, `max`, `std`, `var`, `sem`, `skew`, `kurt`) silently accepted any truthy/falsy value since pandas 2.0. title: BUG: rolling on ArrowDtype timestamp/duration returned float64 instead of raising
body:
needs_i8_conversion is False for ArrowDtype, so Rolling._prep_values did not reach the NotImplementedError it raises for datetime-like input. Arrow timestamps and durations fell through to the generic ExtensionArray branch and were converted with to_numpy(np.float64), silently returning raw nanosecond counts:

    pd.Series(dti).rolling(2).sum()
    # DataError: No numeric types to aggregate

    pd.Series(pd.array(dti, dtype=ArrowDtype(pa.timestamp("ns")))).rolling(2).sum()
    # 1    3.155760e+18      <- plausible-looking number, unit discarded

expanding and ewm share _prep_values and were affected identically. Both now match their NumPy counterparts.

This is the same root cause as GH#66338: a guard written against needs_i8_conversion silently fails to cover ArrowDtype. Rather than add a fourth inline copy of the "is this an Arrow timestamp/duration" test, promote the helper added there to pandas.core.dtypes.common as is_arrow_temporal_dtype and route the existing sites through it -- missing.py (3 sites, was _is_arrow_temporal) and arrow/array.py (2 sites in searchsorted and to_numpy, which tested self._pa_array.type inline).

The helper matches on pa.types.is_timestamp/is_duration rather than dtype.kind, so date32/date64 are excluded: they report kind "M" but are not backed by a DatetimeArray. Verified date32, date64, time64, decimal, bool, string, int64[pyarrow], Int64 and datetime64 all behave exactly as before.

title: API: reconsider returning read-only arrays from DataFrame/Series .array/.values/__array__

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
**Context**: during the implementation of the Copy-on-Write feature (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/48998), there was the idea to make returned arrays read-only for APIs that return underlying arrays (`.values`, `to_numpy()`, `__array__`).

This was initially only done for numpy arrays (the first two PRs), and recently also for columns backed by ExtensionArrays (both for when returning an EA (`.values` / `.array`) or returning the EA as a numpy array (`to_numpy()`, `__array__`)):

- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/51082
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/53704
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/61925

The idea behind returning a read-only array is as follows: with Copy-on-Write, the guarantee we provide is that mutating one _pandas_ object (Series, DataFrame) doesn't update another pandas object (whose data is shared as an implementation detail). But users can still easily get a viewing numpy array, and mutate that one. And at that point, we don't have any control over how this mutation propagates (it might update more objects than just the one from which the user obtained it, for example if other Series/DataFrames were sharing data with this object with CoW). 

Example to illustrate this:

```python
# creating a dataframe and a derived dataframe through some operation
# (that in this case didn't need to copy)
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
>>> df2 = df.sort_values(by="a").reset_index()

# getting a column and mutating this -> CoW gets triggered and only `ser` is changed, not `df`
>>> ser = df["a"]
>>> ser[0] = 100
>>> ser
0    100
1      2
2      3
Name: a, dtype: int64
>>> df
   a  b
0  1  4
1  2  5
2  3  6

# however, when the code is mutating the numpy array it got from the series (or dataframe)
# (though .values, or np.asarray(ser), etc), then even the derived `df2` is silently mutated
>>> ser = df["a"]
>>> arr = ser.values
>>> arr.flags.writeable = True  # <-- this is now needed because we made .values readonly
>>> arr[0] = 100
>>> df2
   index    a  b
0      0  100  4
1      1    2  5
2      2    3  6
```

Right now, with returning read-only arrays, I have to include `arr.flags.writeable = True` to make this work (otherwise the above example would raise an error in `arr[0] = 100` about the array being read-only). 

But if we didn't make the returned arrays read-only, this would work, and such mutations of the underlying numpy array would propagate unpredictably to other pandas series/dataframe objects.

title: BUG: Timedelta/Timestamp overflow guards broke on ndarray subclasses (GH#66552)
body:
Follow-up to the GH-66552 overflow-guard series (#66581, #66661, #66668, #66670, #66692) and to GH-43178 (#65515), all unreleased.

Every guard those PRs added either reduces with `np.max(..., initial=/where=)` or views the operand as `i8`, and both assume an exact `np.ndarray`:

```python
pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.ma.array([2.0, 3.0])
# TypeError: MaskedArray.max() got an unexpected keyword argument 'initial'
#   (initial= makes numpy dispatch to the subclass's own max(); np.matrix too)

pd.Timedelta(5, "ns") + np.ma.MaskedArray(np.array([10, 20], "M8[ns]"), mask=[False, True])
# array(['...015', '...025'], dtype='datetime64[ns]')   <- mask silently dropped,
#   masked payload exposed as a real timestamp; numpy gives masked_array([15, --])
```

Affected: `_addsub_timedelta64_array` and `_addsub_datetime64_array` in both `timedeltas.pyx` and `timestamps.pyx`, `_mul_numeric_array`, `_check_div_float_array`, and `TimedeltaArray._mul_float_overflowsafe` — the last one via `TimedeltaIndex`/`Series`, and it left the EA holding a `MaskedArray` whose `repr` raised `MaskError` even before #65515.

Each guard now measures a plain view of the operand and leaves the arithmetic itself on the subclass, so the overflow raise survives and so does the subclass. `_mul_float_overflowsafe` instead strips the subclass up front, since its result has to be a `TimedeltaArray` either way — that also makes its float branch agree with its integer branch, which already read through to the raw values.

The same `_addsub_*` helpers also read only the *base* unit out of the operand's dtype, so a multiplier was discarded:

```python
pd.Timedelta(1, "s") + np.array([1], "m8[10s]")
# array([2], dtype='timedelta64[s]')   <- every value came back divided by 10
```

`m8[10s]` is not a resolution pandas can hold, and GH-25611 (#68072) already rejects those dtypes everywhere an array of them can enter — the constructors, `pd.array`, a `dtype=` argument, and `DatetimeIndex`/`Series`/`TimedeltaIndex` arithmetic. These three helpers were the remaining hole, so they raise `ValueError` too. The whatsnew note for GH-25611 covers the added case.

`TimedeltaIndex` is otherwise unaffected throughout because it goes through `np.asarray` first.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which reproduced each case against numpy, wrote the fix and the regression tests, and verified the tests red against a pre-fix build.

title: BUG: isinstance(obj, DateOffset) deadlocked when called from a C extension under a tracer
body:
`OffsetMeta.__instancecheck__` and `__subclasscheck__` passed
`stacklevel=find_stack_level()` to their deprecation warnings. `find_stack_level`
walks the Python stack, and these two hooks are reachable from a C extension's
callback — `pa.array()`'s type inference calls `isinstance(obj, pandas.DateOffset)`
on each element of an object array. Running Python there re-enters the active
tracer, and `coverage`'s `data_lock` is not reentrant, so the process hangs:

```python
import warnings, numpy as np, pandas as pd

arr = pd.array([pd.Timedelta("1h"), None], dtype="duration[ns][pyarrow]")
other = np.empty(2, dtype=object)
other[:] = [pd.offsets.Hour(1)] * 2

warnings.simplefilter("error")
arr != other
```

`python repro.py` completes. `python -m coverage run repro.py` never returns.

| | warnings normal | warnings as errors |
|---|---|---|
| no coverage | ok | ok |
| `coverage run` | ok | **hangs** |

The hung stack, with pyarrow's C++ frames invisible to `faulthandler` between
`pa.array` and `find_stack_level`:

```
coverage/collector.py:242 in lock_data
pandas/util/_exceptions.py:41 in find_stack_level
pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py:876 in _box_pa_array   # pa.array(value, mask=mask)
pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py:723 in _box_pa
pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py:1176 in _cmp_method
```

`find_stack_level` exists to skip pandas-internal frames when a warning is raised
deep inside pandas. `isinstance`/`issubclass` are builtins that add no Python
frame, so in a metaclass hook there is never anything to skip and the walk can
only ever return the immediate caller. `stacklevel=1` is therefore equivalent and
free. Note it is `1` rather than `2`: the Cython-compiled hook does not
materialise a frame that `warnings` counts, so `2` would point one frame too far
out. The new test pins the attribution rather than the literal.

Only the two `OffsetMeta` hooks change. The other `find_stack_level()` calls in
`offsets.pyx` are in ordinary functions, where the walk is still needed.

This is what has been timing out every py312/py313 job on GH-68456 since
2026-09-11; those jobs run under `--cov` with warnings as errors.

title: BUG: where/mask mishandled a list `other` for extension dtypes (GH#63842)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
closes #63842

`ExtensionArray._where` and `._putmask` index `value[~mask]` directly, which only works if `value` is already an ndarray/ExtensionArray of exactly `len(self)`. Nothing upstream converts a plain list, so a list `other` silently fell back to `object` for `str`/`string[pyarrow]`/`interval` and raised `TypeError: only integer scalar arrays can be converted to a scalar index` for `Int64`/`Float64`/`boolean`/`ArrowDtype` — the reported bug is only the string half of that. `Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and boolean-mask setitem are fixed with it, since they route through the same two methods.

The conversion is done in a new `EABackedBlock._align_listlike_arg`, not in `ExtensionArray`. `_where`/`_putmask` keep their existing contract ("arraylike with the same length as self"), so an EA author still reads the same short method, and `EABackedBlock.where`/`.putmask` are their only callers outside the EAs themselves. Handling it at the block level also reaches `NDArrayBackedExtensionArray` and `SparseArray`, which override `_where` so a fix on the base class never applied to them, and the 2-D datetimelike blocks, where a list reached `np.where` unaligned and silently filled **every** masked position with `other[0]`.

A 2-D block now gets one alignment order: one entry per selected position (putmask only — the analogue of the `np.place` call `putmask_without_repeat` makes for numpy dtypes), then one value per column, then one value per row filling every column. A length that fits none of them raises `ValueError`. The order matters because a consolidated `datetime64[ns]`/`timedelta64[ns]` block holds every column of the frame while `Int64`/`ArrowDtype`/`Categorical`/`datetime64[ns, tz]`/`period` get a block each: before this they gave different answers for the same input, and now they agree.

Non-`Sequence` list-likes — `dict`, `set`, `MultiIndex` — are passed through untouched, so the EA holds them as a scalar (the object-backed dtypes) or rejects them (masked, Arrow, `Categorical`), exactly as before. A tuple is likewise left alone: object dtype holds one as a scalar (GH-37681), and `Index.fillna` admits one.

Note on the conversion: it goes through `com.asarray_tuplesafe` rather than `_from_sequence(dtype=self.dtype)`. `_from_sequence` coerces where we need it to raise — `str` turns `9` into `"9"` and `Categorical` turns an unknown category into `NaN` — and it is the setitem call raising that triggers the block's upcast to `object`.

Base extension tests cover the list shapes, xfailed for `SparseArray` (no item assignment) and `JSONArray` (its `__setitem__` mishandles a boolean mask, which is also the cause of the pre-existing `test_where_series` xfail there).

Not reconciled here: 1-D EA dtypes get one block per column, so they cannot see the frame's column count, and a multi-column EA frame still reads a row-length list per column (`df[key] = [10, 20, 30]`) where the numpy and object spellings raise. That needs the rule moved into `NDFrame._where`, which changes behavior for every dtype and belongs in its own PR. The whatsnew entries are scoped to what actually changed.

title: BUG: sparse binary ops left stored values equal to the result's fill_value (GH#45126)
body:
closes #45126
closes #45284

`SparseArray` binary operations left stored values equal to the result's `fill_value` in `sp_index`: the splib kernels return the union of the operands' indexes, and the other arms reuse an operand's own. Indexing a `SparseArray` with such a comparison result then selected every element, and `density`/`npoints`/`memory_usage` overstated how much the result stores. The same operation also gave a different `sp_index` depending on subtype, because the object route already re-sparsified while the numeric one did not.

`_wrap_result` now prunes stored values that would densify as the fill. Deciding that is not plain equality, so it is factored into `_differs_from_fill`: `-0.0` compares equal to a `0.0` fill but densifies differently, `isna` is true for a complex with either part NaN, and an object array can hold several NAs at once of which only the fill's own spelling densifies back as the fill.

Unary operators and single-input ufuncs have the same defect and are left alone here — they build results through `_simple_new` rather than `_wrap_result`, and pruning them turns `abs()` on a complex subtype into a `TypeError` for a reason that wants its own fix. The whatsnew is scoped to binary operations accordingly.

GH-45284's underlying cause also survives: `__getitem__` reads a boolean key's `sp_index` rather than its `sp_values`, which `fillna` can still trigger. This PR removes the route that made a comparison produce such a key.

title: BUG: SparseArray is not implemented as index first
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s1 = pd.arrays.SparseArray([1,0,-1,np.nan], fill_value=np.nan)
s1
# [1.0, 0.0, -1.0, nan]
# Fill: nan
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([0, 1, 2])
s2 = s1 + 1

# wrong SA after comparison with other SA
s1 > s2
# [False, False, False, False]
# Fill: False
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([0, 1, 2])
# should be 
# Indices: array([])

# wrong SA after comparison with other ndarray
a = np.array([0,1,2,3])
s1 > a

# [True, False, False, False]
# Fill: False
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([0, 1, 2, 3])
# should be
# Indices: array([0])

# wrong SA after filling na values
s1.fillna(-1)

# [1.0, 0.0, -1.0, -1]
# Fill: -1
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([0, 1, 2])
# should be
# Indices: array([0, 1])

# wrong SA in case of changing the fill_value
s1.fill_value = -1
s1
# [1.0, 0.0, -1.0, -1]
# Fill: -1
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([0, 1, 2])
# should be 
# Indices: array([0, 1])

# wrong SA in case of arithmetic operations:
sa = pd.arrays.SparseArray([0,0,np.nan,-2,-1,4,2,3,0,0],fill_value=0)
sa
# [0, 0, nan, -2.0, -1.0, 4.0, 2.0, 3.0, 0, 0]
# Fill: 0
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])

sa + 1
# [1.0, 1.0, nan, -1.0, 0.0, 5.0, 3.0, 4.0, 1.0, 1.0]
# Fill: 1.0
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])

# Indices of result are wrong. It should be:
pd.arrays.SparseArray([1.0, 1.0, np.nan, -1.0, 0.0, 5.0, 3.0, 4.0, 1.0, 1.0], fill_value=0)
# [1.0, 1.0, nan, -1.0, 0, 5.0, 3.0, 4.0, 1.0, 1.0]
# Fill: 0
# IntIndex
# Indices: array([0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
```



### Issue Description

In current implementation of SparseArray class usually doesn't work with own indices.

When I has starting to work with SparseArray in pandas, I've noticed, that many operations (unary, binary and some methods) work with SparseArray the same as basic ndarray. In some case it uses explicit (to_dense) cast, in the other case it apply operations only to internal sp_values array and doesn't check the indices.
As a result we have wrong SparseArray instances (see examples above). Pay attention that printed arrays are correct, but indices are not.

Anyway in both case the logic doesn't fit the nature of Sparse array.

I suggest to discuss new private api that will be based on sparse logic, because only this way will lead us to effective structure that Sparse Array represents.

There are few open questions about the API:

- [ ] __Deprecation of setting fill_value__
       I'm not sure that changing fill_value is good point and what is crucial that is the real life case. In the one of examples that I wrote above, e.g. SA that contains both nan and some fill_value (e.g. -1) is looks no natural. I think in such case user should cast own data to using only one fill_value before loading it to SA. See #21818.

- [ ] __Fill_value dtype should match with SparseDType__
       See #23124. Now we can create boolean sparsearray and set fill_value as any value of other type.

- [ ] __Implement index first logic__
      The idea is that all operation with SparseArray should be based on indices, because as I understand it this is the meaning of sparse array. Here I don't have concrete suggestion. I will try to add something later. Perhaps we should use as example scipy and other frameworks that have such types.

- [ ] __Should operations touch the whole array?__
       Perhaps any operation should work only with non zero elements. In this case we just to check if some of values became fill_value and in case of true remove it from sp_values and sp_indices.


Links for study:
- Theory:
  - [Sparse matrix - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_matrix)
- APIs from other frameworks:
  - [Sparse matrices (scipy.sparse) — SciPy v1.7.1 Manual](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/sparse.html)
  - [pydata/sparse: Sparse multi-dimensional arrays for the PyData ecosystem](https://github.com/pydata/sparse)
  - [Boost. vector_sparse](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_78_0/libs/numeric/ublas/doc/vector_sparse.html)
  - [Enhanced C#: Loyc.Collections.SparseAList< T > Class Template Reference](http://ecsharp.net/doc/code/classLoyc_1_1Collections_1_1SparseAList.html#details)
  - [Sparse Arrays · The Julia Language](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/stdlib/SparseArrays/#Sparse-Arrays)
  - [Create sparse matrix - MATLAB sparse](https://www.mathworks.com/help/matlab/ref/sparse.html)
  - [Eigen: Eigen::SparseVector< _Scalar, _Options, _StorageIndex > Class Template Reference](https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/classEigen_1_1SparseVector.html)
- Application examples:

title: BUG: DataFrame.sparse.from_spmatrix gave the unstored entries a missing value (GH#59212)

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
closes #59212

`scipy.sparse` defines a matrix's unstored entries as zero, and every dtype it supports (bool, int8-64, uint8-64, float32/64, complex64/128) has a representable zero. GH-59063 reported that `from_spmatrix` raised `ValueError` for a bool matrix, because it hardcoded an integer `0` as the fill value, which `SparseDtype` rejects for a bool subtype. GH-59064 fixed that by dropping the fill value entirely, falling back to `SparseDtype`'s NA default — so float and complex matrices came back with `NaN` in the unstored positions and the frame no longer held the same values as `spmatrix.toarray()`. The minimal fix for GH-59063 was a subtype-appropriate zero, which `SparseArray.from_spmatrix` has used all along; this uses the same expression, so the two entry points agree again.

GH-59064 also deleted `to_coo`'s `fill_value != 0` guard and its test, which made `to_coo` silently write zeros in the unstored positions of a column with a non-zero fill value. Restored, made NA-safe (`pd.NA != 0` is `pd.NA`, which cannot be used as a condition), with `pd.NA` added to the test's parametrization.

The two halves have to land together: with the guard restored and `from_spmatrix` left as-is, the `to_coo` example in `doc/source/user_guide/sparse.rst` raises.

title: DEPR: out-of-bounds scalar setitem into a numpy-nullable integer array (GH#48867)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
closes #48867

Redo of GH-68943 (reverted by GH-68971) as a deprecation rather than an immediate raise.

`BaseMaskedArray.__setitem__` now emits a `Pandas4Warning` when numpy stored a scalar altered to fit instead of rejecting it; the 3.x result is unchanged. numpy range-checks a python scalar whatever the key, but a numpy scalar only for a signed dtype under an integer or slice key — so an unsigned dtype with any key, or a signed one with a fancy or boolean key, silently stored the wrong value. That second case covers `where`/`mask`/`replace`/`putmask`, which all arrive with a mask key: `pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="Int8").where(mask, np.int64(1000))` gives `-24` today. Warning after the store rather than before keeps the paths where numpy raises untouched, without having to encode which key/dtype combinations it checks.

Two notes on the GH-68943 thread. The premise there — that the fillna et al cases "currently actually gave a correct but upcasted result" — holds for the *numpy-backed* dtypes, not the masked ones: every masked path either raises `OverflowError` or stores the value altered, and none upcast. And `Series.fillna` is not covered by this PR, on main or on the branch — it raises `OverflowError` from `scalar_fillna_inplace` before reaching `__setitem__`. Since numpy-backed `where` does upcast, the consistent 4.0 endpoint for masked may be to upcast rather than to raise; worth settling before enforcement.

`shift(fill_value=)` and the float-overflow arm are left alone, as in GH-68943.

title: BUG: DataFrame.isetitem and __setitem__ silently corrupted the frame when the value's column count did not match the target

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
Found by a post-merge audit of GH-65491, which deleted a FIXME reading "refactor, clearly separate broadcasting & zip-like assignment" on the grounds that it was stale. It was not — it marked this defect. No issue was open for it.

`BlockManager.iset` only validated the value's column count under `if lib.is_integer(loc)` — the GH-46544 guard added in GH-66001. With a sequence or slice `loc` nothing checked that `value` had one column per position, so the zip-like branch's `value[placement.indexer]` stored a block narrower than its placement when the value was too narrow, and silently dropped the extras when it was too wide.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.isetitem([0, 1], np.array([7, 8, 9]))   # no exception
df.shape        # (3, 2)
df._mgr.blocks  # (NumpyBlock: slice(0, 2, 1), 1 x 3, dtype: int64,)
repr(df)        # IndexError: index 1 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 1
df.to_numpy()   # (3, 1) -- column "b" silently gone
```

`DataFrame.__setitem__` reaches the same code whenever the key matches several columns (duplicate or `MultiIndex` columns) and the value is one that `_set_item`'s `np.tile` broadcast skips — a timezone-aware `datetime64` or `period` value, or a 2D array:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3]] * 3, columns=["a", "a", "b"])
df["a"] = pd.Series(pd.date_range("2030", periods=3, tz="UTC"))  # same corruption
```

Both reproduce on released 3.0.5 and on 2.3.3; `iset` there has only the row-shape `AssertionError`.

The fix compares against `blklocs`, which is already computed one line above and normalizes int, slice, boolean-mask and integer-array `loc` into a single length, so one check covers every form. The integer-loc guard stays: `_iset_single` returns before the new check, so it is still load-bearing. An empty `loc` writes nothing, so it is exempt and stays the no-op it is on main.

Two things the guard would otherwise have broken are carried here rather than deferred:

- A scalar `value` sanitizes to one column, so `df.isetitem([0, 1], 5)` — which the method's own docstring documents as `value : scalar or arraylike` — would have hit the new check with a message about "1 columns". It now fills every selected position, as the label spelling does, for each `loc` spelling that selects several (list, slice, boolean mask, and the empty forms).
- `_set_item`'s tiling gate was `not isinstance(value.dtype, ExtensionDtype)` where `iset` uses `is_1d_only_ea_dtype`, so exactly two dtype families — tz-aware `datetime64` and `period` — fell between the two and would have gone from silent corruption to `ValueError` while every neighbouring dtype broadcasts. They now broadcast as well; `np.tile` would degrade the EA to object, so that arm uses `reshape`/`repeat`.

The `isetitem` docstring now states the shape rule the new `ValueError` enforces, which was previously only in the error string.

Not fixed here, and filed locally instead: 1d-only EA values still broadcast for a sequence `loc` (`df.isetitem([0, 1], pd.Categorical([...]))`), so `isetitem` semantics still depend on `value.dtype`; a zero-column 2D value slips past the `len(value) > 1` guards in `_iset_single` and `insert` and corrupts the same way, so repairing only the `iset` arm would leave `df[new] = <0-col>` broken; and the `DataFrame`-value branch of `isetitem` counts `len(loc)`, so a boolean-mask loc is counted by the mask's length.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which investigated the audit finding, wrote the fix and tests, and ran a multi-round review loop over the branch; reviewed by me before opening.

title: API: should the _supports_2d contract require repeat(axis=...)?

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: ExtensionArray - New Method Request
labels.description: Suggestion to add a new method to the EA base class/interface.

body:
`ExtensionDtype._supports_2d` documents what a third-party array must provide to
declare itself 2-D capable (`pandas/core/dtypes/base.py`):

> Arrays that support 2D values should:
>
> - implement Array.reshape
> - subclass the Dim2CompatTests in tests.extension.base
> - `_concat_same_type` should support `axis` keyword
> - `_reduce` and reductions should support `axis` keyword

`repeat` is not on that list, and the base implementation actively rejects an axis:

```python
# pandas/core/arrays/base.py
def repeat(self, repeats, axis: AxisInt | None = None) -> Self:
    nv.validate_repeat((), {"axis": axis})
```

while the backing-array implementation both defaults to and honours one:

```python
# pandas/_libs/arrays.pyx
def repeat(self, repeats, axis: int | np.integer = 0):
```

In-tree this never shows, because the only dtypes with `_supports_2d = True` are
`DatetimeTZDtype` and `PeriodDtype`, whose arrays are `NDArrayBacked`. A third-party
array that implements the four documented requirements and inherits
`ExtensionArray.repeat` would raise
`ValueError: the 'axis' parameter is not supported in the pandas implementation of repeat()`.

This matters because the gate internals use to decide "may I treat this as 2-D" is

```python
def is_1d_only_ea_dtype(dtype) -> bool:
    return isinstance(dtype, ExtensionDtype) and not dtype._supports_2d
```

so anything reaching a 2-D code path is exactly the `_supports_2d` audience. Broadcasting
a 1-D value across several columns wants `value.reshape(1, -1).repeat(ncols, axis=0)`, which
works for both in-tree types and for any `NDArrayBacked` array, but is not something the
documented contract entitles pandas to call.

Two ways to resolve it:

1. Add `repeat` with `axis` support to the `_supports_2d` requirements, and relax the base
   signature/validation for 2-D-capable arrays. This documents what pandas already needs and
   costs existing third-party authors nothing until they opt into `_supports_2d`.
2. Treat `repeat(axis=)` as out of contract and require internals to spell 2-D broadcasting
   with only the four documented operations, e.g. `value.repeat(ncols).reshape(-1, ncols)`.
   That is contract-clean but produces a C-contiguous result where the current spelling gives
   an F-contiguous one, which changes the stored block's layout on the NumPy path.

No in-tree caller passes `axis=` to an ExtensionArray's `repeat` today, so nothing is broken
right now; this is about whether such a call is legitimate going forward.

title: BUG: arithmetic on length-zero ExtensionArrays (GH#40624)

labels.name: Testing
labels.description: pandas testing functions or related to the test suite

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
closes #40624

The extension-array arithmetic tests never exercised a length-zero operand. This adds that
coverage and fixes the three bugs it turns up.

**Coverage.** Rather than new test methods, `_check_length_zero` is called from `_check_op`
and `_compare_other` in `pandas/tests/extension/base/ops.py`, asserting
`op(obj[:0], other[:0]) == op(obj, other)[:0]`. That placement is deliberate: subclasses such
as `TestNumpyExtensionArray` set `self.series_scalar_exc` and friends *inside* their overrides
of `test_arith_series_with_scalar`, so a separately-named test runs against the class-level
defaults instead (348 spurious failures when I tried it that way). Folding the check into the
shared helpers means every existing subclass override and xfail applies unchanged, which also
keeps third-party EAs — pint-pandas, the reporter here — from needing new overrides.

**Bugs fixed.**

1. `PeriodArray.__sub__` raised `TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a real number,
   not 'NaTType'` for any length-zero operand (array, `Period` scalar, `PeriodIndex`, `Series`).
   `np.array()` over an empty list of `DateOffset`s infers float64, so the `new_data[mask] = NaT`
   write failed. Long-standing; not a regression from GH-66682.
2. `lib.is_string_array` is `False` for an empty array, so length-zero `string[python]` /
   `str[python]` arithmetic fell back to `object` dtype instead of the string dtype.
3. A length-zero object-dtype operand boxes to the pyarrow `null` type, which has no
   `binary_join_element_wise` kernel, so e.g. `Series[string[python]] + Series[str]` worked at
   full length but raised `TypeError` when empty. The fix is scoped to null-typed *and*
   length-zero so that a length-zero `int64[pyarrow]` operand still raises as it should.

Comparison ops turned out to be consistent on every dtype; the new check covers them anyway.

Full suite green locally.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the test-placement
experiment, bisected the three failures to their root causes, and drafted the patch and tests
under my review.

title: BUG: list-of-tuples setitem silently written column-major (GH#65264)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
Follow-up to GH-65264. That PR is unreleased (its note is in the `v3.1.0` whatsnew and there is no 3.0.x backport), so the bug below never shipped and no separate whatsnew entry is added here. It is still worth fixing before 3.1.0: checked against a released 3.0.5, both routes below raise `ValueError` there, so shipping 3.1 as it stands would be a silent-wrong-data regression from 3.0.x.

GH-65264 added an escape hatch out of the 2D dispatch in `_setitem_with_indexer_split_path`, so that a list of mismatched-length tuples aimed at a single object column is stored per cell rather than treated as a 2D value (GH-37629). The hatch was unconditional on the number of target columns, so it also fired for multi-column selections whenever the tuple width happened to disagree with the column count:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x", "y", "z"], "b": [1, 2, 3], "c": [4.0, 5.0, 6.0]})
df.loc[:, ["b", "c"]] = [(10, 20, 30), (40, 50, 60)]   # 2x3 value into a 3x2 target
```

That is a genuine shape mismatch, which `_setitem_with_indexer_2d_value` used to reject. Instead it fell through to the `len(ilocs) == len(value)` branch and wrote each tuple as a whole column — `b == [10, 20, 30]`, `c == [40, 50, 60]`, silently. The same value spelled as a list of lists or as an ndarray still raised `ValueError: Must have equal len keys and value when setting with an ndarray`, so identical data either raised or was silently transposed depending only on whether its rows were tuples. A second route through the same hatch, an all-False row mask with a value as long as the frame, silently discarded the assignment rather than rejecting it.

Gating the hatch on `len(ilocs) == 1` restores the pre-GH-65264 behaviour for multi-column selections. With a single target column the old `len(value[0]) != len(ilocs)` condition is exactly `len(value[0]) != 1`, so the single-column path — and the GH-37629 fix — is unchanged. Since GH-68021 landed on main, that condition lives in the `_is_2d_value_for_columns` helper, so the gate is applied there as `ncols == 1` rather than at the call site.

The gate also affects one multi-column route that the hatch was handling *correctly*, which is worth calling out since it is not a shape mismatch: with a scalar row key,

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [None] * 3, "b": [None] * 3, "c": [1, 2, 3]})   # object, object, int
df.loc[0, ["a", "b"]] = [(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)]   # one tuple per column, into one row
```

stored one tuple per cell on the split path and now raises. Raising is the right outcome — 3.0.5 raises here, and the list-of-lists and ndarray spellings of the same value already raised on main — but nothing pinned it, so `test_setitem_2d_value_scalar_row_multi_column` does. Note this spelling still succeeds on a *consolidated* frame; that split-vs-consolidated divergence predates this PR and is left alone.

Deliberately not changed:

- The hatch is **not** narrowed to object dtype. A pyarrow list column legitimately uses it: `df.loc[:, ["a"]] = [(1, 2), (3, 4)]` on `ArrowDtype(pa.list_(pa.int64()))` correctly gives `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]`, and an object-only gate would also make the list-key spelling raise while the equivalent scalar-label spelling kept working. There is a test pinning this.
- Length-1 tuples into a single column still unwrap (`[(1,), (2,)]` -> `[1, 2]`), which is what `list`, `ndarray`, `Series`, `Index` and `pd.array` rows already do (GH-64230). `tuple` was added to that test's parametrization.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and the tests and ran the review loop that produced them.

title: BUG: loc/iloc setitem raised for a 2D value in a single object cell

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
Follow-up to a post-merge review comment on GH-66702, where @jorisvandenbossche asked why a 2D value set into a single `object` cell is a shape mismatch rather than simply stored.

It shouldn't be. The answer depended on block layout:

```python
value = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

# more than one dtype -> split path
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.zeros(2, dtype=object), "b": [0, 0]})
df.iloc[0, 0] = value
# ValueError: Must have equal len keys and value when setting with an ndarray

# single block -> stored
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.zeros(2, dtype=object), "b": np.zeros(2, dtype=object)})
df.iloc[0, 0] = value  # df.iloc[0, 0] is value
```

Same divergence for a list of `ndarray`/`Series`/`Index`/`ExtensionArray` rows and for a 2-D `ndarray`. Verified identical in 2.3.3, 3.0.6 and `main`, so this is long-standing rather than a regression; GH-64230 and GH-66702 only moved which value kinds reach the raise.

Cause is branch order in `_setitem_with_indexer_split_path`: the `_is_2d_value_for_columns` check runs ahead of the branch that stores nested data in a single cell, so the shape rules for a multi-column selection get applied to a one-cell selection. Single-block frames never take that path, which is why they store.

This moves the single-cell branch above the 2-D check, canonizing the single-block answer. It also hops the "multiple rows in a single column" branch, which is inert here: that branch requires `not is_scalar(pi)`, and `_is_scalar_access` implies `is_scalar(pi)`.

`raise` -> `store` is strictly widening, so nothing that works today changes.

The test that pinned the old behavior is inverted and re-aimed at the property: it now parametrizes the second column's dtype, which is what decides single- vs multi-block, so the block-layout equivalence is what is under test. With the code change reverted, exactly the 12 multi-block parametrizations fail and the 12 single-block ones pass.

Still divergent after this, left alone deliberately: `df.iloc[0, 0] = some_dataframe` stores the single column as a `Series` on the split path and the whole frame on the single-block path, because the `ABCDataFrame` branch sits above the one moved here.

title: BUG: read_json(orient="table") could not read back non-string labels (GH#19129)
body:
closes #19129

The issue title asks for a `ValueError`, but on current main the symptom is worse than the 2018 report: an ordinary frame with default `RangeIndex` columns round-trips through `orient="table"` to all-NaN with no error at all.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1.5, 2.5], [3.5, 4.5]])
pd.read_json(StringIO(df.to_json(orient="table")), orient="table")
#     0   1
# 0 NaN NaN
# 1 NaN NaN
```

An int-dtype frame instead raises `IntCastingNaNError` (`Error while type casting for column '0'`), as does a non-string index name; a `MultiIndex` with a non-string level name raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'startswith'` on the *write* side.

The schema field `name` is JSON-serialized from the label, so an int label stays the JSON number `5`, while the record keys in `"data"` are `str(label)` (`"5"`). `parse_table_schema` looked the data up by the schema name and matched nothing.

So this makes the labels round-trip rather than rejecting them. Matching is done on the field name's string form, with the original labels restored at the end.

The fast parser perturbs `0.3` into `0.30000000000000004`, which would otherwise make the match fail for a perfectly ordinary frame. A key that parses back to the same double as the perturbed field name spells that label exactly, so `float()` on the key recovers it. The two are not always the same text — `1e16` is written `10000000000000000.0` in the schema and `1e+16` as the key — so the match is on the parsed value, not the spelling. Labels that no key recovers, including every label when `"data"` has no keys at all, fall back to decoding the document a second time at full precision; worth avoiding, since that decode costs a transient roughly 10x the payload size.

A `"data"` payload of arrays rather than objects has no keys at all, so those labels are used as written. Where `"data"` holds objects, two cases raise `ValueError` instead of reading as NaN: two distinct labels that share a string form (`5` and `"5"`), and a label no key matches when some key matches no field — that orphan key is the evidence the label was spelled differently. Without one the column reads as all-missing, which is what a string label already does.

Two write-side fixes come along because the round-trip needs them: `set_default_names` is guarded against a non-string `MultiIndex` level name, and a falsy `Series` name (`0`, `False`, `""`) is no longer replaced by the `"values"` placeholder — only a `None` name is a missing name.

Not addressed here, and left for a follow-up on the write side: `None`, tuple, and duplicate labels still emit a schema `name` that disagrees with the data keys. The full remedy is to derive the schema `name` from the same stringification the C writer uses for object keys, which is a larger change to `build_table_schema` than this needs. GH-25488 proposed switching the data payload to `orient="values"` arrays — correct diagnosis, too invasive.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which reproduced the symptoms on main, wrote the fix and tests, and ran a multi-round adversarial review of the branch that caught several defects in its own earlier drafts.

title: BUG: MultiIndex setops split a string operand entry into its elements (GH#39699)
body:
Note: this does **not** close GH-39699, which asks for the opposite change — see the last section.

`MultiIndex._convert_can_do_setop` passes a raw list-like operand straight to `MultiIndex.from_tuples`, which accepts any indexable row and so decomposes a string or bytes entry into its elements. When the entry's length matches `nlevels`, the setop treats it as a tuple of level values:

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]])
mi.intersection(["ac"])              # MultiIndex([('a', 'c')])  -- "ac" is not in mi
mi.union([b"ac"])                    # adds (97, 99)
mi.intersection([("a", "c"), "bd"])  # "bd" matches ('b', 'd')
```

The four setops now raise the existing `TypeError("other must be a MultiIndex or a list of tuples")` for such an operand. Everything else keeps its existing path through `from_tuples`, including `np.void` rows and null entries, which `lib.to_object_array_tuples` deliberately expands to an all-null row.

Two deliberate behavior changes worth a reviewer's attention:

- Splitting a length-`nlevels` label has two outcomes today — it matches spuriously when the characters line up, and returns the right answer by accident when they don't. Both now raise, so e.g. on 2-level columns `cols.difference(["id"])` returned both columns before and now raises. A deprecation cycle isn't really available, since it would mean continuing to return `('a', 'c')` from `mi.intersection(["ac"])` for another release; the `MultiIndex.isin` change in GH-20252 is the local precedent for going straight to raising.
- On a one-level `MultiIndex` a single-character label used to match. Any longer label already raised.

On GH-39699 itself: it asks for `mi.intersection(["some_col"])` to return an empty index, as it did on 1.1.5. That result was the same split — `"some_col"` became an 8-level MultiIndex, which then intersected to empty. Ten existing assertions pin `TypeError` for a raw list of non-tuples, so raising seemed the consistent reading, and I've left the issue open for that separate question.

title: BUG: Timestamp rejected fold with positional date components (GH#52117)
body:
closes #52117

`Timestamp.__new__` validates `fold` before the `if/elif` chain that decides which of the three calling forms is in play. The guard accepted only the keyword-component form or a naive datetime, so the *positional* by-component form — where `ts_input` holds the integer year — fell through to the "possibly unambiguous input" error, whose own advice is to build from components:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
ValueError: Cannot pass fold with possibly unambiguous input: ...
>>> pd.Timestamp(year=2020, month=1, day=1, hour=0, minute=0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
Timestamp('2020-01-01 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC')
```

The fix exempts that form too, keyed on both leading arguments being integers rather than on `year` alone, so the guard cannot admit an input the dispatch chain routes to an earlier arm (null-like, `float` and `bool` first arguments all reach `elif` arms above the positional one).

This also removes a limitation GH-31930 documented in the 3.1.0 whatsnew: `datetime.__replace__` reconstructs subclasses through the 8-positional-argument form and passes `fold` when it is nonzero, so `copy.replace()` raised on any `fold=1` timestamp. That clause is deleted and the test pinning it now pins the fixed behavior.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which investigated the issue, wrote the fix and tests, and ran a differential sweep against `main` and stdlib `datetime`; reviewed by me before opening.

title: BUG: replace silently discards a compiled regex on ArrowDtype strings

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

body:
`Series.replace`/`DataFrame.replace` silently discarded a compiled `re.Pattern` on arrow-backed string dtypes:

```python
pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string())).replace(re.compile("^a"), "z")
# ['a', 'b']   <- discarded; object, str, string[python] and string[pyarrow] all substitute
```

`Block._replace_regex` gated compiled patterns on a literal allowlist, `_regex_target_dtype(self.dtype) not in [object, "string"]`. `ArrowDtype(pa.string())` matches neither, so the pattern never reached `replace_regex`. The string spelling of the same pattern was unaffected — `is_re("^a")` is False, so it never hit the guard.

The allowlist is now `is_string_dtype(target) and target.kind != "S"`. The `kind != "S"` half keeps numpy bytes out, since `is_string_dtype` counts them and a regex can never match bytes (without it a `|S2` Series silently upcast to `object` on what is still a no-op). The predicate is still applied to `_regex_target_dtype`, which resolves a `Categorical` to its categories' dtype (GH-68928), so a `Categorical` of arrow strings stops being a silent no-op too.

Widening the gate is not enough on its own: the object-upcast escape hatch on the next lines asks `can_hold_element`, which returns `True` for every `ArrowDtype` (`pandas/core/dtypes/cast.py`, under the comment "This is technically incorrect"), so an unholdable replacement never triggered the upcast. That is already visible on the released string spelling — `replace("^a", 1, regex=True)` raises `ArrowInvalid` and `replace(regex={"^a": 1})` silently stores `"1"`, where every other string dtype upcasts to `object` — and the compiled spelling would join them once the gate admits it. For an arrow string block the decision is now made directly: a `str`, a regex (left to raise on write, as `StringDtype` does), or a scalar NA fits, and anything else upcasts. That branch is gated on the same string predicate, so a non-string arrow column keeps its dtype through a frame-wide sweep like `df.replace(r"^\s*$", 0, regex=True)`.

Not covered here, each a separate defect with its own review surface: dictionary-encoded arrow strings, which `is_string_dtype` rejects, and `pa.string_view()`, where the direct path discards silently just as `string` did while the `regex=` dict path raises `NotImplementedError` from `ArrowDtype.type`, so admitting it to `is_string_dtype` would not be enough.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix, the tests and this description; reviewed and verified by me.

title: BUG: Rolling/Expanding skew and kurt wrong on data with a large shared offset
body:
The sliding moment accumulators behind `Rolling.skew`/`kurt` (and `Expanding.skew`/`kurt`, which
share the kernels) take every deviation against a running mean. On a series carrying a large
offset the mean dwarfs the spread, so the deviations lose most of their significant digits and the
results are silently wrong — on a 4-wide window of values one ulp apart at 1e8, `kurt` returned
213, where the attainable range for 4 points is [-6, 4]. Separately, once a window's observation
count dropped to zero the accumulators divided by it and every later window returned `NaN`.

This anchors the accumulators to each window's first value so an offset shared by the window
cancels exactly, retires that anchor once the window's centre drifts away from it, and replaces
the per-kernel cancellation tests with a shared detector (a NaN arm, an anchor-drift arm, and a
peak-deviation arm). It is the treatment `Rolling.cov`/`corr` already received in GH-66678.

The NaN-forever half is a long-standing bug; the low-variance half surfaced in GH-64366, which
dropped the `m2 <= nobs * 1e-14` guard that had been returning `NaN` there instead of a wrong
number. The underlying precision loss predates both — 2.3.3 pre-centred the values by the rounded
global mean, and GH-62863/GH-63143 dropped that when they introduced the incremental instability
machinery.

Dropping the two per-kernel arms also removes the rescan-every-window fallbacks they triggered, so
this is a speedup as well as an accuracy fix:
`pd.Series(np.tile([-1., 0., 1., 0.], 25_000)).expanding().skew()` goes from 5.3s to 0.7ms (the
old behaviour was quadratic in the length of the series), and
`pd.Series(rng.lognormal(0, 5, 50_000)).rolling(1000).kurt()` from 54ms to 0.6ms.

Accuracy, measured against an exact rational oracle over 83,772 windows per statistic (142 series
× 6 window widths, covering shared offsets, drifting levels, lognormal, mixed-magnitude and
NaN-holed data):

| | p99 rel err | max rel err |
|---|---|---|
| `skew` before | 3.3e+01 | 4.6e+23 |
| `skew` after | 1.0e-11 | 4.9e-08 |
| `kurt` before | 4.8e+02 | 2.9e+32 |
| `kurt` after | 1.8e-10 | 3.5e-07 |

No window in that sweep comes back worse than `main` by more than 1e-6 relative.

Two consequences worth calling out. A window of identical values reached incrementally on offset
data used to come back as a number rather than `NaN`, because the digits the accumulators had lost
left `m2` nonzero; it is `NaN` now, which is what GH-62864 already specifies for a degenerate
window. And the new detector is not free on data that never needed it: in an ABBA-ordered
measurement with untouched `rolling.median`/`var` as controls, `rolling(100).skew()` is 2.6% slower
on uniform data and 12.5% slower on lognormal data, against the wins above.

One known limit, pre-existing and deliberately not widened into here: the same
overflow-in-the-detector shape affects `roll_var` and the `cov`/`corr` diagonal.

and reviewed across several passes before opening.

title: BUG: DataFrame.agg with a list of funcs rounds uint64 results (GH#65031)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65031, which added the list-of-reductions fast path in
`FrameApply._agg_list_like_frame_reductions`. That path computes DataFrame-level reductions per
dtype group and stacks one 1-row frame per function with `concat`. When the functions return
different dtypes for a column, the stack reconciles them to a common dtype that need not hold
the results:

```python
big = 2**64 - 3
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.Series([big, 1], dtype="uint64")})

df.agg(["max", "count"])
# main:   max -> 1.8446744073709552e+19, dtype float64   (true value 18446744073709551613)
# 3.0.6:  max -> 18446744073709551613,   dtype object
```

`max` returns unsigned and `count` signed, and the dtype that holds both is float64. The
`uint64[pyarrow]` spelling raised `ArrowInvalid` on the same cast instead of rounding.

Now, when the functions disagree on dtype, the stacked frame has to still hold every result
exactly; the columns where it does not are replaced with object, individually, so a column's
output dtype does not depend on its siblings' values. When the cast is refused outright — a
`uint64[pyarrow]` column raises rather than rounding — each column is retried on its own.
Results are compared as object arrays, because a numpy scalar widens the original back to the
stacked dtype and so compares a rounded value against itself; `Series.tolist` is not enough,
since a `Sparse` column's elements stay numpy scalars. `pandas/core/array_algos/quantile.py`
already decides a result dtype with a cast-round-trip check, in the float-to-int direction where
a numpy comparison suffices.

Groups whose functions agree on dtype, and groups whose stacked dtype does hold every result,
are untouched — `df.agg(["sum"])` and ordinary magnitudes keep both their dtype and the speedup
from GH-65031.

The fast path is unreleased, but the check also changes released behavior, so there is an
*Other API changes* entry: `df.agg(["sum", "mean"])` on an int64 column whose sum is not
representable in float64 now returns object where 3.0 returns a rounded float64. Sparing that
case would mean special-casing unsignedness. `Series.agg(["max", "mean"])` and
`df.agg({"a": ["max", "mean"]})` still round, via a different assembly path that this PR does
not touch.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests
and ran a dtype x function-list differential against the pre-GH-65031 path; reviewed by me.

title: BUG: DataFrame.clip with an extension-dtype array/Index bound degrades to object

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
`NDFrame._clip_with_one_bound` converts a non-`Series` list-like bound via `_align_for_op(threshold, axis, flex=None)` and passes the result to `where`. Since GH-61828 that routes an extension-dtype operand through `_maybe_align_series_as_frame`, which now returns an EA-columned `DataFrame` instead of the `Series` it used to return. `DataFrame.where` has an EA-aware column-wise path for a 1-D `other` but none for a 2-D one, so the bound interleaves to an object ndarray.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[10, 20], [30, 40]])

df.clip(lower=pd.array([15, 25], dtype="Int64"), axis=1).dtypes
# object, object   (int64, int64 before GH-61828)

df.clip(lower=pd.array([15, 25], dtype="Int64"), axis=1, inplace=True)
# TypeError: Invalid value '[[15]]' for dtype 'int64'
```

`_align_for_op` now skips that broadcast when `flex is None` — clip is that flag's only caller — so the bound stays a `Series` and takes the working 1-D path; the helper is renamed `_align_series_as_frame` since it no longer has a fallback. `_clip_with_one_bound` then pins `axis=1` when it gets a `Series` back with `axis=None`, since `_align_for_op` had already aligned the bound against `self.columns` and `DataFrame.align(Series, axis=None)` raises.

The object degradation never shipped, so against released 3.0 the only `clip` change is that `df.clip(lower=<extension-dtype array>)` with `axis` omitted no longer raises `ValueError: Must specify axis=0 or 1`.

Routing the bound back through the 1-D path made it reach `np_can_hold_element`'s `dtype.itemsize < tipo.itemsize` comparison, which runs before the `not isinstance(tipo, np.dtype)` guard and so raised `AttributeError` for any non-NumPy `tipo` carrying no `itemsize`. That is a released bug in its own right, not just a `clip` one: on 3.0 it fires for every setitem-shaped path that hands a `SparseArray` into an integer-dtype NumPy column.

```python
ser = pd.Series([10, 20, 30])
sp = pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, 2, 3])

ser.where([True, False, True], sp)                              # AttributeError on 3.0
ser.mask([True, False, True], sp)                               # AttributeError on 3.0
ser[[0, 1]] = sp[:2]                                            # AttributeError on 3.0
pd.Index([10, 20, 30]).putmask(np.array([True, False, True]), sp)  # AttributeError on 3.0
```

The comparison is now skipped when the dtype carries no `itemsize`; such an element falls through to the extension-array branch below, which re-runs the same guards on its densified values, so a `SparseArray` is accepted or rejected exactly as the nullable `Int64` spelling already was.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which diagnosed the regression, wrote the fix and tests, and ran a differential sweep against released 3.0.

title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray silently truncated a value an integer dtype cannot hold (GH#68638)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(2, 1.5)` returned `[1, 1, 3]` — the replacement landed, truncated toward zero, with no error and no warning. The numpy-backed Series upcasts to float64 and stores 1.5; the masked `Int64` Series raises `TypeError`. Only the arrow-backed one silently corrupted the value.

`ArrowExtensionArray._validate_setitem_value` boxed the value with `pa.scalar(value, type=pa_type)`, which converts unsafely — `pa.scalar(1.5, type=pa.int64())` is `1`. Because that never raised, the block-level machinery above it never engaged and `putmask_inplace` wrote the truncated value. The same boxing pattern appeared a second time in `fillna`.

This rejects a lossy value in `_validate_setitem_value` with `TypeError`, matching `BaseMaskedArray._validate_setitem_value`, and routes `fillna` through that same validation. `Series`/`DataFrame` now raise; `Index.fillna`/`Index.where`/`Index.putmask` upcast, since `Index` has no column-dtype contract to protect — both matching the nullable integer dtypes.

The check is a deny-list rather than masked's allow-list on purpose: an allow-list would also turn `arr[0] = "x"` from `ArrowInvalid` into `TypeError`, which is a separate change with its own test fallout.

It runs over list-likes as well as scalars. `pa.array` applies a safe cast to a numpy array but not to a Python list, so `arr[:2] = [9.5, 8.5]` truncated exactly as `arr[0] = 1.5` did while `arr[:2] = np.array([9.5, 8.5])` raised `ArrowInvalid` — the same operation, spelled three ways, silently corrupting in two of them. A non-finite `Decimal` and a `Fraction` fold into the same `TypeError` for the same reason. The scan short-circuits on a container whose own dtype is integer or boolean; other containers pay a few extra passes (measured at 1e6 elements: float64 ndarray 4.8 -> 6.0 ms, object-of-ints 27.1 -> 32.9 ms, int64 ndarray unchanged).

Routing `fillna` through the validator also tightens the PyArrow-backed `StringDtype`, where `pd.array(["a", None], dtype="str").fillna(b"z")` stored `"z"` and `fillna(np.array([1, 2], dtype=object))` stored `"2"`. `ExtensionArray.fillna` now validates exactly as item assignment does, which in turn accepts a PyArrow *string* scalar; `Series.where` with one stops falling back to `object`.

One behavior change is left unfinished: a 0-d ndarray fill into `Index.where`/`putmask`/`fillna` now raises `ArrowInvalid` after the upcast, where it previously truncated — `_box_pa` cannot box a 0-d ndarray for the widened type. Hoisting the `item_from_zerodim` unwrap out of the integer gate fixes it but regresses `timestamp`/`duration` setitem, so it is left for its own PR.

Adjacent defects found while working on this and deliberately left out: `insert` truncates through `_from_sequence`; `_box_pa_scalar` raises `AttributeError` for a `Timestamp` against a non-matching type; `interpolate`'s linear fast path integer-divides; a dictionary-encoded integer type is not `pa.types.is_integer` and so still truncates.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which diagnosed the root cause, wrote the fix and tests, and ran a multi-round adversarial review that caught two regressions in earlier versions of this branch.

title: BUG: iloc/loc setitem broadcast a 1-D value down rows on an all-datetimelike frame

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
`EABackedBlock.setitem` adapts a 2-D EA block's `(ncols, nrows)` storage layout by swapping the two entries of the indexer tuple rather than transposing `values`, since `EA.T` may not be a view (GH-45419). It reoriented only a 2-D ndarray value to match, so a **1-D value was broadcast down rows instead of across the selected columns**:

```python
arr = np.arange(12).reshape(4, 3).astype("i8")
df = pd.DataFrame(arr.view("M8[s]"), columns=list("abc"))

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::2] = np.array([100, 101], dtype="i8").view("M8[s]")
# each value lands in the wrong column, silently:
#   a=101, c=101 in row 0 and a=100, c=100 in row 2
#   expected (and what a float64 frame does): a=100, c=101 in both rows
```

Where the selection could not absorb the misplaced value it raised instead, as `OutOfBoundsDatetime: Incompatible (high-resolution) value` — the `coerce_to_target_dtype(..., raise_on_upcast=True)` fallback reporting a swallowed shape `ValueError` as a resolution problem, which is not something a user can act on.

The swap is also **not** a reorientation at all when both indexer entries are advanced indexers, since those broadcast against each other, so the unconditional `value.T` was wrong there too — with two list keys this raised, and with two boolean masks it silently wrote the transposed cells.

Both reorientations are now gated on whether the swap actually transposes the selection — it does only when the entries index separate axes, so a scalar entry (which drops one) and two advanced indexers (which broadcast against each other) both opt out, as does a key of two or more dimensions, which makes the selection 3-D.

An indexer tuple short of the column axis, which is what a trailing comma in the key produces, is padded before that gate, since the missing entry is a full slice. `Ellipsis` is normalized to a full slice as well, because `np.ndim(...)` is `0` and it would otherwise read as an axis-dropping scalar when it is the opposite — but only when there is exactly one, so numpy still rejects a duplicate. `np.newaxis` is the mirror case and is carved out: it adds an axis rather than consuming one, so neither the padding nor the gate applies to it. A value that is not an ndarray goes through `_validate_listlike` first, so a `list`, `tuple`, `Index`, `Series`, `Categorical` or other 1D-only EA is reoriented the same way; each of those spellings wrote the wrong cells silently before.

When the value genuinely cannot be broadcast, a 2-D block now names the shapes in frame order rather than the datetime resolution — unless the selection is deeper than 2-D, where no shape would correspond to anything the caller can see, and the original error stands.

Measured against a numpy-backed frame as the oracle: over a 2160-combination sweep (9 row keys × 8 column keys × 9 value shapes × 5 value spellings, `M8[s]` and `m8[s]`), **388 divergences before, 40 after**; over a wider 118,656-cell sweep adding `M8[ns]`, `M8[ns, UTC]` and `period[D]`, **no cell where this writes a value the numpy-backed frame does not**. The divergences that remain are pre-existing families in other layers.

Scope notes, each verified pre-existing and left alone:
- an integer column key means the swap is not a transpose, so `df.iloc[1, 1] = np.array([x])` still raises where a numpy-backed frame broadcasts;
- a 2-D *list* value is rejected upstream of the block, in `_setitem_with_indexer`;
- a 0-d ndarray row key (`df.iloc[np.array(1)] = [...]`) raises `TypeError: len() of unsized object` from `check_setitem_lengths` on a numpy-backed or mixed frame, so the datetimelike path tested here is the one that works, not the odd one out;
- with a 2-D row key the selection is 3-D and the value is passed through unreoriented, so one of the two length-1 2-D value shapes still writes where a numpy-backed frame rejects both. Dropping the unconditional `.T` swaps which one; making that arm raise is a new user-visible rejection and wants its own PR;
- a 1-D block reports a shape failure through the same upcast fallback, as `TypeError: Invalid value ...` or, for `datetime64[s]` with a `datetime64` value, `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. Giving it the new message would change the exception type of `Series` setitem, which wants its own PR.

Two narrowings worth calling out, both of them an all-datetimelike frame giving up a broadcast that no other frame dtype allows:

- an empty value assigned into an empty *row* selection (`df.iloc[[]] = np.array([])`) was a no-op and now raises. The mirror case, an empty *column* selection, went the other way — from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to the no-op a numpy-backed frame gives.
- a column vector into a single column (`df.iloc[mask, 0] = value.reshape(4, 1)`) used to succeed here, because the unconditional `.T` turned it into a row vector; a numpy-backed frame and numpy itself both reject it, and so does this now. A *row* vector into a single row (`df.iloc[1] = value.reshape(1, 3)`) is the shape numpy does accept, and that one went from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to writing.

Both are pinned.

title: BUG: DataFrame.rank did not retain extension dtypes (GH#52829)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

labels.name: pyarrow dtype retention
labels.description: op with pyarrow dtype -> expect pyarrow result

body:
closes #52829

`NDFrame.rank` cast a DataFrame to a single common dtype through `data.values` before ranking, so `DataFrame.rank` dropped the extension dtypes that `Series.rank` retains. With `axis=0` each block is now ranked in its own dtype via `_mgr.apply`, and the two agree.

Besides the dtype, this fixes two value bugs that came from the common-dtype cast:

- an ordered `Categorical` column was ranked by the natural ordering of its values rather than by the declared category order — the `DataFrame` half of GH-15420, fixed for `Series` in 0.20.0;
- distinct integers above `2**53` got tied ranks when another column made `float64` the frame's common dtype.

Both are silent numeric changes, so they get a `notable_bug_fixes` entry.

`axis=1` is unchanged: ranking a row needs all of its entries in one dtype, so it still goes through `data.values` and still returns `float64` for an extension-dtype frame.

title: BUG: indexing a SparseArray with a boolean SparseArray mask (GH#45284)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
closes #45284

`SparseArray.__getitem__` read a boolean `SparseArray` mask off its `sp_index` alone, which assumes no stored value ever equals the mask's own `fill_value`. An op result violates that — `_sparse_array_op` gives the result the union of both operands' indices — so `arr[arr > other]` returned the wrong elements. Comparisons against an array-like and logical ops between two boolean `SparseArray`s both produce such a mask; a scalar comparison does not, since that result is re-sparsified. The fix selects on `sp_values` instead.

That same fast path returned before reaching `check_array_indexer`, so a mask of the wrong length was never rejected — every other spelling of the same mask raises `IndexError`. Added the check there, with the message `check_array_indexer` uses.

`Series`/`DataFrame`-level indexing was unaffected throughout: those routes densify the mask before it reaches `SparseArray.__getitem__`.

The issue also asks for `s > [3, 3, 4, 1, 0, 0]` to report `Indices: array([3])` rather than storing every position. That is the density of the op result rather than its values, and it is left to GH-45126 — re-sparsifying comparison results conflicts with `test_cmp_object_subtype_scalar_keeps_sparse_index` (GH-68586).

title: BUG: DataFrame.apply/agg with a callable dropped the extension dtype (GH#61812)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
closes #61812

`DataFrame.agg`/`apply` with a callable that reduces each column (or row) to a scalar built the result from the raw Python scalars, so the frame's extension dtype was lost — `df.agg(lambda x: x.mean())` on a `double[pyarrow]` frame returned `float64`, where the string alias `df.agg("mean")` returned `double[pyarrow]`. This routes those results through `ExtensionArray._cast_pointwise_result`, the mechanism `DataFrameGroupBy.agg` already uses for a callable, when the frame has a single extension dtype. Masked and `category` frames lost the dtype the same way and are fixed too.

Sparse frames are excluded: a reduction result has no sparsity to preserve, and `SparseArray`'s cast drops a timezone (GH-61812 does not fix that; it is reachable today through `groupby.agg`).

`DataFrame.nunique` and `DataFrame.corrwith` are implemented via `self.apply`, so each casts its result back to what it returned before — `nunique` to `int64` (matching `count()` and `groupby.nunique`) and `corrwith` to `float64` (a correlation coefficient would otherwise come back as `Int64` for an all-NA result, or as a `category`). Neither method changes behavior.

Not covered here: `df.agg([f])` and `df.agg({"col": f})` assemble results through a different path and still drop the dtype, as they already do on main relative to `df.agg(["mean"])`.

title: BUG: partial string indexing that matches no entries raises KeyError (GH#57596)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
closes #57596

`DatetimeIndexOpsMixin._partial_date_slice` raised `KeyError` when a partial-string key fell outside the index's range, but returned an empty selection when it fell inside and matched nothing. Callers that need presence semantics — `Index.__contains__`, `.at`, and `.loc`-setitem's missing-key path — read that as a match of length zero, so the assignment in the issue silently set nothing. It now raises `KeyError` whenever the selection is empty, which also makes an in-range miss consistent with the out-of-range case that already raised, and with a `MultiIndex` datetime level, which already raised.

The two `# we are out of range` pre-checks are removed as part of this: they fire only when both bounds lie past the extreme element of a sorted index, which is exactly when the new check raises anyway.

This is a behavior change for getitem — `ser["2024-05"]` where May is absent but in range now raises instead of returning an empty Series — so it has a notable-bug-fix whatsnew entry. Nothing in the test suite asserted the old behavior.

title: DOC: `DataFrame.agg` and `Series.agg` documentation is unclear on which function we can use
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.agg.html
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.agg.html


### Documentation problem

During discussion for issue #49352 we found that the documentation of the `agg` function for both DataFrame and Series is unclear on 
- which function will work
- what will be passed to the function
- how function names are looked up (and so which optional parameter can be used if we use function names)

### Suggested fix for documentation

For `DataFrame.agg`, it must be explained that:

The passed function must accept either a Series and return a scalar, or a DataFrame and returns a Series. If the axis is 0 and the function accept a Series, the passed Series will be a column, otherwise, it will be a row.  If function names are passed, the called function will be the first function found according to the MRO from a DataFrame object (that is, the result of getattr(df, 'func_name')). For instance, passing `mean` will match DataFrame.mean.

For `Series.agg`,  it must be explained that:

The passed function must accept either a Series and return a scalar. If function names are passed, the called function will be the first function found according to the MRO from a Series object  (that is, the result of getattr(s, 'func_name')).

title: PERF: avoid building _pd_timedelta on every subtraction
body:
Written with Claude Fable 5.1.
Ref: https://github.com/pandas-dev/asv-runner/issues/159
Ref #66331

`_pd_timedelta` is cached, but `datetime - offset` goes through `__rsub__` and creates a fresh offset on every call, so the cache was always cold. Constructing the `Timedelta` dominated the runtime.

This adds a `_pd_timedelta_unit` property that derives the unit from the keyword names alone, and skips the coercion entirely when the unit is seconds (a `Timestamp` built from a `datetime` is never coarser than microseconds, so `apply_wraps` would undo that coercion anyway).

`OffestDatetimeArithmetic.time_subtract` with `DateOffset(months=2, days=2)`, median per call:

| | |
|---|---|
| parent of #66331 | 31.5us |
| #66331 | 57.1us |
| this PR | 32.1us |

title: BUG: DateOffset silently truncated non-integer date components

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

body:
Applying a `DateOffset` multiplies its `relativedelta` by `n`, and dateutil's
`relativedelta.__mul__` casts every component through `int()`, so a fractional
value was discarded without warning:

```python
>>> datetime(2020, 1, 1) + pd.DateOffset(days=1.5)
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2, 0, 0)     # a whole day, not a day and a half
>>> datetime(2020, 1, 1) + pd.DateOffset(hours=1.5)
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 1, 30)    # correct
```

The second is correct because a lone sub-daily keyword is handled by `timedelta`,
which represents fractions exactly. Adding any date component switches to the
relativedelta path, so `DateOffset(days=1, hours=1.5)` lost the half hour too.

This raises `ValueError` on the relativedelta path instead, per @jbrockmendel's
comment on the issue. The timedelta path is unchanged, and a float that is a whole
number, such as `days=2.0`, is still accepted.
