title: API: `freq` or `step` for base class Index?

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
Brainstorming, not advocating:

Thinking about #60561 about how to make `Index[timestamp[pyarrow]]` either _be_ a DatetimeIndex or behave like one, one approach is to take DTI methods and move their logic to the base class behind a `self.dtype.kind == "M"` check.  This almost works, but some of those methods check for `self.freq` which the base class doesn't have.

But `freq` for DTI/TDI means basically the same thing as `step` does for `RangeIndex`.  And `step` could be well-defined for any dtype where subtraction is defined.

What if we defined `step` on the base class, had it be an alias for freq on DTI/TDI?  Could get rid of a ton of special-casing in the DTI/TDI classes.  When it is present, it would enable some optimizations (e.g. we know we are monotonic, can fastpath some setops).

Downside: it would have a different type for numeric and datetime/timedelta indexes

xref #46484 about extending RangeIndex to support floats, #47227 about fixing the overloading of the word "freq".

title: BUG: rolling skew/kurt returned NaN after a window emptied

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

body:
- [x] closes #69037
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

`remove_skew` and `remove_kurt` decrement `nobs` and then immediately divide by it:

```cython
nobs[0] -= 1
n = <float64_t>(nobs[0])
delta = val - mean[0]
delta_n = delta / n
```

When the observation being removed is the last one in the window, `n` is `0.0`, so `delta_n` is `inf` or `nan` and the running `mean`, `m2`, `m3` (and `m4` for kurt) are poisoned for every window after it. That is why the reported series return `NaN` even where the final window itself has no missing values.

There is already a recompute path for exactly this kind of damage, but **it cannot fire here**. The guard is

```cython
if (fabs(m3_update) + fabs(m3[0])) * InvCondTol > fabs(new_m3):
    numerically_unstable[0] = True
```

and once `m3_update` is `NaN` that comparison is `NaN > NaN`, which is `False`. So the one case the guard exists to catch is the single case that slips past it silently.

The fix zeroes the moments when `nobs` reaches zero, since an empty window has no moments to carry forward. That addresses the root cause rather than widening the instability check.

This is the same shape as the already-fixed `.Rolling.corr`/`.Rolling.cov` bug in #65739 ("returning NaN for all later windows once a window contained no valid pairs").

Verified by rebuilding both ways. Before the change, both reproducers return `nan`; after, they match a fresh computation over the final window, and independently match scipy:

| | pandas | scipy |
|---|---|---|
| `skew` | `0.0` | `0.0` |
| `kurt` | `-0.41610621014935756` | `-0.41610621014935845` |

Added a parametrised regression test covering both functions. `pandas/tests/window/` is 9003 passed, 45 skipped, 1 xfailed.

title: TST: Fix CoW alias corruption in DataFrame.eval (#65664)
body:
- [x] closes #65664
- [x] Tests added and passed if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [x] All code checks passed.

**Bug Description:**
In Pandas >= 3.0, using `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)` bypassed Copy-on-Write reference tracking. The evaluation engine returned the raw memory of the evaluated column back to the DataFrame. Because `inplace=True` bypasses standard `__setitem__` CoW tracking, writing to the new column mutated the original column's memory.

**The Fix:**
In `pandas/core/computation/eval.py`, if the evaluated result is being assigned back to the DataFrame and it supports `.copy()`, we now explicitly force a copy. This guarantees the CoW perimeter is maintained and intra-DataFrame aliasing does not result in memory corruption during `inplace` evaluations.

title: BUG: ops with an iterator raised TypeError instead of treating it as a scalar (GH#31646)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
closes #31646

Comparison and arithmetic between a pandas object and an iterator — a generator, `iter([...])`, `map`, `filter`, `reversed` — raised `TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len()` (or `len() of unsized object`), because the op sites gated on `is_list_like(other)` or `lib.is_scalar(other)` and then took a length. NumPy arrays and NumPy-dtype Series already treat an iterator as a scalar.

Two helpers in `pandas/core/ops/common.py` replace those gates across the array and frame op sites:

- `is_listlike_for_op(other)` = `is_list_like(other) and not is_iterator(other)`, replacing `is_list_like`.
- `is_scalar_for_op(other)` = `is_scalar(other) or is_iterator(other) or not (is_list_like(other) or hasattr(other, "__len__") or has_castable_attr(other))`, replacing `lib.is_scalar`. Deliberately not the negation of the first: a sized sequence with `__getitem__` but no `__iter__`, and an operand carrying only `__array__` or `__array_interface__`, are not `is_list_like`, yet NumPy coerces them, so they have to stay element-wise.

Only iterators change. A list-like with no length that can be read more than once — an `Iterable` that is not an `Iterator` — stays on GH-62423's deprecation path and keeps its `Pandas4Warning`.

Iterators become scalar-like now rather than after a deprecation cycle, because the current behavior is a crash rather than a result worth preserving — and the merged GH-62423 deprecation already says non-standard list-likes become scalar-like in 4.0. Two of the three user-visible changes replaced a wrong answer rather than a crash: a `Sparse` dtype and an `ExtensionScalarOpsMixin`-based array consumed a length-matching iterator and computed elementwise, and `ArrowDtype` arithmetic looped forever on an endless one (`ser + itertools.count()`).

Two smaller fixes ride along, since they are the same gate being too narrow to serve as a `len()` guard. An object that is neither list-like nor a recognized scalar now operates as a scalar against a `Sparse` dtype, instead of raising `ValueError` about mismatched lengths, and raises `TypeError` from `&`/`|`/`^` instead of a bare `AssertionError`.

`has_castable_attr` gains `__array_interface__` and `__array_struct__`, which `np.asarray` honors and the widened `is_scalar_for_op` would otherwise misclassify as scalars. That also narrows GH-62423 by the same amount: an operand exposing only one of those warned before and no longer does, so it stays element-wise in 4.0 rather than becoming scalar-like.

GH-31646 is labelled *Needs Discussion*, and the objection recorded there is to returning a boolean array when the lengths do not match. Merged GH-62423 settles that direction for every non-standard list-like, so this PR follows it rather than reopening it.

Related, not addressed here: GH-62423 (the deprecation this follows), and `where`/`mask`/`__setitem__`, which have the same shape but want the opposite resolution, since `pd.Series(gen)` materializes.

title: BUG: concat(union_categories=True) conflated True with 1
body:
`concat(union_categories=True)` silently replaced `True` with `1` when unioning bool-category and integer-category Categoricals:

```python
a = Series(Categorical([1, 2, 3]))
b = Series(Categorical([True, False]))

concat([a, b], ignore_index=True, union_categories=True).tolist()
# [1, 2, 3, 1, False]     <- True became 1
concat([a, b], ignore_index=True).tolist()
# [1, 2, 3, True, False]  <- the default gets it right
```

`union_categories_compat` casts categories with differing dtypes to a common dtype, which for bool and integer categories is object. `union_categoricals` then unions the categories through a hashtable, where `True` and `1` collide, so one replaces the other. The existing `is_unique` guard only caught collapse within a single input, not across inputs.

A Categorical's categories must be unique and uniqueness is decided by hash, so no Categorical can hold both `1` and `True` and there is nothing to return here. `union_categories_compat` now returns `None` when the categories cannot be shown to be all distinct, and the caller casts to object before continuing — returning `None` is not enough on its own, because two object-dtype `CategoricalDtype`s compare equal whenever their categories do, so `dtypes_all_equal` would send the inputs straight back into `union_categoricals`. The result is object dtype with both values intact.

The check is a single pass keyed by the category itself: it refuses a key that turns up under two different types, so `1`/`True` and `1`/`1.0` are refused while duplicate column labels still read back as duplicate columns, and it refuses a pair whose comparison raises rather than letting the error out of `concat` (`Decimal("1")` and `np.int64(1)` hash equal and raise on `==`). Inputs that share one categories object are scanned once, since a categories Index cannot collide with itself. An `inferred_type` shortcut was tried and dropped — an `IntEnum` infers as `"integer"` just as `int` does, so it could not see that case.

Follow-up to GH-65098, which added the `union_categories` keyword in the unreleased 3.1.0 — no whatsnew entry for that reason.

body: Currently there are ways of performing a ``to_json()`` method with the desired output formatting but the procedure is a bit cumbersome: ``` df = pd.DataFrame(data=[[1.9999, 1.9999, 1.9999, 1.9999, 1.99]], columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']) df['A'] = df['A'].apply(lambda x: float(f'{x:,.00f}')) df['B'] = df['B'].apply(lambda x: int(f'{x:,.00f}')) df['C'] = df['C'].apply(lambda x: f'{x:,.01f}') print(df.to_json(double_precision=3)) ``` > {"A":{"0":2.0}, "B":{"0":2}, "C":{"0":"2.0"}, "D":{"0":2.0}, "E":{"0":1.99}} The ``Styler`` has its own formatter which can make things a little more aesthetic, and has the advantage of not affecting the underlying data: ``` df = pd.DataFrame(data=[[1.9999, 1.9999, 1.9999, 1.9999, 1.99]], columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']) print(Styler(df, uuid="", precision=3).format({ 'A': lambda x: float(f'{x:,.00f}'), 'B': lambda x: int(f'{x:,.00f}'), 'C': '{:,.01f}'.format }).render()) ``` > 0 2.0 2 2.0 2.000 1.990 But Styler does not have a ``to_json()`` method. #### Describe the solution you'd like I would like to add a simple extension to the Styler to create JSON from the formatted Styler Object, in a similar way as it constructs HTML tables: ``` class Styler: ... def to_json(self, **kwargs): """ Applies the ``:meth:DataFrame.to_json`` method to the ``Styler`` object including existing formats. Parameters ---------- **kwargs Any additional keyword arguments are passed to ``DataFrame.to_json()``. Useful to control the output structure of the JSON return. Returns ------- None or str Examples -------- >>> df = pd.DataFrame(data=[[1.9999, 1.9999, 1.9999, 1.9999, 1.99]], columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']) >>> df.style.format({ ... 'A': lambda x: float(f'{x:,.00f}'), ... 'B': lambda x: int(f'{x:,.00f}'), ... 'C': '{:,.01f}'.format ... }).to_json() {"A":{"0":2.0},"B":{"0":2.0},"C":{"0":"2.0"},"D":{"0":"1.999900"}} """ df = self.data.copy() for r in range(len(df.index)): for c in range(len(df.columns)): formatter = self._display_funcs[(r, c)] df.iloc[r, c] = formatter(self.data.iloc[r, c]) return df.to_json(**kwargs) ``` #### API breaking implications None - new feature Might be useful to make some minor adjustments to Styler factory default formatter, but this is optional and can happen later. #### Describe alternatives you've considered - Building a formatter for a DataFrame without using styler and applying `to_json` to that. - Adding a `formatter` argument to `DataFrame.to_json` which performs the necessary adjustments before Since Styler is inherently a 'display' context component and specifically designed for the web I thought it more suitable to add `to_json` to the `Styler` object. Opinions welcome.. I will probably submit a PR if consensus approval..

title: BUG: tz_localize `nonexistent` shift took the offset from the wrong side of the DST transition
body:
The offset to apply after a `nonexistent` shift — a timedelta, `"shift_forward"` or `"shift_backward"` — was picked by bisecting the shifted *wall* time against `info.tdata`, which holds *UTC* transition instants. That lands within one transition of the answer but not on it, and the ad-hoc corrections layered on top (`delta_idx_offset`, and the `deltas[delta_idx - 1] >= 0` branch) were tuned to the zones the tests covered. Whether a call came back right depended on the signs of the zone's offsets as much as on the shift; when it came back wrong it was off by exactly the DST delta — silently, and contradicting the documented contract that "timedelta objects will shift nonexistent times by the timedelta".

```python
pd.Timestamp("2011-03-27 02:30").tz_localize("Europe/Warsaw", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(hours=-2))
# 2011-03-26 23:30:00+01:00   <- an hour early
# 2011-03-27 00:30:00+01:00   <- expected

pd.Timestamp("2021-03-14 02:30").tz_localize("America/Anchorage", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(hours=1))
# 2021-03-14 04:30:00-08:00   <- an hour late, on a one-hour shift
# 2021-03-14 03:30:00-08:00   <- expected
```

Same on `DatetimeIndex`, `Series.dt` and the scalar path, at every resolution.

The whole computation is replaced by a `_delta_idx_for_local()` helper: bracket the search by a day either side of the wall time — no zone offset reaches a day, the same assumption `_get_utc_bounds` already makes — and return the index whose *own* offset places the wall time inside that index's own interval, `tdata[idx] <= local - deltas[idx] < tdata[idx + 1]`. On an ambiguous wall time it lands on the earlier offset. `delta_idx_offset`/`first_delta` and their precompute block go away with it.

Verification: a wall-time oracle over every zoneinfo zone's spring-forward gaps × 14 shifts is **0 wrong in 280,105 cases** on this branch, against **66,201 wrong** on `main`.

Where the shift lands inside *another* gap, no offset can reproduce the requested wall time. That is a separate pre-existing defect — `shift_forward`/`shift_backward` move by whole hours off `val % pph`, so they do not clear a multi-hour gap either (Pacific/Apia's skipped day, Kwajalein's date-line jump, `Canada/Newfoundland` whose gap starts at 00:01). The helper falls back to the side being shifted toward, so those results change too; `main` moved several of them in the direction opposite to the one requested.

title: ENH: Support `tz_convert` on naive timestamps when naive tz specified

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

It is quite common to defensively convert-or-assume timestamps to UTC, which means writing something like this:

```python
def my_function(df: pd.Dataframe, time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Dataframe:
    if time.tzinfo is None:
        time = time.tz_localize("UTC")
    else:
        time = time.tz_convert("UTC")
    ...
    return df.assign(time=time)
```

Alternatively an inline if can be used

```python
time = time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")
```

But this is slightly longwinded, so often helper functions are repeated in loads of modules

```python
def _ensure_utc(time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Timestamp:
    return (
        time.tz_localize("UTC")
        if time.tz is None
        else time.tz_convert("UTC")
    )
```

My opinion is that neither the rather long if..else expression nor the usually-not-consistently-named helper method are very readable. There can also be challenges around proper typing on the helper method, when support for e.g. series and datetime index is required as well. This feature request is essentially asking for a shorthand that is native to Pandas for this pattern.

### Feature Description

Add a keyword argument to `tz_convert` which specifies how naive timestamps should be interpreted, instead of raising an error:


```python
time = time.tz_convert("UTC", naive_tz="UTC")
```

It would be functionally equivalent to `time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")` - just a shorthand. Of course, `tz_convert` on series, datetime index etc should have the same support.

### Alternative Solutions

"Keeping the status quo" is more verbose and works. The feature request is mainly to make the convert-or-assume pattern easier to both write and read.

But some alternatives that go along the same lines:

- Different keyword arg names, e.g. `.tz_convert("UTC", assume_naive="UTC")`
    - Particularly, putting the verb "assume" might be good for clarity of what the arg does. It's just longer so I didn't put it in the main suggestion (I think the main suggestion is clear enough).
- "Policy style" instead of specific tz, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_utc")`, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_local")`
    - This could have a default of `naive="raise"` which neatly describes the current behaviour correctly while keeping `tz=None` semantics constant. However it obviously loses the ability to set an arbitrary naive timezone to use. 
- Different specific method, e.g. `.tz_ensure("UTC", assume="UTC")`
    - If someone thinks we're changing the semantics of `tz_convert` too hard. I don't think so, but had to be mentioned.

title: PERF: default read_csv parallel workers to available physical cores
body:
Replaces the fixed default worker count for parallel `read_csv` with detection: the machine's **physical core count** (SMT siblings excluded, efficiency cores included), clamped to the CPUs actually available to the process — CPU affinity (`taskset`, SLURM cpusets) and cgroup CFS quotas (Docker `--cpus`, Kubernetes limits) — and to an absolute cap of 16. This keeps a default read from oversubscribing a shared many-core server or a CPU-limited container, which a plain `os.cpu_count()` default would. `mode.max_threads` still overrides everything. Where the topology is not readable — an unsupported platform, or a container without `/sys/devices/system/cpu/*/topology` — detection falls back to the logical CPU count, as the option doc and `io.rst` now state.

The availability clamp this builds on merged separately as GH-66613, so this branch is now standalone: the diff here is just the part that *raises* the default.

Main's default is `min(os.cpu_count(), 4)`, so on a machine with more than 4 physical cores this PR is what actually raises the worker count. The tables below are main's default versus this PR's default — the change a user sees.

### Benchmarks

**Re-measured 2026-09-17 against `main @ dbca7b6a8c7`.** The numbers previously in this description were taken against `main @ c0aee4cea2` (2026-07-20); ~570 commits have landed since, several of them on the parallel path itself — GH-66798 scales the chunk count with file size, GH-68379 and GH-68380 batch the string and numeric conversion sweeps, and GH-66276, GH-66277 and GH-68314 cut per-chunk GIL work. Every win is smaller than it was, and **two shapes now regress.**

M3 Pro, 12 physical cores, no SMT, so the policy resolves to 12 workers against main's 4. Milliseconds, best of 3 reads per round over 7 rounds, worker counts interleaved within each round.

| fixture | 1 worker | 4 (main) | 12 (this PR) | 4 → 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bool, 1M x 10 | 136.2 | 37.7 | 21.7 | **1.74x** |
| mixed, 1M x 10 | 109.6 | 31.7 | 18.9 | **1.68x** |
| int, 1M x 10 | 100.0 | 29.6 | 17.9 | **1.66x** |
| float, 1M x 10 | 128.3 | 35.9 | 22.2 | **1.62x** |
| str, 1M x 10 | 68.5 | 19.7 | 12.8 | **1.54x** |
| str_highcard, 1M x 10 | 73.6 | 21.9 | 15.6 | 1.40x |
| str_mixed_width, 300K x 3 | 21.6 | 5.8 | 6.0 | 0.97x |
| wide, 100 cols x 100K | 126.3 | 45.2 | 51.1 | **0.88x** |
| medium, 70K x 10 (6 MB) | 8.9 | 3.8 | 8.3 | **0.46x** |

The `tall-narrow` row from the previous table is absent because the asv replication suite added here has no such fixture; it has not been re-measured.

The serial path is untouched by construction — the diff only chooses a worker count — and files below `_PARALLEL_READ_MIN_BYTES` stay serial; they pay the one-time core-count probe on the first read of the process and are otherwise unaffected.

### The two regressions

Worker-count sweeps on the same machine:

```
fixture      1      2      4      6      8     12     16
wide     125.7   71.5   44.9   38.2   39.7   50.5   67.5
float    129.3   67.1   36.1   25.9   23.7   21.7   23.0
str       69.1   35.4   20.2   14.7   13.4   12.8   16.7
medium     8.7    4.9    3.6    3.8    5.2    8.0    8.5
mixed    109.8   56.9   31.1   22.3   20.1   18.5   21.1
```

Both problem curves are U-shaped with an interior optimum, so this is not a measurement-order artifact: `wide` peaks at 6 workers and `medium` at 4, and past those points both degrade monotonically. 16 workers is slower than 12 on every fixture, and for the cases that do still scale, 8 → 12 buys only 5-8%.

The mechanism is that the chunk count is derived from the worker count: `n_target = min(n_workers * 3, ...)` in `readers.py`, and every chunk pays a full column-conversion epilogue. For `medium` that is 35 chunks of 2000 rows for a 6 MB file. For `wide` the gather cost grows as `n_columns * n_chunks`, so 100 columns at 12 workers is three times the piece count it has at 4. Reducing that per-(column, chunk) cost is being looked at separately; this PR does not depend on it.

### x86 Linux

Amazon Linux 2023, 8 physical cores available to the process, so the policy resolves to 8 workers there:

| fixture | 1 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 4 → 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| wide | 231.1 | 117.5 | 70.1 | 58.6 | 56.6 | 1.24x |
| medium | 14.6 | 8.6 | 6.6 | 6.7 | 8.7 | **0.76x** |
| mixed | 207.5 | 95.8 | 53.6 | 38.5 | 32.1 | 1.67x |
| float | 250.3 | 119.0 | 65.8 | 47.1 | 39.0 | 1.69x |
| str | 139.5 | 58.8 | 34.1 | 26.9 | 21.9 | 1.56x |

`wide` is still improving at the top of this range — its reversal happens past 8 workers, which this allocation cannot reach; the Windows sweep below does reach it.

### x86 Windows

Windows Server 2025, 16 physical cores and no affinity restriction, so the policy resolves to 16 workers against main's 4 — the only configuration here that reaches the cap:

| fixture | 1 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 12 | 16 | 4 → 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| wide | 359.9 | 219.9 | 136.4 | 109.4 | 102.3 | 107.5 | 129.0 | 1.06x |
| medium | 29.8 | 17.1 | 12.5 | 12.6 | 15.8 | 21.9 | 24.9 | **0.50x** |
| mixed | 312.7 | 183.4 | 109.6 | 83.3 | 72.3 | 62.4 | 58.5 | 1.87x |
| float | 462.8 | 265.5 | 151.8 | 112.6 | 95.5 | 80.1 | 71.7 | 2.12x |
| str | 179.4 | 116.3 | 71.7 | 58.9 | 52.5 | 49.6 | 49.9 | 1.44x |

Both problem shapes reproduce on a third platform, with the same interior optima as the M3 Pro sweep: `wide` turns over at 8 workers and `medium` at 4, ending at half main's speed. So neither regression is arm64-specific, and `wide`'s reversal is confirmed on x86, where the Linux allocation could not reach it.

SMT siblings stay excluded (a hyperthread adds no memory bandwidth to the bandwidth-bound parse its sibling is running); Windows is in scope because GH-66751 enabled parallel reading there by default. Efficiency cores are included: on GH-66275's worker-queue structure a slower core just pulls fewer chunks from the queue instead of straggling the gather.

### Reproducing the numbers

The last commit adds `asv_bench/benchmarks/io/csv_parallel_replication.py`, a port of the suite above so reviewers can rerun it on their own hardware. Because this PR changes only the *default* worker count, `mode.max_threads` reaches both behaviours from a single build — no second build and no `asv continuous` needed:

```
python -m asv_bench.benchmarks.io.csv_parallel_replication          # A/B table
python -m asv_bench.benchmarks.io.csv_parallel_replication --sweep  # worker-count curve
```

That commit (and the Cython pin it adds to the asv matrix, working around a 3.2.9 build that fails to import) is temporary and reverts before merging.

title: BUG: tz_convert/tz_localize failing or silently wrong with a ZoneInfo built by from_file (GH#64379)

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
GH-64379 routed every `zoneinfo` timezone through a transition cache that rebuilds the pure-python `ZoneInfo` from `tz.key`. That key only describes the object when it was loaded from the installed tzdata under that key — which is exactly what `ZoneInfo.from_file` need not do. Four ways it goes wrong today:

```python
data = open("/usr/share/zoneinfo/US/Eastern", "rb").read()
naive = pd.date_range("2025-06-15", periods=3, freq="h")

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data)))
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "NoneType") to str

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data), key="my/custom"))
# ZoneInfoNotFoundError: 'No time zone found with key my/custom'

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data), key=5))
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

tokyo = open("/usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Tokyo", "rb").read()
naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(tokyo), key="US/Eastern"))
# silently uses the installed US/Eastern rules; wrong by 13 hours
```

The last one is the nastiest: it's silent, and it's the realistic case, since pinning a tzdb release via `from_file` under the correct key is a large part of why `from_file` exists. `date_range(..., tz=tz)`, `Timestamp.tz_localize` and the `Series.dt` counterparts all follow the same paths.

## Fix

Gate the fast path on whether `tz.key` is a usable handle at all, rather than assuming it is. `get_zoneinfo_twin` returns a verified pure-python twin or `None`, memoized in a `WeakKeyDictionary` so `from_file` objects don't pin entries; `tz_cache_key`, `is_fixed_offset` and `Localizer.__cinit__` all consult it. When there is no twin, values go down the tzinfo-API path that other zones already use past their last cached transition — no new conversion code.

The test for "was this built by `from_file`" is to ask the object to pickle. The stdlib documents that a `from_file` `ZoneInfo` cannot be pickled, for precisely the reason its key is not a usable handle: the data is not recoverable from the key. So a `__reduce__` that raises `PicklingError` means fall back, and one that succeeds means the object came from the installed tzdata under its key. That is an exact test rather than a heuristic, so `ZoneInfo(key)` and `no_cache(key)` both keep the full fast path and are unaffected.

The cost is that a `from_file` object whose data *does* match the zone its key names cannot be told apart from one whose data does not, so it takes the fallback too — correct, but slower (roughly 30x on a large `tz_localize`; 3ms vs 106ms for 100k values here), and without the fixed-offset shortcut in `DatetimeIndex` set operations, so an empty `intersection` comes back with `freq=None`. Anyone who needs both a non-default tzdb and the fast path can point `zoneinfo.reset_tzpath()` at that release *before the first conversion* and load by key — neither the stdlib’s `ZoneInfo` cache nor pandas’ transition cache is invalidated afterwards.

An earlier revision of this PR tried to close that gap, verifying a candidate twin by probing its transitions and a monthly grid — 0 false rejects across all 598 installed zones, but ~120 lines and a documented residual hole before each zone's first transition. Per review it was dropped in favour of the exact-but-coarser test above; the [commit](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/66828/commits/e8a05a8a8f39c27a6a92c0db4d0685066dff8138) is kept for the record.

`tzdata` stays a Windows-only pixi target. The tests here read a known tzdb file off `zoneinfo.TZPATH`, and fall back to `importorskip("tzdata")` only when the zone is not on `TZPATH` at all — in practice Windows, where `TZPATH` is empty and `tzdata` is already installed. `validate_test_dependencies` cannot see `[target.win.dependencies]`, so it gets an allowlist entry saying why.

The other half of the report this came from — wrong offsets for `Africa/Casablanca`/`Africa/El_Aaiun` in 2088-2099 — is **not** live; GH-65712 and GH-65733 already fixed it. Re-checked against the stdlib across all 598 IANA zones for 2020-2099 (`tz_convert` and `tz_localize`, exact) plus a synthetic reverse-DST zone, so nothing is added for it here.

title: BUG: IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__, concat and shift with an ExtensionDtype subtype (GH#64297)

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
closes #64297

`IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` built its endpoints with `np.asarray(arr.field("left"), dtype=self.subtype)`, which raises `TypeError: Cannot interpret ... as a data type` for any `ExtensionDtype` subtype. That includes `DatetimeTZDtype`, which `IntervalArray` explicitly supports. Delegate to the subtype's own `__from_arrow__` in that case.

Two supporting hunks, both of which fix user-visible bugs of their own:

* `IntervalArray._concat_same_type` used `np.concatenate`, which downgraded a masked subtype to its NumPy counterpart (`interval[Int64]` -> `interval[int64]`) and boxed tz-aware endpoints to object. A non-empty result was re-inferred back, but an empty one has nothing to infer from, so `pd.concat([pd.Series(empty_tz_interval)])` raised `TypeError: category, object, and string subtypes are not supported`. `concat_compat` fixes both, and `Index.append` with it.
* `IntervalArray.shift` built its NA fill piece with `from_breaks([na_scalar] * (n + 1))`, which infers `datetime64[s]`. Once the endpoints are concatenated dtype-faithfully that stops being a loud failure and becomes a silently wrong one — `Series(interval[timedelta64[us]]).shift(1)` returned `interval[datetime64[s]]`. Building the fill piece with `take(..., allow_fill=True)` keeps the subtype, and also stops `float32` being upcast to `float64`.

Two related things deliberately left out of scope, both filed:

* The write side, GH-67753. `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` computes its arrow subtype with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype` and so rejects every extension subtype, which is why the tz-aware array in GH-64297 has to be built by hand. Lifting that alone would produce unreadable parquet: `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_serialize__` stores `str(subtype)` and deserializes with `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for `timestamp[us, tz=Europe/Brussels]`. Making that round-trip needs a metadata-format change on a registered extension type.
* `__from_arrow__` ignores the struct-level validity bitmap, GH-67754, so a null struct entry whose children are non-null reads back as `(0.0, 0.0]` instead of NaN. Pre-existing, and not reachable from pandas-written data since `__arrow_array__` nulls the children too.

title: DEPR: deprecate top-level pandas.to_pickle (GH#48402)
body:
closes #48402

`to_pickle` is exported from `pandas/__init__.py` but is not in the API reference, and it is
the only `to_<IO>` writer at the top level — the others are `DataFrame`/`Series` methods, and
only the `read_*` readers are top-level functions. Deprecated per the dev meeting of 2025-09-09.

The name is dropped from `pandas/__init__.py`'s import list and `__all__` and re-exposed through
a module-level `__getattr__` emitting `Pandas4Warning`, following GH-43695 (`Float64Index` et al.)
and GH-68937 (the `pandas.api.typing` `Groupby` spellings). As in GH-68937 the shim sits behind
`if not TYPE_CHECKING:`, since a `__getattr__` visible to type checkers resolves every unknown
`pandas` attribute to `object` and silences `attr-defined` repo-wide.

`pandas.io.pickle.to_pickle` is unchanged and still backs `DataFrame.to_pickle` and
`Series.to_pickle`; it loses `@set_module("pandas")` so that reflective lookups — `pickle.dumps`
of the function object, `inspect.getmodule`, `help` — no longer route back through the deprecated
name. `pandas/_testing/_io.py` and `pandas/tests/io/test_pickle.py` now import it directly. The
`pandas.io.api` re-export is deliberately kept, since this deprecates `pandas.to_pickle` and not
that name.

One thing worth a second opinion: `Index`, `Categorical`, `dict` and friends have no `.to_pickle`
method, so for them the warning names no replacement. Nothing public reproduces what `to_pickle`
did for an arbitrary object on a compressed or remote path — `pickle.dump` infers neither
compression from the suffix nor `storage_options` — and pointing at `pandas.io.pickle.to_pickle`
would advertise a private path. Since the top-level name was never in the reference docs, the
message names the documented replacement and stops, but I'm happy to add wording if we'd rather
say something to those callers.

when a list of sheets is passed, dtype could be a dictionary with {elem_on_list: usual_dtype_parameter}

title: BUG: factorize trusted a pre-encoded pyarrow dictionary

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
`ArrowExtensionArray.factorize` short-circuited when the input was already `pa.dictionary`-typed and returned the stored dictionary as `uniques`. That dictionary is not a factorization of the values the array currently holds: entries can be unreferenced, they can be duplicated, and a null can live in the dictionary rather than in the indices.

So after an ordinary boolean filter, `groupby` invented a group for a value that was no longer in the frame, while `unique`/`value_counts` on the same column disagreed with it:

```python
enc = pa.array(["a", "b", "c", "a"]).dictionary_encode()
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": pd.array(enc, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(enc.type)), "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
sub = df[df["v"] > 2]

sub.groupby("k", sort=False)["v"].sum()
# k
# a    4
# b    0   <- "b" appears nowhere in `sub`
# c    3
```

A dictionary holding the same value in two slots additionally split that value across two groups, and a null stored in the dictionary could end up in `uniques`.

The fix re-factorizes in index space — dedupe the stored dictionary, map the indices through it, re-encode, take the uniques back out — so it never materializes the decoded values. Decoding instead silently overflows the 32-bit offsets once the values pass 2 GiB, and the following kernel segfaults. Value types that have no `dictionary_encode` or `take` kernel (nested and view types, `float16`) keep the existing behaviour rather than raising — except under `use_na_sentinel=False` with a null present, where keeping the stored dictionary would leave the null in index space and `factorize` would hand back the `-1` that flag promises not to use; that combination re-raises, as `main` does today.

`uniques` now come out in order of first appearance rather than in the stored dictionary's order, which is what every other dtype does and is visible through `groupby(sort=False)`.

Adjacent defects with the same root cause are left alone deliberately: `_factorize_keys` in `merge`, the `Categorical` constructor, and `unique`/`value_counts`/`mode` all read a stored dictionary the same way, and each needs its own change.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and reviewed the branch over several rounds; the index-space approach was chosen after review found the first version segfaulted.

title: BUG: args offset in Timestamp.__new__ causes bugs
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
# Pandas 1.5.x
import pandas as pd

ts1 = pd.Timestamp(2023, 3, 30, 10, None, None, 30)
ts2 = pd.Timestamp(2023, 3, 30, 10, day=30)

> 2023-03-30 10:00:00.000030
> 2023-03-30 10:00:00.000030

# Pandas 2.x
ts1 = pd.Timestamp(2023, 3, 30, 10, None, 30)
ts2 = pd.Timestamp(2023, 3, 30, 10, second=30)

> 2023-03-30 10:00:00.000030
> 2023-03-30 10:00:00.000030
```


### Issue Description

When we build `Timestamp` from components through positional args, the year initially ends up in `ts_input`, and we need to shift args one to the right, which we do with some kludges (normally by calling a constructor and passing it arguments in offset positions).

The problem is that we cannot tell the difference between the construction calls given in the example from inside the current `Timestamp.__new__`. This is the cause of both the bug outlined here and also of #52117 .

The two available solutions are  to either decorate `Timestamp`, which causes a performance hit (see #52221) or to refactor `Timestamp` to be built from `*args, **kwargs` and handle the logic internally.

### Expected Behavior
```python
# Pandas 2.x
ts1 = pd.Timestamp(2023, 3, 30, 10, None, None, 30)
ts2 = pd.Timestamp(2023, 3, 30, 10, second=30)

> 2023-03-30 10:00:00.000030
> 2023-03-30 10:00:30
```

title: BUG: Index.difference treating parsable strings as datetimelike members (GH#58971)

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
closes #58971

`Index._difference` resolves membership with `other.get_indexer_for(self)`, and `get_indexer` begins by running the target through `other._maybe_cast_listlike_indexer` — the same label parsing `.loc` and `get_loc` use. For a `DatetimeIndex`/`TimedeltaIndex`/`PeriodIndex` `other`, that turns `"2022-02"` into `Period("2022-02")`, so the string counts as a member. Because the cast is applied to one operand only, the answer depends on which side is `self`: `index2.difference(index1)` came back empty. GH-55108 flipped the lookup direction for perf, which moved which direction shows it rather than introducing it.

Aligning the dtypes before the lookup, as `union` and `intersection` already do, puts that cast out of reach. Membership is then decided by equality, matching `union`, `intersection`, `symmetric_difference` and `isin` — all of which already treat `"2022-02"` and `Period("2022-02")` as distinct, as does `==` on the scalars. `test_float64_index_difference` (GH-35217) pins the same reading, symmetrically, for the float-vs-string version of this case.

Note this makes `index2.difference(index1)` return `["2022-02", "2022-03"]` rather than making `index1.difference(index2)` drop the two periods, so it is the opposite of what the issue asks for and of the stale GH-59148. The dtype comparison is the only added work on the same-dtype path, so GH-55108's speedup is unaffected.

title: BUG: named agg result depended on the output name matching the column name (GH#63743)
body:
GH-63743 added a fast path to `reconstruct_func` that skips normalization when every named-aggregation output name equals its source column name. That function is shared by four callers (`frame_apply`, `reconstruct_and_relabel_result`, `window/rolling.py`, and `DataFrameGroupBy.aggregate`), so the fast path leaked out of `groupby.agg` and made results depend on whether the output name happened to match the column name.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4.0, 5.0, 6.0]})

df.agg(A=("A", "max"))   # Series  <- wrong
df.agg(x=("A", "max"))   # DataFrame

df.agg(A=("A", "min"), axis=1)   # silently aggregated row "A"
df.agg(x=("A", "min"), axis=1)   # NotImplementedError

d = pd.DataFrame({"A": [0, 0, 1, 1], "B": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
d.groupby("A").agg(B=("B", "ohlc")).shape   # (2, 4)  <- 4 columns for 1 keyword
d.groupby("A").agg(x=("B", "ohlc")).shape   # (2, 1)
```

`"describe"` widened to eight columns the same way, `"expanding"` changed the return type from `DataFrame` to `Series`, and on a frame with duplicate column labels `agg(B=("B", "sum"))` produced one output column per matching column instead of one per keyword.

This makes the fast path opt-in. `reconstruct_func` takes a positional-only `allow_skip_normalization` flag — positional-only so that a column literally named `allow_skip_normalization` cannot collide with `**kwargs` — and only `DataFrameGroupBy.aggregate` passes `True`, and only when its columns are unique. The fast path additionally requires a non-list-like aggfunc that, if a string, names a scalar reduction (gated on `pandas.core.groupby.base.reduction_kernels` rather than a hand-maintained blocklist, since `describe`, `ohlc` and `expanding` all had to be excluded).

GH-63743's performance win is preserved: on its own benchmark the named form still skips normalization (0.56 ms vs 0.43 ms for the equivalent unnamed dict form, against 1.36 ms when normalized).

No whatsnew note: the regression is not in any released version — no tag contains 9591444e34c.

title: BUG: sparse cumsum propagated a stored missing value instead of skipping it (GH#68187)
body:
Follow-up to GH-68187, which added `SparseArray._accumulate` and routed numeric `cumsum` with `skipna=True` to the existing `SparseArray.cumsum`.

`SparseArray.cumsum`'s null-fill-value branch reduced `sp_values` with a bare `ndarray.cumsum()`, so a missing value held *among the stored values* -- rather than left as a gap -- propagated into every later stored value instead of being skipped:

```python
a = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, np.nan, 2, 0, 5], fill_value=0))
b = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, 1, np.nan, np.nan, 1], fill_value=np.nan))
(a + b).cumsum()  # [2, nan, nan, nan, nan], where dense gives [2, nan, nan, nan, 8]

pd.DataFrame.sparse.from_spmatrix(csr_matrix([[1.0], [np.nan], [3.0]]))[0].cumsum()
# [1, nan, nan], where dense gives [1, nan, 4]
```

Sparse arithmetic, `DataFrame.sparse.from_spmatrix`, and an explicit `sparse_index` all produce such an array. The fix masks those NAs to the additive identity, accumulates, then restores them -- the shape `nanops.na_accum_func` uses, which cannot be reused directly because it asserts against `datetime64`/`timedelta64`.

The defect predates GH-68187: `git log -L` puts `self.sp_values.cumsum()` with GH-62703/GH-65494. GH-68187 made it reachable from `Series.cumsum`/`DataFrame.cumsum`, which previously raised `NotImplementedError`. Fixing the array method rather than the `_accumulate` routing also repairs a `timedelta64` subtype, where `arr.cumsum()` gave `[1ns, NaT, NaT]` instead of `[1ns, NaT, 4ns]`.

Off-PR I ran a dense-vs-sparse differential over ~11000 cells -- float16/32/64, complex64/128, `m8[ns]`/`[s]`/`[us]`, int64, bool and object subtypes x `IntIndex`/`BlockIndex` x lengths 0-8 x NA placement x `inf`/`-inf`/`-0.0`/imaginary-only NaN x `axis` variants x Series, DataFrame and array entry points -- with no divergence, and confirmed the fix mutates nothing the caller still holds.

title: BUG: read_sas held a SAS7BDAT file open until a cyclic collection
body:
`SAS7BDATReader` stored a list of its own bound methods on the instance, making every reader a reference cycle: dropping one did not free it, and its file stayed open until the next cyclic collection. So `pd.read_sas(path, chunksize=n)` without a `with` block leaked the file descriptor. `XportReader`, which has no such list, already closed on drop.

The list moves to a class attribute of plain functions, with `collect_page_subheaders` passing the reader explicitly.

This also fixes a flaky CI failure seen mostly on the free-threading build: the suite treats `ResourceWarning` as an error, and a reader leaked by `test_encoding_default_deprecated_header_text_only` (added in GH-66477) was collected at an arbitrary later point, so the failure was charged to whichever unrelated test was running then. That test now closes its reader.

title: BUG: SparseArray.fillna mishandled a datetimelike fill value

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
`SparseArray.fillna` passed the caller's scalar `value` straight to `np.where(isna(self.sp_values), value, self.sp_values)`, leaving numpy to decide what the result held. Only an `np.datetime64`/`np.timedelta64` in the subtype's own unit or a coarser one came through correctly. Every other spelling of a value the subtype can hold left the array wrong under a dtype that still reported the original subtype:

- a boxed `Timestamp`/`Timedelta`, a stdlib `datetime`/`timedelta`, `NaT`, `None`, or `pd.NA` made `sp_values` `object`, holding raw `int64` on a nanosecond unit;
- a lossless numpy scalar in a *finer* unit left `sp_values` in the fill value's unit;
- `np.nan` and date strings raised `DTypePromotionError`.

The dense path is correct for all of them.

The fix unboxes the scalar into the subtype when the subtype can hold it. That needed `_promote_for_fill` split into `_can_hold_for_fill` + `_unbox_for_fill` and recomposed from them: its `maybe_promote` fall-through raises `ValueError: Cannot losslessly convert units` for a `timedelta64` it would have to widen, so it cannot be called speculatively just to ask whether the subtype can hold the value. The split is a pure extraction; the other eight call sites are unchanged.

A value the subtype *cannot* hold still reaches numpy's own promotion untouched, exactly as before. `Series.where`/`DataFrame.where` on a sparse datetimelike column has the same shape but needs a different fix — the result subtype has to come from the fill value rather than from `np.where`'s promotion — so it is left for a follow-up.

title: BUG: Index.replace raised instead of widening for a value the dtype cannot hold

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
`Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and `Index.insert` all catch a value the current dtype cannot hold, find a common dtype, and retry on it — `where` was aligned with `putmask` deliberately in GH-39412, on the grounds that an Index has no column-dtype contract to protect the way a DataFrame column does.

`Index.replace` was added later (GH-65099, still unreleased) and delegates straight to `Series.replace`, so it never got the retry:

```python
ci = pd.CategoricalIndex(["a", "b", "c"])

ci.where([True, False, True], "z")   # Index(['a', 'z', 'c'], dtype='str')
ci.replace("a", "z")                 # TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical ...
```

The dtypes affected are Categorical, masked and Sparse — the ones whose `Series.replace` raises `TypeError` for a value it cannot hold. Every numpy-backed dtype already widened, because `Series.replace` upcasts there itself.

Four implementation notes:

- Only `TypeError` is caught, not `ValueError` as in `Index.where`: `replace`'s argument validation raises `ValueError`, and no dtype raises it for a value it cannot hold.
- A replacement whose `to_replace` matches nothing is left out of the common dtype, since `Block.replace` skips those pairs rather than widening for them. Matching goes through `mask_missing`, the predicate `Block.replace` itself matches with — a containment check disagrees with it, notably for an ns-resolution `Timestamp` against object.
- An NA `to_replace` is matched against `hasnans`, and needs no re-check after widening.
- Widening can change how `to_replace` compares (a str, or an ns-resolution `Timestamp`, against datetime categories). When it does, the retry re-raises rather than returning data with the replacement silently dropped. On the regex paths there are no matched literals to re-check, so the retry instead re-raises when it replaced nothing — otherwise a `TypeError` raised for some unrelated reason (`mask_missing` crashes comparing datetime categories against a partial datetime string) would come back as an Index whose only change is its dtype.

Not covered: `Sparse` only widens when the value escapes the Sparse family entirely. `replace(1, 5)` still raises, because the widened dtype is Sparse too and `SparseArray.__setitem__` refuses it just the same (GH-21818) — out of scope here. The behaviour is pinned by a test.

Arrow-backed dtypes are out of scope too, pinned by a test alongside the Sparse one: `pyarrow` raises `ArrowInvalid`, a `ValueError` subclass, so the retry never fires for them. Catching it here would not be enough on its own — arrow's `Series.replace` silently no-ops for a value it cannot hold (`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(1, 1.5)` returns the input unchanged), so that path wants fixing before the Index retry can rely on it.

title: BUG: to_datetime parsed a time-only string with a one-digit minute as year 1 (GH#46509)
body:
closes #46509

`pd.Timestamp("11:00")` is parsed relative to today's date, but `pd.Timestamp("11:0")` comes back as `1-01-01 11:00:00`. `_does_string_look_like_time` requires a two-digit minute, so the one-digit spelling is not recognized as a time-only string and falls through to `dateutil_parse` with `_DEFAULT_DATETIME` (year 1) instead of today.

The issue as filed reports this as a confusing `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. That framing is out of date: now that 3.x defaults to `datetime64[us]`, year 1 is representable and nothing raises at all, so `pd.to_datetime(["11:00", "12:00", "11:0"])` silently returns a year-1 value in the middle of the data.

Leading whitespace defeats the same check (`" 11:00"` is also parsed as year 1) — a different cause, left for a separate PR.

title: BUG: DataFrame.isetitem with an out-of-order loc corrupted the block structure

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
`BlockManager._iset_split_block` passed the caller's `blk_locs` order straight to `Block.delete`, whose docstring says "Assumes `loc` is strictly increasing when list-like". So `df.isetitem([2, 0, 1], value)`, where those positions share a block and only part of it is replaced, left stale and overlapping blocks behind.

The values read back correct, which is what makes this easy to miss. The sum of block placement lengths exceeds the column count, so `_verify_integrity` fails: a later `merge`, `join` or `describe` raises `AssertionError`, and `to_pickle` writes a file that `read_pickle` rejects.

`np.unique` normalizes for the `Block.delete` call only — `blk_locs` is reused two lines down at `locs = blk.mgr_locs.as_array[blk_locs]`, where its order pairs with `value`'s columns. `BlockManager.setitem` already did this (GH-65446); `iset` was the unfixed sibling. The comment there credited `Block.delete`'s precondition, which this change makes obsolete, but the sort is still needed for `_iset_split_block`'s `_blklocs` bookkeeping, so that comment is corrected rather than the code.

Not fixed here:

- A duplicated position (`df.isetitem([0, 0], value)`) still builds a block whose placement repeats that column. This change makes that raise `IndexError` instead of corrupting when the block has a single column; the real fix is to reject a duplicated `loc`, which covers the multi-column case too.
- `_iset_split_block`'s whole-block early return skips the `_blklocs` update, so an unsorted `blk_locs` leaves the cache stale. Not reachable from any public API today, and `BlockManager.setitem`'s `np.unique` is what keeps it that way.
- A reversed-contiguous `BlockPlacement` — which a descending `loc` produces, correctly, both before and after this change — makes default-axis `concat` raise `ValueError: unbounded slice`. Pre-existing and independent: `_iset_split_block` is not called at all for the two-column case that shows it.

title: ENH: Expose PEP249 DB API "rowcount" in read_sql_query iterator

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
### Feature Type

- [X] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

When using `pd.read_sql_query` with `chunksize=` set, the result is an iterator of data frames.

Often the underlying database library exposes a total row count for the query, which can be used to estimate task completion time, allocate resources, etc.

However this is not exposed anywhere in the `pd.read_sql`/`pd.read_sql_query`/`pd.read_sql_table` interface. It would be very useful if users could access this, perhaps as an attribute on the iterator object itself.

One hypothetical usage among many:

```python
df_iter = pd.read_sql_query(query, engine, chunksize=k)
for chunk in tqdm(df_iter, total=df_iter.rowcount):
    ...
```

Ideally `.rowcount` would also be exposed as `__len__`, so `len(df_iter) == df_iter.rowcount`.

### Feature Description

This can be facilitated by pulling out the implementation of `pandas.io.sql.SQLDatabase._query_iterator` into a helper class:

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Any

import sqlalchemy as sqla

class QueryIterator:
    def __init__(self, result: attribute sqla.engine.CursorResult) -> None:
        self.result = result

    def __iter__(self) -> 'QueryIterator':
        return self

    @property
    def rowcount(self) -> int:
        return self.result.rowcount

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return self.result.rowcount

    def __next__(self) -> Sequence[sqla.engine.Row[Any]]:
        ...  # implementation here
```

### Alternative Solutions

Pre-computing `SELECT count(*)` is not always an option, and generally is not a great design, partly because of TOCTOU inconsistentcy and partly because it's just not necessary in most cases.

### Additional Context

I'm happy to block out some time to work on this, if the feature is of interest and it's not already WIP somewhere.

title: ENH: Add pyarrow/auto engine options to DataFrame.to_csv

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
Adds an `engine` parameter ("python", "pyarrow", "auto") to to_csv/Series.to_csv. "auto", the new default, uses the pyarrow writer when it's installed and the data/options are fully supported, and transparently falls back to "python" otherwise -- never changing the values written or their round-trip fidelity through read_csv, only formatting for the calls where pyarrow ends up being used.

"auto" avoids pyarrow for: MultiIndex columns; rows that are entirely missing values (would collapse to a blank line that read_csv silently drops); and data pyarrow's CSV writer can't represent (Period, Interval, complex, Sparse, object columns of list/dict values, etc). bool, timedelta64, timezone-aware datetime64, and whole-number-float columns render differently under pyarrow (and the float case can change the dtype read_csv infers on round-trip), so "auto" skips pyarrow for those too, while explicit engine="pyarrow" proceeds anyway with a warning.

Rewrites pandas/tests/io/formats/test_to_csv.py to exercise all three engines, asserting the actual (possibly different) rendering per engine. Also fixes pre-existing tests elsewhere that hard-coded python-engine-only to_csv output, now that "auto" is the default.

title: DEPR: pinning group key to name attribute in groupby UDFs
body:
closes #41090

## Summary
- Deprecate pinning the group key to the ``name`` attribute of the group passed to a user-defined function in groupby ``apply``, ``transform``, and ``filter``, and in the ``Resampler`` equivalents (GH-41090). The warning's migration recipe is given per method: ``pd.concat({key: func(group) for key, group in gb})`` reproduces ``apply``, while ``transform`` and ``filter`` return an object indexed like the original and need their own recombination
- The key is still pinned exactly as before (no behavior change), but flagged via a private ``NDFrame._groupby_pinned_name`` attribute; ``Series.name`` and ``DataFrame.__getattr__`` emit a ``Pandas4Warning`` when user code reads the pinned name. Internal reads (e.g. result-name propagation in ops) are exempted by classifying the single frame that did the read, so UDFs that never touch ``.name`` see no warning
- Compared to a call-without-name-then-retry approach: the UDF runs exactly once per group, Series groups keep returning the group key (rather than silently returning the column name), and exceptions from UDFs surface unchanged
- The key is no longer written into the group's instance ``__dict__``, so two paths need explicit handling to keep the pre-deprecation behavior. ``NDFrame.__setattr__`` short-circuits ``group.name = value`` so that it sets an attribute and unpins, rather than falling through to assigning a *column* named ``"name"``. And ``_pin_deprecated_group_name`` drops a ``name`` that ``__finalize__`` propagated from a subclass's ``_metadata``, which would otherwise shadow ``__getattr__`` and hide the key entirely
- Groupby plotting (``.plot`` accessor, ``hist``) goes through ``_python_apply_plot``, which labels each Series group with its key explicitly, so enforcement can delete the deprecation machinery without touching plotting. That helper has since landed on ``main`` separately; this branch now just rebases onto it
- Removed the docstring notes advertising the ``name`` attribute from ``GroupBy.apply``, ``SeriesGroupBy.apply``, both ``transform`` docstrings, and ``DataFrameGroupBy.filter``

**Known limitation:** the warning fires only on direct ``.name`` access. A UDF that hands the group to pandas code that consumes the name internally (e.g. ``x.to_frame()`` naming the column after the key) does not warn now and will change behavior at enforcement. Exempting only the readers that use ``self._name`` explicitly was tried and rejected: instrumenting the hook across the groupby, resample and apply suites turns up 13 distinct internal readers, so that variant would warn on ``group + 1`` and ``group.value_counts()``.

**Cost:** ``Series.name`` reads go from ~37.5ns to ~62.8ns locally, worth ~4% on ``small + small``. The guard is one attribute load in a property whose body is otherwise a single load, so the cost is inherent to intercepting reads; spelling it as an instance-``__dict__`` membership test measured no better.

The exemption check itself is a single-frame lookup rather than ``find_stack_level``: the question is only whether the frame that read ``.name`` is pandas' own code, and ``find_stack_level`` answers it by walking the whole pandas prefix — 10+ frames inside a groupby transform — on a path taken about five times per group.

## Test plan
- [x] Full groupby, resample, and plotting suites pass (warnings escalate to errors in the test suite, so this also verifies no spurious warnings)
- [x] Plotting suite additionally passes with pinning disabled entirely (enforcement simulation)
- [x] New tests: Series group ``.name`` returns the group key with a warning; UDFs not touching ``.name`` don't warn; name set inside a UDF unpins; ``SeriesGroupBy.plot(legend=True)`` legend labels are group keys; ``DataFrameGroupBy.filter`` and the three ``Resampler`` entry points warn; setting ``group.name`` does not clobber a ``"name"`` column; a subclass with ``name`` in ``_metadata`` still sees the key
- [x] mypy, pyright, pre-commit clean

df.filter(df["age"] > 18)  # same as `df[df["age"] > 18`

title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray ops leak pyarrow errors for unconvertible operands (GH#62682)
body:
closes #62682

`ArrowExtensionArray` binary ops let pyarrow's own `ArrowInvalid`/`ArrowTypeError` escape when the
other operand holds objects pyarrow cannot convert — `Categorical`, `Interval`, `DateOffset`, a bare
`object()`. Arithmetic and logical ops now raise pandas' own `TypeError`; comparisons compare
elementwise for `==`/`!=` and raise `TypeError` for ordered comparisons, matching the NumPy-nullable
dtypes.

Note that the issue's *literal* repro already gives a clean `TypeError` on `main` — `pd.array(["a", np.nan])`
is the arrow-backed `str` dtype, which GH-65677 routed through an object-dtype fallback. The bug is
live for every other arrow dtype:

```python
pd.array([1, 2], dtype="int64[pyarrow]") + pd.DataFrame([[pd.Categorical(["test"])] * 2])
# main:    pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: ... did not recognize Python value type
# this PR: TypeError: operation 'add' not supported for dtype 'int64[pyarrow]' with dtype 'object'
```

This also fixes `duration[ns][pyarrow] == Hour(1)`, which raised `ArrowTypeError` while the reflected
`Hour(1) == arr` worked. `!=` against an offset scalar needs the reflected-`__ne__` detour:
`BaseOffset.__ne__` is `not self == other`, which raises on an array result, so `ne` is evaluated as
a negated `eq`.

The 2-D-ndarray guard and the comparison length-mismatch `ValueError` from the same issue are a
separate PR. The two touch adjacent lines in `_evaluate_op_method`, so whichever lands second needs
a rebase.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and ran a multi-round blind review of the branch.

title: BUG: fix stream buffer overflow in read_csv c engine on short rows
body:
1. read_csv with the ``c`` engine reserves the token stream once per read buffer for a 1:1 copy of the input, and the SIMD/scalar bulk-copy fast paths in ``tokenize_bytes`` then write field bytes with no per-copy capacity check.
2. a row with fewer fields than expected is padded in ``end_line`` with one synthetic NUL terminator per missing field; those writes take stream space but consume no input, and only ``make_stream_space(ex_fields - fields)`` was reserved for them, not the input still waiting to be copied.
3. a read buffer with many short rows before a wide field then leaves the stream smaller than that field, so the bulk copy runs past ``self->stream`` (heap-buffer-overflow under ASAN; without a sanitizer the field is truncated or corrupted, and larger inputs crash).

Reserve room for the terminators plus the rest of the chunk so the reservation the bulk copies rely on survives the padding.

title: BUG: find_stack_level treating third-party pandas* packages as pandas-internal
body:
Closes #67992.

### What changed

`find_stack_level` in `pandas/util/_exceptions.py` compared frame filenames with a bare prefix match against `os.path.dirname(pd.__file__)` (no trailing separator). Any sibling install directory merely starting with `pandas` (`pandas_ta`, `pandas_gbq`, `pandas_datareader`, ...) matched, so warnings raised on behalf of user code in those packages got a `stacklevel` pointing past the real caller (and anywhere the return value is used as a decision, e.g. warning suppression by depth, user code could get no warning at all).

The fix caches `_pkg_dir`/`_test_dir` with a trailing `os.sep`, making the comparison directory-scoped, as suggested in the issue. In production code, `_pkg_dir`/`_test_dir` are only read inside `find_stack_level`, so nothing else can observe the trailing separator; the new test derives the sibling paths it simulates from `_pkg_dir`.

### Verification

- Ran the issue's repro script against unpatched code: the `pandas_ta` path mis-reports at the outer script while `/somewhere/else/strategy.py` reports correctly. Bug confirmed.
- After the fix, a differential battery over 15 caller paths (internal files, `tests/` dir, `pandas_ta`/`pandas2`/`pandasbackup`/`pandas-tests`/`pandasx` siblings, nested sibling paths, unrelated and lookalike paths like `apandas`): every non-degenerate case classifies correctly; the only deltas vs old behavior are the intended sibling family. The repo contains no `tests*`-prefixed sibling directory other than `tests` itself, so no in-tree path changes classification.
- End-to-end: a warning raised from a (simulated) pandas-internal frame still resolves to the user file, and depth counting is unchanged (user frames add nothing, each pandas frame adds one).
- Added `pandas/tests/util/test_find_stack_level.py`. An earlier revision wrote a fake module next to `pd.__file__` and removed the tree afterwards; on a non-editable install that path is `site-packages/pandas_ta`, so it could delete a real installed package. The reworked test compiles the caller source with the sibling path as its filename and execs it, so nothing is created or removed while the frame still reports the same `co_filename`. All three cases fail without the fix and pass with it.
- Existing suites on the patched code, no new failures: `pandas/tests/util` (973 passed, 1 known env failure locally), `tests/generic` + `test_register_accessor` + `frame/methods/test_fillna` (1017 passed), `series/indexing/test_setitem` + `tools/test_to_datetime` (2420 passed), `groupby/test_apply` + `groupby/test_groupby` (2370 passed). The single failure in `tests/util` (`test_datapath`) also fails on pristine code, because the wheel does not ship `io/data/csv/iris.csv`, so it is environmental and unrelated.

Added a whatsnew entry in v3.1.0 (Other).

title: BUG: find_stack_level treats third-party `pandas*` packages as pandas-internal
body:
### Problem

`find_stack_level` (`pandas/util/_exceptions.py`) walks the stack while

```python
filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir)
```

`pkg_dir` is `os.path.dirname(pandas.__file__)`, e.g. `.../site-packages/pandas`, with no trailing `os.sep`. So `.../site-packages/pandas_ta/strategy.py` matches too, and the walk keeps climbing past it. Every sibling distribution whose install directory merely *starts with* `pandas` — `pandas_ta`, `pandas_gbq`, `pandas_datareader`, `pandasql`, ... — is invisible to the walk, so warnings raised on behalf of user code in those packages get a `stacklevel` that points past the real caller.

### Reproducible example

No third-party package needed; only the filename matters.

```python
import warnings

import pandas.util._exceptions as pue

pue.find_stack_level()  # populate the cache
pkg_dir = pue._pkg_dir

src = (
    "import warnings\n"
    "from pandas.util._exceptions import find_stack_level\n"
    "def caller():\n"
    "    warnings.warn('boom', UserWarning, stacklevel=find_stack_level())\n"
)

for path in (pkg_dir + "_ta/strategy.py", "/somewhere/else/strategy.py"):
    ns = {}
    exec(compile(src, path, "exec"), ns)
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as rec:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        ns["caller"]()
    print(f"{path}\n  -> reported at {rec[0].filename}:{rec[0].lineno}")
```

```
/.../site-packages/pandas_ta/strategy.py
  -> reported at repro.py:22            # wrong: skipped past the warning site
/somewhere/else/strategy.py
  -> reported at /somewhere/else/strategy.py:4   # correct
```

The consequence is sharper anywhere the *return value* is used as a decision rather than just a pointer (e.g. suppressing a warning when `find_stack_level()` exceeds some depth): user code living in such a package can end up getting no warning at all.

### Suggested fix

Cache `_pkg_dir` as `os.path.dirname(pd.__file__) + os.sep` (and `_test_dir` likewise) so the comparison is directory-scoped. One line, no new imports.

Expect some churn: tightening the walk shifts stacklevels across the codebase, and `pandas/_testing/_warnings.py::_assert_raised_with_correct_stacklevel` asserts the reported filename, so a full test run is needed to see what moves.

title: DEPR: rename Groupby classes to GroupBy (GH#49578)
body:
closes #49578

`pandas.api.typing` spelled "group by" two ways: `DataFrameGroupBy`/`SeriesGroupBy` with a capital B, and six others without — `RollingGroupby`, `ExpandingGroupby`, `ExponentialMovingWindowGroupby`, `DatetimeIndexResamplerGroupby`, `PeriodIndexResamplerGroupby`, `TimedeltaIndexResamplerGroupby`. Those six are renamed to the `GroupBy` spelling, and the old names still resolve through a module-level `__getattr__` with a `Pandas4Warning`.

Since this module exists for type-hinting, the old spellings are also bound under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` so annotating with one keeps type-checking for the deprecation period. Without that the deprecation has no period at all for its primary use case: `x: pd.api.typing.RollingGroupby` becomes an immediate mypy error, and under `from __future__ import annotations` no runtime warning fires either. `TYPE_CHECKING` itself is deleted at runtime so it does not enter the public namespace.

The private `BaseWindowGroupby` and `GroupbyIndexer` are renamed outright with no shim; neither is re-exported from a public module.

Only `pandas.api.typing` is shimmed. The old names are gone from `pandas.core.window` and `pandas.core.resample`, so `from pandas.core.window.rolling import RollingGroupby` now raises `ImportError` — pandarallel and mapply both do this, and pandarallel subclasses it. That is deliberate, since `pandas.core` is private and the downstream fix is a one-line rename, but flagging it in case reviewers would rather shim those modules too.

One follow-up outside this repo: pandas-stubs re-exports all six old spellings from `pandas.core.window`/`pandas.core.resample`, and stub packages shadow pandas' inline types. Until a companion pandas-stubs PR lands, pandas-stubs users won't see the new names at all, and won't see the deprecation either.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which implemented the rename and shim, wrote the tests, and ran a multi-round blind review loop over the diff.

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment

body:
- [x] closes #66080
- [x] All code checks passed.
- [x] Added tests to cover the bug.

**Bug Description:**
In `DataFrame.to_html(render_links=True, escape=True)`, the visible text was properly escaped, but the generated `href` attribute intentionally bypassed the escaping dictionary. If a DataFrame contained a URL with double quotes (e.g., `q="hello"`), it would prematurely close the anchor tag, breaking the table layout and exposing the render to arbitrary HTML injection.

**The Fix:**
In `pandas/io/formats/html.py`, the unescaped raw URL string (`rs_unescaped`) is now securely routed through the standard python `html.escape()` library before being formatted into the `href` attribute. A regression test has been added to prove both the visible text and the link destination are consistently and safely done!

title: BUG/DEPR: low_memory keyword in read_csv

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
`low_memory=True` (the default) can give incorrect results in corner cases, which is the reason why the keyword exists.  Minimal example:

```
N = 65536  # rows in the first internal chunk of an 8-column table
data = (
    "a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\n"
    + "1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n" * N          # chunk 1 -> int64
    + f"{2**64 - 1},1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n"   # chunk 2 -> uint64
    + f"{2**64 - 2},1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n"
)

res = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data))["a"]
exp = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), low_memory=False)["a"]

assert exp.iloc[-1] != exp.iloc[-2]
assert res.iloc[-1] != res.iloc[-2]  #  <- fails because of unwanted casting
```

In the `low_memory=True` case, we do dtype inference in chunks.  In cases where different chunks get different dtypes, the concat does a cast which can be lossy.  `low_memory=False` avoids that by doing the dtype inference on the whole column instead of in chunks.

The alternative I think we should consider is to detect when this casting occurs and then re-parse (with `usecols` restricted to the affected column) in the `low_memory=False` mode.  Then we get the correct result and don't need the user-facing keyword.  The downside is a perf penalty in these corner cases.

Passing `low_memory=False` disables the parallel path, which is what brought this to my attention.

title: BUG: comma read as a decimal separator silently corrupts parsed dates (GH#17265)

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
closes #17265

dateutil's tokenizer folds `<2+ digits>,<digits>` into a single decimal number, and `int()` discards the fraction when that number lands in a year/month/day slot. So `Timestamp("2013,11,04")` returned `2013-04-01` and `Timestamp("Nov 14,2013")` returned year 1 — silently, and through `to_datetime`, `DatetimeIndex`, `Period`, `astype` and `read_csv(parse_dates=)` alike.

`dateutil_parse` now rejects exactly those strings. Everything dateutil handles correctly is preserved: a comma it leaves as punctuation (`"Nov 4,2013"`, `"Nov 14, 2013"`, `"Thu, 14 Nov 2013"`), the ISO 8601 decimal comma for fractional seconds (`"01:02:03,456"`, GH-59256), the same comma on minutes and hours (`"01:02,5"`), and unit-label forms (`"12,5h"`). An explicit `format=`/`date_format=` is unaffected either way.

Three adjacent defects turned up on the way and are deliberately left out, since each needs a different rule rather than a wider version of this one: the `.` spelling of the same bug (`Timestamp("Nov 14.2013")` is year 1 — but `.` is a *supported* date separator, so the guard cannot simply be widened), `_find_subsecond_reso`'s dot-only regex (`Period("2013-11-04 01:02:03,456")` truncates to whole seconds, a gap left by GH-59256), and comma handling in `Timedelta` string parsing (`Timedelta("0 days 00:00:01,500")` is 25 minutes).

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and validated the guard by differential sweep against dateutil's own lexer.
